scoring.rule: Five statements, each true or false, 1 point each. The student checks the statements they believe are true. A statement scores 1 point if it is checked and true, or unchecked and false; otherwise 0.

questions.section: 1. Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.stem: A fraud team reports that its transaction classifier "catches 90% of fraud" and "wrongly flags only 4% of legitimate transactions". In the traffic being scored, 0.5% of transactions are fraudulent. Consider 100,000 transactions and assume the two rates hold exactly (90% of the fraudulent ones flagged, 4% of the legitimate ones flagged). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If 5% of transactions were fraudulent instead, with the same two rates, more than half of the flagged transactions would be fraudulent.
statements.explanation: 4,500 true flags and 3,800 false flags give about 54% fraudulent; a higher base rate raises the share of correct flags.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the false-flag rate were halved to 2%, more than 30% of flagged transactions would be fraudulent.
statements.explanation: With a 2% false-flag rate there would be 450 true and 1,990 false flags, about 18% fraudulent, well under 30%.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Roughly one in ten flagged transactions would be fraudulent.

statements.label: D
statements.text: About 450 fraudulent and about 3,980 legitimate transactions would be flagged.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A flagged transaction has a 90% chance of being fraudulent.
statements.explanation: 90% is P(flagged | fraud); the chance that a flag is correct, P(fraud | flagged), also depends on how common fraud is.

questions.section: 1. Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.stem: A help desk logged 1,000 tickets. Of the 300 billing tickets, 30 were escalated. Of the 700 technical tickets, 140 were escalated. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: P(escalated) is 0.15, the simple average of 0.10 and 0.20.
statements.explanation: The overall rate weights each group's rate by its share of tickets: 0.3 × 0.10 + 0.7 × 0.20 = 0.17.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Ticket type and escalation are independent in this data.
statements.explanation: Independence would need P(escalated | type) to equal P(escalated) = 0.17 for both types, but the rates are 0.10 and 0.20.

statements.label: C
statements.text: P(billing and escalated) = 0.10.
statements.explanation: The joint probability is 30 / 1,000 = 0.03; 0.10 is the conditional P(escalated | billing).

statements.label: D
statements.text: P(billing | escalated) equals P(escalated | billing), which is 0.10.
statements.explanation: Of the 170 escalated tickets 30 are billing, so P(billing | escalated) is about 0.18; swapping the conditioning event changes the number.

statements.label: E
statements.text: P(escalated | technical) = 0.20.

questions.section: 1. Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.stem: Two automated checkers each miss a given defect with probability 0.10. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The probability that both checkers miss is 0.01 even if both were built with the same method and tend to miss the same defects.
statements.explanation: Shared blind spots make the misses positively dependent, so P(both miss) is larger than 0.01.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the two checkers miss independently, the probability that both miss a given defect is 0.01.
statements.explanation: Independence means the joint probability is the product, 0.10 × 0.10.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the checkers miss independently, the probability that exactly one of them misses is 0.18.
statements.explanation: Exactly one misses: 2 × 0.10 × 0.90 = 0.18.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If P(second misses | first misses) = 1, the two misses are independent events.
statements.explanation: Independence needs P(second misses | first misses) to equal P(second misses) = 0.10; a conditional probability of 1 is extreme dependence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the second checker only misses defects that the first checker also misses, the probability that both miss is 0.10.
statements.explanation: The second checker's misses are then a subset of the first's, and both have probability 0.10, so they are the same set of defects.

questions.section: 1. Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.stem: Assume 365 equally likely birthdays and people whose birthdays are independent. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If birthdays cluster on certain dates instead of being uniform, a shared birthday becomes less likely than in the uniform case.
statements.explanation: Unequal birthday frequencies raise the chance of a match; the uniform case is the least likely to produce one.

statements.label: B
statements.text: P(at least two share a birthday) equals 1 minus P(all birthdays are different).
statements.explanation: This is the complement rule, and it is how the probability is computed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With 23 people the probability that at least two share a birthday is above 50%.
statements.explanation: The probability is about 50.7% at 23 people, which give 253 pairs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With 30 people the probability that at least two share a birthday is about 30/365, roughly 8%.
statements.explanation: With 30 people the probability is about 71%; the number of pairs (435), not the number of people, drives it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In a group of 23, the probability that one particular person shares a birthday with at least one of the other 22 is also above 50%.
statements.explanation: For one named person the chance is 1 − (364/365)^22, about 6%; the 50% figure is about any two people in the group.

questions.section: 1. Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.stem: A mail filter's statistics: 30% of all messages are spam. The word "urgent" appears in 60% of spam messages and in 10% of legitimate messages. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If spam were only 5% of messages, the same word would give P(spam | "urgent") of about 0.24.

statements.label: B
statements.text: P(spam | "urgent") is about 0.72.

statements.label: C
statements.text: P(spam | "urgent") is 0.60, because the word appears in 60% of spam.
statements.explanation: 0.60 is P("urgent" | spam), the reverse conditional; the base rate and the word's frequency in legitimate mail change the answer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Prior odds of 3 to 7 multiplied by the likelihood ratio give posterior odds of about 2.6 to 1.
statements.explanation: (3/7) × 6 is about 2.57, which corresponds to a probability of 0.72.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The likelihood ratio for "urgent" (spam versus legitimate) is 6.

questions.section: 2. Random variables and distributions
questions.stem: An agent retries a failing tool call before giving up. Let X be the number of retries in one run, with P(X=0) = 0.50, P(X=1) = 0.30, P(X=2) = 0.15 and P(X=3) = 0.05. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Over 1,000 independent runs the total number of retries will be exactly 750.
statements.explanation: The expected total is 750, but the actual total varies from run to run (a standard deviation of about 28).

statements.label: B
statements.text: The standard deviation of X is about 0.89.
statements.explanation: E[X²] = 1.35, so Var(X) = 1.35 − 0.5625 = 0.7875 and the standard deviation is about 0.89.

statements.label: C
statements.explanation: Adding a constant does not change the variance and multiplying by 2 multiplies it by 4, so Var(2X + 1) = 4 Var(X) = 3.15.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The most likely value of X is also its expected value.
statements.explanation: The most likely value is 0 (probability 0.5); the mean of 0.75 is not even a possible value.

questions.section: 2. Random variables and distributions
questions.stem: X is a continuous random variable that is uniformly distributed on the interval from 0 to 0.5 (for example, a measured delay in seconds). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The cumulative distribution function reaches 1 at x = 0.5 and stays at 1 beyond it.
statements.explanation: P(X ≤ x) cannot rise above 1, and all the probability lies at or below 0.5.

statements.label: B
statements.explanation: By symmetry the mean is the midpoint of the interval, 0.25.

statements.label: C
statements.explanation: For a continuous variable the probability of any single exact value is 0; the density value 2 is not a probability.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The density equals 2 everywhere on the interval, and a density value above 1 is allowed.
statements.explanation: The density must integrate to 1 over a width of 0.5, so it is 2; a density is not a probability and can exceed 1.

statements.label: E
statements.explanation: Probability is the area under the density: 2 × 0.1 = 0.2.

questions.section: 2. Random variables and distributions
questions.stem: A model answers each of 20 test prompts correctly with probability 0.8, independently, so the number of correct answers is Binomial(20, 0.8). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The probability that all 20 answers are correct is about 1.2%.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The probability of at least 18 correct answers is about 0.5, because 18 is close to the mean of 16.
statements.explanation: P(X ≥ 18) is about 0.21; 18 is more than one standard deviation (1.79) above the mean.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If many of the 20 prompts are near-duplicates, the number correct would vary more than the binomial variance of 3.2 suggests.
statements.explanation: Positively correlated outcomes violate independence and make the count more variable than the binomial formula says.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The expected number correct is 16 and the variance is 3.2.
statements.explanation: The mean is np = 16 and the variance is np(1−p) = 20 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 3.2.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The probability of exactly 16 correct answers is 0.80.
statements.explanation: 16 is the mean, but the probability of exactly 16 is C(20,16) × 0.8^16 × 0.2^4, about 0.22.

questions.section: 2. Random variables and distributions
questions.stem: Request latency for a service is modeled as a normal distribution with mean 200 ms and standard deviation 40 ms. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: About one third of requests would be faster than 160 ms.
statements.explanation: 160 ms is one standard deviation below the mean (z = −1), which has about 16% below it, roughly one in six.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If real latencies are fat-tailed but have the same mean and standard deviation, the fraction of requests over 280 ms must still equal the fraction this normal model predicts.
statements.explanation: Tail mass depends on the whole shape of the distribution, not just the mean and standard deviation, so the fraction beyond 280 ms can differ from the normal model's figure (in either direction).

statements.label: C
statements.text: A 360 ms request is a 4-standard-deviation event that the model expects about once per 1,000 requests.
statements.explanation: z = 4 has an upper tail of about 3 in 100,000, roughly one request in 31,600.

statements.label: D
statements.text: About 2.3% of requests would take longer than 280 ms.
statements.explanation: 280 ms is z = 2 and the upper tail beyond it is about 2.3%.

statements.label: E
statements.text: About 95% of requests would fall between 120 ms and 280 ms.
statements.explanation: 120 ms and 280 ms are 2 standard deviations on either side, which contain about 95.4%.

questions.section: 2. Random variables and distributions
questions.stem: A team sets an alert threshold at the mean plus a multiple of the standard deviation and wants to know how often values would exceed it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A two-sided "six-sigma" failure probability of about 2 in a billion, computed from the normal curve, remains valid when the real distribution is fat-tailed with the same mean and standard deviation.
statements.explanation: The normal tail figure depends on the normal shape; heavier tails put far more probability at extreme distances.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For any distribution with finite variance, at most 1/9 (about 11%) of its probability lies more than 3 standard deviations from the mean.
statements.explanation: This is Chebyshev's inequality, P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k², which needs only a finite variance.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A Student t distribution with 3 degrees of freedom, rescaled to a standard deviation of 1, has about 1.4% of its probability beyond 3 standard deviations, around five times the normal figure.
statements.explanation: The two-sided tail beyond 3 SD is about 1.38% for this t distribution against 0.27% for the normal.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For a standard Cauchy distribution, the average of 1,000 independent observations is no more concentrated than a single observation.
statements.explanation: The mean of n independent standard Cauchy variables is itself standard Cauchy, so averaging does not help (there is no finite mean).

statements.label: E
statements.text: For a normal distribution about 0.27% lies beyond 3 standard deviations, so the distribution-free bound of 1/9 is loose in that case.
statements.explanation: The normal tail beyond 3 SD is about 0.27%, much smaller than the worst-case 11% that Chebyshev allows.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.stem: An engineer runs 400 independent evaluation prompts and 320 pass (an observed pass rate of 0.80). Treat the prompts as an independent random sample and use the normal approximation, with 1.96 for a 95% interval. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The standard error of the observed pass rate is 0.02.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With 400 prompts, the standard error would be smaller if the observed rate were 0.50 instead of 0.80.
statements.explanation: √(p(1−p)/n) is largest at p = 0.5, giving 0.025 here, which is larger than 0.02.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A 95% confidence interval for the true pass rate is about 0.76 to 0.84.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Cutting the margin of error to ±1 percentage point would need about 1,600 prompts.
statements.explanation: The present margin is about ±3.9 points; a margin of ±1 point needs about 1.96² × 0.16 / 0.01² ≈ 6,150 prompts.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Running 800 prompts at the same observed rate would cut the margin of error in half.
statements.explanation: The standard error scales with 1/√n, so doubling n shrinks it by a factor of about 1.41; halving it takes four times as many prompts.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Statistical inference, estimation and hypothesis testing
questions.stem: An A/B test compares a new answer-ranking feature with the old one, with 20,000 users per arm. Conversion is 10.0% in the control arm and 10.6% in the treatment arm. A two-sided test of equal conversion rates gives p = 0.048. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: There is a 4.8% probability that the feature has no effect.
statements.explanation: A p-value is computed assuming no effect; it is not the probability that the no-effect hypothesis is true.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the feature had no effect, a difference at least this large would arise in about 4.8% of repeated experiments.
statements.explanation: This is the definition of a p-value: the probability, assuming no effect, of data at least as extreme as observed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With the same observed rates but only 2,000 users per arm, the p-value would still be below 0.05.
statements.explanation: With ten times fewer users the standard error is about three times larger and the same gap gives a p-value near 0.5.

statements.label: D
statements.text: There is a 95.2% probability that the feature truly raises conversion.
statements.explanation: The p-value does not give the probability that the alternative is true; that would need a prior and a different calculation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The small p-value shows that the effect is large.
statements.explanation: The observed gap is 0.6 percentage points; with large samples even small effects can give small p-values.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Statistical inference, estimation and hypothesis testing
questions.stem: A research group screens 200 independent hypotheses. Exactly 20 of them are true effects and 180 are true nulls. Each test uses significance level 0.05, and the tests of the true effects have power 0.80. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because the significance level is 0.05, about 95% of the significant results are real effects.
statements.explanation: The significance level is the Type I error rate (false positives among true nulls), not the share of significant results that are real; that share depends on the base rate of true effects.

statements.label: B
statements.text: About 64% of the significant results are real effects.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Raising the power of every test to 100% (a Type II error rate of 0) would make every significant result a real effect.
statements.explanation: With full power the 20 true effects are detected, but the 180 nulls still yield about 9 false positives, so about 69% are real.

statements.label: D
statements.text: About 25 significant results are expected, of which about 16 are real effects and 9 are false positives.
statements.explanation: Power 0.8 × 20 = 16 detections and 0.05 × 180 = 9 false positives.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If only 4 of the 200 hypotheses were true effects (same significance level and power), roughly a quarter of the significant results would be real.
statements.explanation: Then 3.2 true detections and 9.8 false positives, so 3.2 / 13 is about 25% real.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Statistical inference, estimation and hypothesis testing
questions.stem: A team tests 20 independent prompt variants against a baseline, each with a two-sided test at significance level 0.05. Suppose that, unknown to the team, none of the variants truly differs from the baseline. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The expected number of variants reaching p < 0.05 is 1.
statements.explanation: 20 × 0.05 = 1 expected false positive.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Requiring p < 0.0025 (that is, 0.05 / 20) for each test keeps the chance of at least one false positive at or just under 5%.
statements.explanation: 1 − (1 − 0.0025)^20 is about 4.9%, the Bonferroni guarantee.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The probability that at least one of the 20 variants reaches p < 0.05 is about 5%.
statements.explanation: The chance of at least one false positive is 1 − 0.95^20, about 64%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure controls the probability of making any false discovery, in the same way as the Bonferroni correction.
statements.explanation: Benjamini–Hochberg controls the false discovery rate (the expected share of false findings among discoveries), a weaker guarantee than controlling any false positive.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If only the best variant is reported, and its raw p-value is below 0.05, the p-value is a valid measure of evidence even when the other 19 tests are not mentioned.
statements.explanation: Choosing the best of 20 results after the fact means a raw p-value understates how easily chance produces such a result.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Statistical inference, estimation and hypothesis testing
questions.stem: A study reports that a reranking change improved accuracy by 2.0 percentage points, with a standard (frequentist) 95% confidence interval of 0.5 to 3.5 points. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A 90% interval computed from the same data would be narrower than this one.
statements.explanation: A lower confidence level uses a smaller multiplier, so the interval is narrower.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the same procedure were repeated on many independent samples, about 95% of the intervals it produced would contain the true improvement.
statements.explanation: That long-run coverage is the meaning of a 95% confidence interval.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A two-sided test of "no improvement" at the 5% level would reject, because the interval excludes 0.
statements.explanation: A 95% interval that excludes zero corresponds to rejecting zero at the 5% level (two-sided).

statements.label: D
statements.text: About 95% of individual queries improved by an amount between 0.5 and 3.5 points.
statements.explanation: The interval concerns the average improvement, not the spread of individual changes, which is much wider.

statements.label: E
statements.text: There is a 95% probability that the true improvement lies between 0.5 and 3.5 points.
statements.explanation: Once computed, a given interval either contains the true value or does not; the 95% describes the procedure, not this particular interval.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.stem: Consider the sample mean of n independent, identically distributed observations from a right-skewed population with finite variance (for example, task completion times). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For an exponential population (skewness 2), the sample mean has skewness 2/√n, about 0.89 at n = 5 and 0.2 at n = 100.
statements.explanation: The skewness of a mean of n independent exponentials is 2/√n, which falls toward 0 as n grows.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The sample mean has standard deviation σ/√n, and its distribution approaches a normal distribution as n grows.
statements.explanation: This is the central limit theorem for independent, identically distributed data with finite variance.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sample of about 30 is a common rule of thumb for the normal approximation, but heavily skewed or outlier-prone populations can need far more.
statements.explanation: The n ≈ 30 figure is a guideline, not a theorem, and skew or extreme values slow convergence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: As n grows, a histogram of the individual observations becomes bell-shaped.
statements.explanation: The data keep the population's shape; it is the distribution of the sample mean that becomes bell-shaped.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the observations are strongly positively correlated, for example many near-copies of the same item, the standard error σ/√n understates the real uncertainty.
statements.explanation: Correlated observations carry less information than n independent ones, so the effective sample size is smaller than n.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Statistical inference, estimation and hypothesis testing
questions.stem: A tutoring app shows a satisfaction survey to its 1.25 million users. A total of 50,000 users (4%) respond, and 92% of respondents say they are satisfied. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If non-respondents averaged 80% satisfaction, satisfaction among all users would be about 80.5%.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A 4% response rate is harmless when the number of respondents is as large as 50,000.
statements.explanation: A large number of volunteers shrinks the standard error but does not remove selection bias, which depends on the response mechanism.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The standard error reflects random variation among respondents but not the effect of who chose to respond.
statements.explanation: Standard errors measure chance variation; they cannot detect a systematic difference between responders and non-responders.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A random sample of 500 users, nearly all of whom respond after follow-up, could give a less biased estimate than the 50,000 volunteers, even though its standard error is larger.
statements.explanation: Bias can dominate error; a smaller probability sample with high response avoids the self-selection that the volunteer sample cannot fix.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The margin of error of about ±0.24 points shows that satisfaction among all 1.25 million users lies between 91.8% and 92.2%.
statements.explanation: The margin describes sampling variation only and holds under random sampling; self-selection can shift the result by far more than 0.24 points.

questions.section: 4. Exploratory data analysis, data quality and missing data
questions.stem: A survey records age for every respondent and asks for income, which some respondents leave blank. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Whether the blank incomes are missing not at random can be confirmed from the observed values alone.
statements.explanation: Missing-not-at-random depends on the very values that are unobserved, so the observed data cannot confirm it; it takes outside knowledge or assumptions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Mean imputation gives an unbiased estimate of average income when higher earners skip the question because of their income.
statements.explanation: The observed incomes are then too low on average, and filling blanks with their mean keeps that bias.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If higher earners tend to skip the question because of how much they earn, income is missing not at random.
statements.explanation: Missingness that depends on the value being reported is missing not at random.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If older respondents skip the question more often, and within each age group skipping is unrelated to income, income is missing at random given age.
statements.explanation: Missingness that depends only on an observed variable (age) is missing at random, and adjusting for age can correct it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the blanks come from a random server glitch unrelated to anything measured, income is missing completely at random.
statements.explanation: Missingness unrelated to any variable is missing completely at random.

questions.section: 4. Exploratory data analysis, data quality and missing data
questions.stem: A column has 10 rows. Five values are observed (10, 20, 30, 40, 50) and five are missing. An analyst fills each blank with the observed mean (30) and treats all 10 rows as real data. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Filling the blanks with the median instead would preserve the original sample variance.
statements.explanation: Any single constant added at the center lowers the variance; filling with the median (here also 30) gives the same result as the mean.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The standard error of the mean computed from the 10 filled rows (about 3.3) is a fair measure of the uncertainty.
statements.explanation: The five invented values add no information; the honest standard error rests on five observations (about 7.1), so 3.3 overstates precision.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The mean of the column stays at 30.
statements.explanation: Adding values equal to the mean leaves the mean unchanged.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Mean imputation is a safe default whenever many values are missing, whatever the reason for the missingness.
statements.explanation: Mean imputation shrinks spread and distorts correlations, and it biases results when missingness depends on the missing value.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The sample variance falls from 250 to about 111.
statements.explanation: The sum of squared deviations stays 1,000 but is now divided by 9 instead of 4: 111.1 against 250.

questions.section: 4. Exploratory data analysis, data quality and missing data
questions.stem: Eleven response times in seconds are 12, 13, 14, 14, 15, 15, 16, 18, 18, 19 and 120. The median is 15, the first and third quartiles are 14 and 18, the mean is about 24.9 and the sample standard deviation is about 31.6. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Whether to keep the 120 depends on how it arose, since it might be a genuine rare event such as a timeout.
statements.explanation: The decision depends on the data-generating process, such as a recording error versus a real slow request.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The mean of 24.9 seconds is a typical response time for this data.
statements.explanation: Ten of the eleven values lie between 12 and 19; the single large value pulls the mean up to 24.9.

statements.label: C
statements.text: By the 1.5 × IQR rule the upper fence is 24, so 120 is flagged.
statements.explanation: IQR = 18 − 14 = 4 and 18 + 1.5 × 4 = 24; 120 is far above it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A value flagged as an outlier by the 1.5 × IQR rule should be deleted automatically.
statements.explanation: The rule flags values for inspection; deleting a real extreme observation can bias the analysis.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Without the 120, the mean would be about 15.4 and the sample standard deviation about 2.3, while the median would stay at 15.
statements.explanation: The median is resistant to one extreme value; the mean and the standard deviation are not.

questions.section: 4. Exploratory data analysis, data quality and missing data
questions.source: Statistical checks: test the data before you trust it
questions.stem: A pipeline joins an orders table to a customer table. The orders table has 50,000 rows; the joined table has 47,500. All 2,500 dropped rows belong to one region that had 10,000 orders. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The region's share of the data fell from 20% to about 15.8%.
statements.explanation: The region goes from 10,000 / 50,000 = 20% to 7,500 / 47,500, about 15.8%.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Range and type checks on the 47,500 remaining rows can all pass even though rows are missing.
statements.explanation: Checks on present rows only test those rows; rows that never arrived leave nothing to flag.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Comparing row counts per region before and after the join would reveal the loss.
statements.explanation: A by-group reconciliation of counts across the join exposes the concentrated loss that the overall total hides.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because only 5% of rows are missing, any statistic computed on the joined table is within 5% of its true value.
statements.explanation: The lost rows can differ systematically from the rest; if they were all the positive cases, a positive rate of 5% could drop to 0%.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The join lost 5% of rows overall but 25% of the affected region's rows.
statements.explanation: 2,500 / 50,000 = 5% overall and 2,500 / 10,000 = 25% for the region.

questions.section: 4. Exploratory data analysis, data quality and missing data
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about summarizing data with statistics and plots.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If X takes the values −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 and Y = X², the Pearson correlation between X and Y is 0 even though Y is fully determined by X.
statements.explanation: The relationship is symmetric and nonlinear, so the linear correlation is exactly 0.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Pearson correlation is resistant to extreme points: a single outlier cannot change it by much.
statements.explanation: One far-away point can move Pearson's r from near 0 to near 1, or the reverse.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A tall spike of values at exactly 0 in a measurement that should be continuous is often a sign of a default or missing-value code.
statements.explanation: A spike at an exact value usually reflects how the data were recorded, not a natural measurement.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Datasets with identical means, variances and correlation can have very different scatter plots, which is why plots are examined in addition to summary numbers.
statements.explanation: Different shapes can share the same summary statistics, so numbers alone can hide structure that a plot shows.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A Pearson correlation of 0.9 in observational data shows that X causes Y.
statements.explanation: Correlation measures association; confounding, reverse causation or selection can produce it without causation.

questions.section: 5. Modeling basics: fit, overfitting and evaluation
questions.stem:
A classifier for a rare event is evaluated on 100,000 cases, 1,000 of which are truly positive. The counts at three decision thresholds are below. Treat a missed positive as costing 20 units and a false alarm as costing 1 unit.

| Threshold | True positives | False positives |
|---|---|---|
| 0.3 | 900 | 3,000 |
| 0.5 | 800 | 800 |
| 0.7 | 500 | 100 |

Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The F1 score is highest at threshold 0.5.
statements.explanation: F1 is about 0.367, 0.615 and 0.625 for thresholds 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7, so it is highest at 0.7.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Total cost is lowest at threshold 0.5.

statements.label: C
statements.text: At threshold 0.7, 83% of the actual positives are caught.
statements.explanation: 83% is the precision at 0.7 (500 of 600 flagged); recall is 500 / 1,000 = 50%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: From threshold 0.3 to threshold 0.7, recall falls and precision rises.
statements.explanation: Recall goes 0.90, 0.80, 0.50 and precision goes 0.23, 0.50, 0.83.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Accuracy ranks the three thresholds in the same order as total cost does.
statements.explanation: Accuracy is 96.9%, 99.0% and 99.4%, so it prefers 0.7, which has the highest cost.

questions.section: 5. Modeling basics: fit, overfitting and evaluation
questions.source: Regularization, model selection, bias and variance
questions.stem:
Polynomial regressions of degree 1, 3, 9 and 15 are fit to 40 training points. Errors (root mean squared error) are measured on the training points and on 40 held-out points.

| Degree | Training error | Held-out error |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4.1 | 4.3 |
| 3 | 2.2 | 2.5 |
| 9 | 0.4 | 3.9 |
| 15 | 0.05 | 11.2 |

Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For the degree-15 model, more training data or a penalty on large coefficients would be expected to reduce the held-out error.
statements.explanation: More data constrains a flexible model, and regularization limits its effective flexibility; both reduce variance.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The problem with degree 15 is that the model is too rigid.
statements.explanation: A training error of 0.05 against 11.2 held out is the signature of an overly flexible model fitting noise.

statements.label: C
statements.text: On these data, degree 3 has the lowest held-out error.
statements.explanation: 2.5 is the smallest held-out error among the four.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Degree 15 is the best model because it has the lowest training error.
statements.explanation: Training error always falls as flexibility rises; it does not measure performance on new data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Degree 1 is underfitting: both of its errors are high and close together.
statements.explanation: A model that is too simple has high error on both sets, with little gap between them.

questions.section: 5. Modeling basics: fit, overfitting and evaluation
questions.stem: A data scientist has 60 examples and 5,000 features. The features are pure noise and the labels are independent coin flips. Procedure X picks the 20 features most correlated with the label using all 60 examples, then runs 5-fold cross-validation of a logistic regression on those 20 features, and reports 92% accuracy. Procedure Y repeats the feature selection inside each training fold only. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Using 10 folds or leave-one-out cross-validation in Procedure X would remove the problem.
statements.explanation: The selection step has already used every label, so the number of folds does not change the leak.

statements.label: B
statements.text: On new data, the model from Procedure X would be expected to be right about 92% of the time.
statements.explanation: The 92% reflects leakage; with noise features the model should be right about half the time on new data.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Procedure X's 92% is optimistic because the held-out labels influenced which features were chosen.
statements.explanation: Choosing the features that happen to correlate with all labels, including the held-out ones, builds the test answers into the model.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Procedure Y would be expected to report accuracy near 50% on average.
statements.explanation: With no real signal, an honest evaluation of a fair-coin task should give roughly 50% accuracy, up to chance variation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Fitting any label-dependent step, such as target encoding, on the whole dataset before splitting causes the same kind of leakage.
statements.explanation: Any step that sees the held-out labels before evaluation contaminates the estimate; such steps belong inside each training fold.

questions.section: 5. Modeling basics: fit, overfitting and evaluation
questions.stem: A logistic regression predicts whether an account is flagged: log-odds of being flagged = −2.0 + 0.9 × x, where x is the number of prior incidents. Use e^(−2.0) ≈ 0.135 and e^(0.9) ≈ 2.46. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For an account with x = 1 the predicted probability of being flagged is about 0.25.
statements.explanation: Odds are 0.135 × 2.46 ≈ 0.33, so the probability is 0.33 / 1.33 ≈ 0.25.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The increase in predicted probability from x = 1 to x = 2 is the same as from x = 0 to x = 1.
statements.explanation: The probabilities are about 0.12, 0.25 and 0.45, so the steps are about 0.13 and 0.20; the probability effect depends on where you start.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Each additional prior incident multiplies the predicted probability of being flagged by 2.46.
statements.explanation: The coefficient acts on the odds, not the probability: 0.12 becomes about 0.25, not 0.29.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Each additional prior incident multiplies the odds of being flagged by about 2.46.
statements.explanation: exp(0.9) ≈ 2.46 is the odds ratio per extra incident.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For an account with x = 0 the predicted probability of being flagged is about 0.12.
statements.explanation: At x = 0 the odds are 0.135, so the probability is 0.135 / 1.135, about 0.12.

questions.section: 5. Modeling basics: fit, overfitting and evaluation
questions.stem: A scorer assigns probabilities of being positive to nine cases. The four positives scored 0.9, 0.8, 0.7 and 0.4. The five negatives scored 0.6, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1. The AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen positive is scored above a randomly chosen negative. Log loss for one case is −ln of the probability the model gave to the outcome that occurred. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The AUC of this scorer is 0.90.
statements.explanation: 18 of the 20 positive-negative pairs are ranked correctly (only 0.4 loses, to 0.6 and 0.5), so AUC = 18 / 20 = 0.90.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An AUC of 0.90 guarantees that cases scored near 0.9 turn out to be positive about 90% of the time.
statements.explanation: AUC measures ranking, not calibration; a well-ranked scorer can still have scores that do not match observed frequencies.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If cases are predicted positive when the score is above 0.5, 90% of the nine cases are classified correctly.
statements.explanation: Above 0.5, three positives and one negative are flagged and one positive is missed, so 7 of 9 (78%) are correct.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Replacing every score with its cube would leave the AUC unchanged.
statements.explanation: AUC depends only on the ranking of the scores, and cubing keeps the order.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Giving probability 0.99 to an outcome that does not occur costs about 4.6 in log loss, about five times as much as giving 0.6 to it.
statements.explanation: The outcome that occurred had been given probability 0.01, so the loss is −ln 0.01 ≈ 4.6, against −ln 0.4 ≈ 0.92 when the model had said 0.6; confident errors are punished heavily.

questions.stem: A launch review for a deployed fraud-detection model hears five sentences from the team, each offered in support of the claim that the model "works in production," meaning that it meets its operating requirements for both scoring speed and fraud detection. A checkable falsifier states an observation, possible to make, that would count against the claim. Check each statement that is a checkable falsifier.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Median scoring latency at the gateway stays under 150 ms across 30 days of production traffic; a 7-day median above 150 ms means the claim has failed."
statements.explanation: Speed is one of the stated operating requirements, and a latency measurement over a defined window with a stated failure threshold can be checked and can fail.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Over 30 days, recall on confirmed fraud in a weekly random audit of 400 labelled transactions stays at or above 0.85; any week below 0.80 counts as failure."
statements.explanation: It names a metric, a sample, a threshold and a window, so a specific audit result can contradict it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "The model performs well across the situations that matter, and the team has high confidence in it going forward based on its experience in the pilot deployment."
statements.explanation: "Performs well" and "high confidence" are compatible with any outcome, so nothing could show them wrong.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "The model stays robust to the many unexpected shifts that production traffic, user behavior and upstream data are likely to bring in the months after launch."
statements.explanation: "Robust" and "unexpected" fix no metric, threshold or window, so no observation could count against the statement.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "If anything looks wrong in production, the team will look into it promptly and take whatever action seems appropriate, escalating to the vendor if the cause is not found within a few days."
statements.explanation: A promise to investigate names no observation that would refute the model's claimed performance.

questions.stem: A team says: "Adding a retrieval step makes our assistant hallucinate less." A reviewer asks them to restate the claim as an explicit prediction, with assumptions and a falsifier, to be tested on a set of 500 held-out questions. Check each statement that would be a sound part of the restatement.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Assumption: the assistant's fluent phrasing shows its answers are supported, so annotators can save time by not checking each answer against the documents.
statements.explanation: Whether answers are supported is exactly what the test measures, so assuming it from phrasing removes the test.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Falsifier, fixed before the run: if the unsupported-claim share with retrieval is not lower than without it on those 500 questions, judged by a significance test or margin stated in advance, the claim counts as refuted for this setup.
statements.explanation: An outcome that is declared in advance to count against the claim is what makes the test capable of failing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Success criterion: the claim counts as supported if no user complains about invented facts during the first week after release, since complaints are the clearest sign of a problem.
statements.explanation: A quiet week is an unmeasured, weak signal that would occur whether or not hallucination fell.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Prediction: on the same 500 held-out questions, the share of answers with a claim unsupported by the supplied documents, as judged by two annotators, will be lower with retrieval than without it.
statements.explanation: It specifies the quantity, the data, the raters and the direction of change, so it can come out wrong.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Assumption, stated so it can be inspected: the 500 questions resemble real user traffic, and the annotators' judgments of whether a claim is supported are accurate.
statements.explanation: Writing down representativeness and rater accuracy turns hidden premises into items someone can check.

questions.stem: A vendor says its content filter "never lets through step-by-step instructions for making the listed hazardous compounds." As evidence it reports that 10,000 test prompts, written by its own staff to resemble ordinary user requests, produced no such instructions. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 10,000 clean results establish that no prompt exists, written by anyone, that would get such instructions through the filter.
statements.explanation: Any number of non-failures leaves open that some untried input fails, so confirming instances cannot prove a universal claim.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A smaller set of prompts written by testers who are actively trying to evade the filter would likely be more informative about the claim than 10,000 ordinary-looking requests.
statements.explanation: Evidence is strongest when it comes from attempts designed to find the failure, since easy cases pass anyway.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The vendor's claim is a real, testable claim because it rules out a specific observable outcome.
statements.explanation: Because the claim forbids an observable outcome, a counterexample could in principle be found, whatever the present evidence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: One failure among the 10,000 test prompts would not by itself refute a different claim, that the filter lets through fewer than 1 in 1,000 such attempts.
statements.explanation: A rate claim is about frequency, so a single failure among many trials can be consistent with a rate under the stated bound.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A single prompt that gets such instructions through would refute the vendor's claim.
statements.explanation: A universal claim of the form "never" is contradicted by one counterexample.

questions.stem: An engineering manager wants her team to treat AI outputs with methodical skepticism rather than with a general attitude of suspicion. Check each practice that fits methodical skepticism, meaning a procedure that can be performed on a particular claim and whose use can be seen.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Accepting an output when it agrees with the reviewer's own recent judgments on similar cases, because that agreement shows the output is sound.
statements.explanation: Agreement with one's own earlier judgments is not independent of them and can repeat their mistakes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Recording how a belief about the system was formed and what conditions it depends on, so that a change in those conditions can be noticed.
statements.explanation: Knowing what a belief rests on is what lets its holder notice when those conditions have changed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Before reading an output, writing down what a wrong answer would look like, so that the output is judged against a criterion fixed beforehand.
statements.explanation: A criterion set before the output arrives cannot be bent to fit whatever the output happens to say.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Declining to rely on any AI output on principle, whatever its track record, the stakes involved or the checks that have been run on it.
statements.explanation: Blanket rejection is a disposition, not a procedure; it ignores evidence and cannot tell good outputs from bad ones.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Examining only the outputs that look strange or implausible, since fluent and polished outputs have already passed an informal quality filter.
statements.explanation: Polish says little about correctness, and errors that look right are exactly what a strangeness filter would miss.

questions.stem: A loan-scoring system outputs "default risk 0.82, decline" for an applicant. A reviewer asks what would have to be true for that score to be wrong about this applicant, intending to produce a list of conditions that can be inspected. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the applicants now arriving come from a different population than the sample used to validate the model, the validation result may not apply to this applicant.
statements.explanation: Validation results carry over to new inputs only to the extent that those inputs resemble the validated sample.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If very few applicants in the training data resemble this one, the score is an extrapolation and deserves less trust.
statements.explanation: Predictions in thinly covered regions of the input space are unreliable, and whether this applicant lies in one can be checked.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The reviewer submitted the same application a second time and received the same score, so the score is probably right for this applicant.
statements.explanation: Reproducing a number shows the system is consistent, not that the number matches the applicant's actual risk.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Writing the list of conditions settles which of them actually hold for this applicant, so no further inspection is needed once the list exists.
statements.explanation: The list names suspects; each condition still needs its own inspection or test to learn whether it holds.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the income field was entered in thousands in one source system and in single units in another, the model may have seen a value 1,000 times too small.
statements.explanation: A unit or data-entry error is a checkable input fault that would make the score describe the wrong applicant.

questions.stem: Before running an experiment, a researcher writes in a dated file: "The new prompt will raise exact-match accuracy on the 1,000-item test set by at least 2 points. A gain below 0.5 points, or any drop, means the claim has failed." The run shows a gain of 1.2 points. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 1.2-point result lies between the stated success and failure thresholds, which shows the prediction left that case undefined.
statements.explanation: Gains between 0.5 and 2 points were assigned no meaning, so the honest report is that the outcome was neither predicted nor ruled out.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Editing the file after the run to say "at least 1 point" would preserve the evidential value of the original prediction.
statements.explanation: Revising a threshold after seeing the result turns a test into a description of what happened.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The 1.2-point gain satisfies the prediction, since it is above the failure threshold of 0.5 points and the direction of the effect is positive.
statements.explanation: The prediction was a gain of at least 2 points; clearing the failure threshold is not the same as meeting the prediction.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Stating the thresholds before the run is what allows the result to count against the claim.
statements.explanation: A criterion fixed beforehand cannot be adjusted to fit the outcome, so the outcome is able to contradict it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Leaving the original entry unchanged and appending the observed result as a separate dated entry preserves what was expected beforehand.
statements.explanation: An append-only record separates prediction from observation and lets others check the order of events.

questions.stem: A team ships a prompt change and sees no overall gain. After looking at the results, an analyst compares 20 customer segments and reports that segment 14 improved with p = 0.03, concluding that "the change works for segment 14 because that segment uses shorter queries." Assume the 20 comparisons are independent and that, in truth, the change has no effect in any segment. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A stronger test is to state the segment 14 hypothesis and a threshold in advance and then check it on new data collected after the hypothesis was written.
statements.explanation: A prediction made before fresh data arrive can fail, so its success is real evidence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because p = 0.03 is below 0.05, the segment 14 result is unlikely to be chance, regardless of how many segments were examined.
statements.explanation: A p-value computed for one comparison does not account for choosing the best of 20 after the fact.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A Bonferroni correction for 20 comparisons would still count p = 0.03 as significant at the 5% family-wise level, because 0.03 is below 0.05.
statements.explanation: The corrected per-segment threshold is 0.05 / 20 = 0.0025, which 0.03 does not meet.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The probability that at least one of the 20 segments shows p < 0.05 by chance alone is about 64%.
statements.explanation: The chance of at least one hit is 1 - 0.95^20, which is about 0.64.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The shorter-queries explanation was constructed after seeing the result, so it has not been tested against any outcome that could have contradicted it.
statements.explanation: An account fitted to a result already seen would have been adjusted to whatever segment looked good, so agreement is guaranteed.

questions.stem: An LLM assistant with no access to a company's systems is asked why a database query is slow. It replies with a well-organized, confident explanation that names a specific table and a specific configuration setting as the cause. The engineer has not looked at the database. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The clarity of the explanation is not evidence that its diagnosis matches this database.
statements.explanation: Well-formed prose is produced by a process that does not depend on being right, so form and correctness are separate properties.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Naming a specific table and a specific setting is evidence that the assistant inspected the database, since a vague answer would not name them.
statements.explanation: With no access to the system the specifics cannot come from inspection; specificity is as easy to generate as vagueness.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Treating the explanation as a hypothesis and testing a prediction that could contradict it, such as whether rebuilding the index speeds up the query, is more informative than rereading it.
statements.explanation: A hypothesis becomes evidence only when a test could have shown it wrong.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A longer and more confident version of the same explanation would reduce the need to measure, because extra detail makes a wrong diagnosis less likely.
statements.explanation: More detail and more confidence change the presentation, not the evidence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Checking the query plan and the table's fragmentation statistics on the real system supplies evidence that the explanation's wording cannot.
statements.explanation: A measurement on the real system is a direct observation of the thing the explanation makes a claim about.

questions.stem: An LLM is given only a table of weekly revenue and asked why revenue fell 8% last month. It writes a fluent, specific account blaming a competitor's price cut. The table would fit several other accounts equally well, such as a shift in billing dates or a holiday moved into the following month. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A coherent account that fits the data is a hypothesis, because other accounts fit the same data equally well.
statements.explanation: Fit to the data does not discriminate among accounts that all fit; only evidence favoring one over the others does.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The mention of a particular competitor shows that the model had access to that competitor's pricing data.
statements.explanation: The model was given only revenue figures, so the competitor detail came from the model's generation habits, not from data it saw.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Obtaining the same price-cut explanation in ten of ten samples from the same model shows that the explanation is true.
statements.explanation: Repetition from one source measures the stability of the model's output, not whether it matches the world.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An account that no conceivable observation could contradict is better supported than one that makes risky predictions.
statements.explanation: Support comes from surviving attempts at refutation, and an unrefutable account has not been tested.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Comparing the date of the competitor's price change with the date the decline began is a check that could contradict the account.
statements.explanation: If the decline began before the price cut, the account fails, so the comparison is a test.

questions.stem: An LLM assistant attaches a stated confidence to each answer. An independent audit of 200 answers for which it stated confidence of at least 90% finds that 150 were correct. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A 95% confidence interval for the accuracy of those 200 answers runs from roughly 69% to 81%, so a true accuracy of 90% is not plausible for this group.
statements.explanation: The normal-approximation interval is 0.75 plus or minus about 0.06, roughly 0.69 to 0.81, which excludes 0.90.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the underlying model or the mix of questions changes, an earlier calibration audit may no longer describe the assistant.
statements.explanation: Calibration is a property of a system on a population of questions, so it can change when either one does.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The observed accuracy of those answers is 75%, which is below the stated confidence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A phrase such as "I am 95% sure" from a language model is a calibrated probability by construction, because the model computes it from its own uncertainty.
statements.explanation: Verbal confidence is generated text; whether it tracks the frequency of being right has to be measured, not assumed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A calibration check compares stated confidence levels with how often the answers at those levels turn out to be correct across many answers.
statements.explanation: Calibration means that among answers given at a stated level, about that fraction are correct, which can only be seen over many answers.

questions.stem: An analyst wants to confirm a model-written answer to "What was Company X's 2022 revenue?" and considers several second checks. Check each statement that is true about whether a second check adds independent evidence.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Looking the figure up in the company's audited annual filing is a check whose errors are unlikely to be tied to the model's errors.
statements.explanation: A primary document produced by a different process has its own error sources, mostly unrelated to the model's.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Two checks are independent to the extent that whatever could make one of them wrong would not also make the other wrong.
statements.explanation: Independence is about whether the errors of two checks are correlated, not about how many checks were run.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Asking a different model that was trained on largely overlapping text is fully independent of the first, because the two systems come from different vendors.
statements.explanation: Models trained on overlapping data and with similar methods can share the same gaps and the same mistakes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Asking the model "Are you sure?" and receiving "Yes" is a second check, since the confirmation was produced after the original answer.
statements.explanation: The model is reading its own answer, so its confirmation shares every assumption of the original.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Asking the same model the question again in a fresh session and getting the same figure adds little, because repeated samples from one model can repeat the same error.
statements.explanation: Resampling one system tests its consistency, and a consistent system can be consistently wrong.

questions.stem: Two reviewers inspect the same batch for a certain defect. Each reviewer catches any given defect with probability 0.8. Consider one defect in the batch. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the two reviewers miss independently, the probability that at least one of them catches the defect is 0.84.
statements.explanation: The probability that at least one catches it is 1 - 0.04 = 0.96, not 0.84.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With three reviewers whose misses are independent, the probability that all three miss the defect is 0.016.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the two reviewers miss defects independently of each other, the probability that both miss this defect is 0.04.
statements.explanation: For independent misses, 0.2 x 0.2 = 0.04.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the two reviewers have identical blind spots, so that each misses exactly the defects the other misses, the probability that at least one of them catches the defect is 0.96.
statements.explanation: With identical blind spots the second reviewer adds nothing, so the probability stays at 0.8.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The probability that at least one of the two reviewers catches the defect can be found as 0.96 from the 0.8 detection rate alone, whatever the relationship between their misses.
statements.explanation: The benefit of a second reviewer depends on how correlated the two reviewers' errors are, not just on each one's detection rate.

questions.stem: A team generates answers to 500 customer-support questions with a language model M and then grades each answer pass or fail by prompting the same model M as a judge. They report a 94% pass rate. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 94% figure is a measurement of how many of the answers are correct.
statements.explanation: It is the rate at which the judge says pass; how well that tracks correctness has to be measured against independent labels.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A judge that shares the generator's blind spots can accept an answer for the same mistaken reason the generator produced it.
statements.explanation: Errors that come from the same knowledge gaps or the same misreading are not caught by a checker with those gaps.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Language-model judges have been reported to favor outputs that resemble their own, so a self-graded score may be inflated.
statements.explanation: Self-preference in model-based grading has been observed, which biases self-graded results upward.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Replacing M with a larger model as judge removes the shared-error problem.
statements.explanation: A larger model may be better, but it can still share training data, framing and failure modes with the generator.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Having a second run of M grade the same 500 answers and finding that its grades match the first run's would show that the 94% pass rate is accurate.
statements.explanation: Agreement between two runs of the same system measures consistency, which a consistently wrong judge also shows.

questions.stem: A reporter finds the statistic "62% of firms have adopted technology X" in five news articles, each citing a different outlet. Tracing the citations back, all five come from a single press release by a vendor that sells X; the release gives no sample size, sampling method or question wording. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The more outlets repeat the figure, the more likely it is to be accurate, since each outlet decided independently to publish it.
statements.explanation: Repetition spreads a claim without testing it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A survey whose methods are published can be trusted without further checks on how it was designed or carried out.
statements.explanation: Published methods make checking possible; they do not show the survey was well designed or carried out.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The five articles amount to one piece of evidence, not five, because they share a single origin.
statements.explanation: Copies of one claim are not separate observations; their errors are perfectly correlated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Independent confirmation would require a source that collected its own data by a separate process.
statements.explanation: A separate sample, collected and analyzed separately, is what can corroborate or contradict the original figure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The vendor's commercial interest in the result is enough, by itself, to show that the figure is false.
statements.explanation: A motive to inflate is a reason to look harder, but whether the figure is true depends on how it was produced.

questions.stem: A data-migration job writes "Migrated 12,000 rows to the new table: SUCCESS" to its log and exits with status code 0. An engineer then runs a row count directly on the destination table and gets 11,400. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The exit status of 0 establishes that the destination table is complete, since the job would otherwise have reported an error.
statements.explanation: A zero exit status means the process did not signal an error; it does not describe the state of the data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Even if the destination count had been 12,000, matching counts would not by themselves show that the row contents were copied correctly.
statements.explanation: Rows can be duplicated, truncated or altered while the total stays the same, so a count checks one property only.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The log line is a statement produced by the process under review, while the destination count is a direct observation of the resulting state.
statements.explanation: A report generated by the system being checked is a claim about the world, not an observation of it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The destination holds 5% fewer rows than the log reports.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because the job exited with status 0, the discrepancy can be set aside without looking at the missing rows.
statements.explanation: A direct observation that contradicts the report calls for investigating the difference, not explaining it away.

questions.stem: A nightly backup job has written "backup completed" to its log and exited with status 0 on each of the last 400 nights. The goal is that the data can be restored after a loss. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A restore test that passed once, when the system was set up, shows that every later backup is restorable.
statements.explanation: Configuration, data and software change over time, so a past test says nothing certain about later backups.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A steadily growing backup file size shows that the backups can be restored, since the files hold more data each night.
statements.explanation: Size can grow while the data are corrupted, incomplete or unreadable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Restoring a recent backup into a scratch environment and comparing it with the source is a direct check of the property that matters.
statements.explanation: A restore into a clean environment tests the outcome that matters rather than a report about the process.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Exit status 0 on 400 consecutive nights shows that the backups are restorable, since errors would have changed the status.
statements.explanation: Exit status describes whether the job raised an error, not whether the files can be restored.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The "backup completed" line is independent confirmation, since it was written after the backup files were created.
statements.explanation: The line is written by the same job whose correctness is in question, so it reports the job's own belief.

questions.stem: A developer says her patch fixes a bug in which exporting a customer record crashes when the customer's name contains an apostrophe. She adds a test that exports a record for "Olivia Smith" and shows that it passes after the patch. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Her explanation of why the patch should work is evidence that it does work, since she wrote the code and understands it best.
statements.explanation: A reason to expect success is a prediction, not an observation of success.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A test that uses a name with an apostrophe, fails on the old code and passes on the patched code would be evidence that the patch addresses this bug.
statements.explanation: A test that fails before and passes after is the kind of observation that distinguishes a fix from no fix.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A passing result on her own machine shows that the deployed build is fixed, since it runs the same source code.
statements.explanation: Her machine and the deployed system can differ, so the check must be made against the thing that actually runs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The test would also have passed before the patch, so it cannot tell a patched build from an unpatched one.
statements.explanation: A test that cannot fail on the broken version does not discriminate between broken and fixed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Seeing no new crash reports for a day after release establishes that the fix is correct, because the bug would otherwise recur.
statements.explanation: A day without reports is weak evidence, since rare inputs may not have occurred in that time.

questions.stem: A safety evaluation runs a chatbot on 100 prompts drawn at random from expected production traffic and records 0 harmful responses. Treat the prompts as independent trials with a fixed probability of a harmful response. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Roughly 3,000 clean trials would be needed to bring the 95% upper bound on the harm rate down to about 0.1%.
statements.explanation: The rule of three gives an upper bound of 3 / 3,000 = 0.1%.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the true harm rate were 2%, observing 0 harmful responses in 100 prompts would still happen about 13% of the time.
statements.explanation: 0.98^100 is about 0.13, so a clean run is quite possible at a 2% rate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The result describes prompts like those that were sampled and says little about prompts written specifically to provoke harm.
statements.explanation: A bound holds for the population that was sampled; adversarial inputs come from a different distribution.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The result shows that the true harm rate is below 1%, since no harmful response was observed in the sample.
statements.explanation: At a true rate of 1% the chance of 0 harms in 100 trials is about 37%, so the data do not rule it out.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A one-sided 95% upper confidence bound on the harm rate is about 3%.
statements.explanation: With zero events in n trials the 95% upper bound is about 3 / n (the "rule of three"), here 3 / 100.

questions.stem: A static-analysis tool finds each instance of a certain class of vulnerability independently with probability 0.6 and raises no false alarms. Of modules like the one under review, 20% contain exactly one instance and 80% contain none. The tool reports nothing for this module. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Given the clean report, the probability that the module contains the vulnerability is about 9%.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The clean report shows that the module is free of this vulnerability class, because the tool raises no false alarms.
statements.explanation: A clean report lowers the probability of a flaw from 20% but does not reduce it to zero.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the module contains one instance, the chance of a clean report is 0.4.
statements.explanation: The instance is missed with probability 1 - 0.6 = 0.4.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the tool were unable to detect this vulnerability class at all, a clean report would carry no information about it.
statements.explanation: A tool that cannot see a class of flaw returns the same clean report whether or not the flaw is present.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A module with two separate instances, each found independently with probability 0.6, would produce a clean report with probability 0.16.
statements.explanation: Both instances must be missed, giving 0.4 x 0.4 = 0.16.

questions.stem: A team's test suite passes on its code. To learn what a pass means, they inject 50 small deliberate faults into the code, one at a time, each confirmed to change the program's behavior on some input that can occur, and rerun the suite for each. The suite fails (detects the fault) for 31 of the 50. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Injecting known faults is a way to measure whether a checking method can detect faults at all.
statements.explanation: Seeding faults of known type lets one count how many the checker catches, which a clean run cannot reveal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The pass on the unmodified code shows that the code contains no faults.
statements.explanation: A suite passes whenever the faults present are ones it does not test for.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The suite detected 62% of the injected faults.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The 19 undetected faults point to behavior that the suite does not check.
statements.explanation: A fault that changes behavior without failing any test marks behavior the tests do not examine.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A detection rate of 62% on injected faults means that 62% of real defects would be caught.
statements.explanation: Real defects may differ in kind from the injected ones, so the rate transfers only roughly.

questions.stem: Consider the general relationship between the effort needed to produce an answer and the effort needed to check it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For some problems, such as factoring a large integer, checking a proposed answer by multiplication is much cheaper than finding the factors by any known classical method.
statements.explanation: Verifying a factorization takes one multiplication, while no efficient classical method for finding factors is known.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because a language model produces an output in milliseconds, checking that output must take longer than producing it.
statements.explanation: How fast something is produced does not determine how hard it is to check; some outputs are cheap to verify.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For a claim such as "this long summary faithfully reflects the source record," a short mechanical certificate that settles correctness generally exists.
statements.explanation: Faithfulness to a long record usually needs a knowledgeable reader, not a quick mechanical test.

statements.label: D
statements.text: How costly it is to verify an AI output depends on whether a cheap check, such as a test, a lookup or an independent ground truth, is available for that kind of output.
statements.explanation: The cost of checking is a property of the task and of what reference is available, so it varies from one output type to another.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If a workflow budgets no effort for checking, unchecked outputs accumulate and, absent other signals, look like successes.
statements.explanation: An output that nobody examined has no visible defects, so it passes by default.

questions.stem: A model drafts 2,000 contract summaries a day at negligible cost. A lawyer needs 10 minutes to check one summary against its contract. Suppose 2% of summaries contain a material error, errors occur independently across summaries, and a lawyer who checks a summary always spots a material error in it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A random sample of 150 summaries has at least a 95% chance of containing at least one erroneous summary.
statements.explanation: 1 - 0.98^150 is about 0.952, just above 95%.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Checking a random 5% sample would take about 33 lawyer-hours per day.
statements.explanation: 5% of 2,000 is 100 summaries, which is 1,000 minutes, about 17 hours.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Checking every summary would take about 333 lawyer-hours per day.
statements.explanation: 2,000 x 10 minutes = 20,000 minutes, which is about 333 hours.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A random sample of 100 summaries has at least a 95% chance of containing at least one erroneous summary.
statements.explanation: The chance of at least one error is 1 - 0.98^100, about 0.87, below 95%.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A random sample of 150 summaries in which no error is found proves, with certainty, that the error rate is below 2%.
statements.explanation: A clean sample of 150 is evidence against a high rate but cannot rule out a 2% rate with certainty, since a 2% rate would give no errors in 150 about 5% of the time (0.98^150 is about 0.048).

questions.source: What you measure and what you care about
questions.stem: A support team rewards agents, and the AI assistant that drafts their replies, for average handle time.
