After six months, average handle time has fallen from 11 minutes to 7, while the share of customers who contact support again within a week about the same issue has risen from 14% to 26%. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The pattern illustrates Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it tends to stop being a good measure.
statements.explanation: Once the measure is rewarded, behavior changes in ways that separate it from what it was meant to indicate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because handle time and resolution moved together before the incentive was introduced, they must still move together now.
statements.explanation: A past correlation is not a guarantee, especially when the incentive itself changes behavior.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The fall in handle time is itself good evidence that more customers are getting their problems solved, since each call is resolved faster.
statements.explanation: Faster closure can come from ending conversations early, which would also raise repeat contacts, as the data show.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The repeat-contact rate is a more direct indicator of the outcome the team cares about than handle time is.
statements.explanation: A returning customer with the same issue is closer to an unresolved problem than a short call is to a solved one.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Handle time was adopted as a stand-in for "customers get their problem solved," and once the stand-in is rewarded the relationship between the two can break.
statements.explanation: Optimizing a proxy puts pressure on the parts of it that are unrelated to the underlying aim.

questions.source: What you measure and what you care about
questions.stem: Two teams report models that score well on their validation metrics but fail the goal the metric was meant to serve. Team 1 trained a model to predict each patient's past healthcare spending as a stand-in for medical need. Team 2 built a demand forecaster whose error was low for two years; a new competitor then changed customers' buying habits, and its error has been rising since. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Team 1's problem would disappear if the model were retrained more often on newer data with the same stand-in label, because the newer data reflect current patients.
statements.explanation: More recent data with the same flawed label reproduces the same gap between label and goal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Team 2, the metric tracked the goal when it was validated, so a one-time review at launch would have found nothing wrong with the measure.
statements.explanation: A relationship that held at launch and later changed cannot be detected by examining launch-time data.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Team 1, the metric and the goal were mismatched from the start, and comparing the stand-in with direct measures of need before deployment could have revealed it.
statements.explanation: A label that never tracked the goal is a design-time flaw that a direct comparison with the goal can expose.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Team 2's problem can be avoided by validating more thoroughly on the original historical data before launch, using more folds and more years.
statements.explanation: The failure arose from a change in the world after launch, which the original data cannot contain.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A strong validation result at launch is enough to show that the metric will still track the goal a year later, provided the model is unchanged.
statements.explanation: A measure's link to the goal can erode as conditions or behavior change, so it has to be checked again.

questions.stem: A delivery-time predictor was within its stated margin on 98% of 50,000 orders during a year of normal operation. The company then opens a new region with a different road network, and the model's inputs now come from that region. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: No number of past correct predictions logically guarantees that the next prediction will be right.
statements.explanation: Induction from past cases is probabilistic support, never a guarantee.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Comparing the input distribution in the new region with the training data can flag a shift, but only comparing predictions with realized delivery times shows whether accuracy fell.
statements.explanation: A changed input distribution is a warning sign; whether outputs have become wrong is settled by comparing predictions with outcomes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The year of correct predictions is evidence about future accuracy to the extent that future cases resemble the past ones.
statements.explanation: Inductive support depends on the future being like the sample from which the track record came.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The model's own output confidence will necessarily fall when it meets inputs from the new region, signaling that its predictions are less reliable.
statements.explanation: A model has no built-in mechanism to notice that its inputs have moved, and can stay confident on unfamiliar data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Accuracy is a property of a model together with the cases it is applied to, not of the model alone.
statements.explanation: The same model can be highly accurate on one population and poor on another.

questions.stem: A pneumonia classifier is trained and tested on a pooled set of chest X-rays from two hospitals. Hospital A contributed 1,000 images, of which 800 show pneumonia; hospital B contributed 1,000 images, of which 100 show pneumonia. Each image carries a scanner tag identifying its hospital, and the tag is visible to the model. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An accuracy of 85% on the pooled set shows that the model is reading features of the lungs and not just the scanner tag.
statements.explanation: A shortcut that uses the scanner tag, which correlates with disease prevalence, produces the same score without any reading of the lungs.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Testing on a third hospital whose scanners and patients were absent from training is a stronger check for reliance on the tag than the pooled held-out set.
statements.explanation: A new site breaks the correlation between tag and disease that the model may have exploited.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Predicting "pneumonia" for every image from hospital A and "no pneumonia" for every image from hospital B would score 85% accuracy on this pooled set.
statements.explanation: The rule is right on 800 of 1,000 from A and 900 of 1,000 from B, so 1,700 of 2,000, which is 85%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Within hospital A alone, a rule that predicts pneumonia for every image would be correct on only 20% of images, since it ignores everything about the patients.
statements.explanation: Within A the rule predicts pneumonia for all images, and 800 of 1,000 do show pneumonia, so it is right on 80%.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Randomly splitting the pooled images into training and test sets removes the hospital confound from the evaluation.
statements.explanation: Both halves of a random split share the same tag-to-prevalence relationship, so the confound remains in the test set.

questions.stem: A company's release pipeline lets an AI reviewer approve routine configuration changes proposed by an AI agent. The approval record reads "Approved by ReviewBot." One of the approved changes causes an outage. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A person who approves several hundred AI-proposed changes a day, a few seconds each, is exercising meaningful review of each change.
statements.explanation: At that volume and speed the approver cannot examine each change, so the approval is nominal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A record of who approved what, and when, supports later review of decisions even though it does not prevent errors.
statements.explanation: Audit trails make it possible to reconstruct what happened and to learn from it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Responsibility for the decision shifts to the AI reviewer because it performed the review.
statements.explanation: A software component cannot be held answerable, so responsibility stays with the people who deployed and relied on it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An approval attributed only to a software component leaves no identifiable person who accepted the risk and can explain the decision.
statements.explanation: Accountability needs someone who can answer for the decision and who had the authority to make it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Naming a human approver adds oversight when that person can see what will change and has the practical ability to stop the change.
statements.explanation: An approver who cannot see the effect or cannot say no is not providing a check.

questions.stem: Reviewers must approve or reject each of 5,000 AI recommendations before it takes effect. They approve 4,850 (97%) and reject 150, spending a median of 4 seconds per item. An independent audit of all 5,000 recommendations finds that 400 (8%) were wrong. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Requiring a human click on every item guarantees that each recommendation received independent verification.
statements.explanation: A click records a decision; it does not show that anything was independently checked.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Had the reviewers rejected 400 recommendations (8%), they would have caught every wrong one, since the rejection count would match the error count.
statements.explanation: Rejecting the right number of items says nothing about whether the rejected ones were the wrong ones.

statements.label: C
statements.text: At least 250 of the 400 wrong recommendations were approved.
statements.explanation: Only 150 items were rejected in total; even if all were correct catches, 400 - 150 = 250 wrong items passed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A high approval rate combined with very short review times is consistent with approvals that do not reflect examination, though the two facts do not prove it.
statements.explanation: Over-reliance on automated suggestions is a documented tendency, and speed plus agreement is a pattern it produces, though other explanations exist.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The 97% approval rate shows that 97% of the recommendations were correct, since reviewers approve only what they have judged sound.
statements.explanation: Reviewers approving an item is not evidence that it is correct, as the audit shows.

questions.stem: A test report reads: "Tested 40 of 40 sample invoices: all processed correctly. Not tested: handwritten scans, invoices in languages other than English, behavior under production load." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because every sampled invoice passed, the report may state that the failure rate on all invoice types is zero.
statements.explanation: Zero failures in a finite sample of one kind of input does not establish a zero rate, still less for other kinds.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The 40-of-40 result supports claims about invoices like those sampled and does not extend to the untested categories.
statements.explanation: A sample supports conclusions about the population it was drawn from, not about different kinds of input.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Since the tool has not failed on handwritten scans, they can be recorded as passing.
statements.explanation: A tool cannot fail on inputs it was never run on, so no failure there is not evidence of success.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Listing what was not tested is part of an honest account, since it marks the limits of what the passing result supports.
statements.explanation: Readers rely on a report to decide what to trust, and a stated scope lets them judge whether it applies to their case.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A record that allows "unknown" as a status, separate from "pass" and "fail", preserves information that a two-state record would lose.
statements.explanation: "Not examined" and "examined and fine" call for different actions, and merging them hides which is which.

questions.stem: A vendor reports that its fine-tuned model reached 91% accuracy on a benchmark test set. Behind that number are eight training runs that differ only in random seed, with test accuracies of 91, 84, 85, 86, 85, 83, 87 and 84 percent. The vendor reported the best run, chosen by looking at test accuracy. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Choosing the best run by its test score means the number was selected using the test set, which biases it upward as an estimate for new data.
statements.explanation: Selecting the maximum of several noisy estimates on the same data overstates what to expect on fresh data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The reported 91% is a fair estimate of the accuracy a new training run with a different seed would reach.
statements.explanation: A typical new run would land near the mean of the runs, not at the maximum.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The spread of accuracies across seeds is noise that a buyer can ignore, since the mean already summarizes the runs.
statements.explanation: The spread, about 2.5 points in standard deviation, shows how much results depend on chance and is part of what the evidence says.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The mean accuracy of the eight runs is about 85.6%.
statements.explanation: The eight values sum to 685, and 685 / 8 is about 85.6.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reporting the best seed is honest as long as the 91% figure was actually observed on the benchmark test set.
statements.explanation: A figure can be literally observed and still misrepresent expected performance when the selection is not disclosed.

questions.stem: A deployment team wants its skeptical checks to happen reliably rather than depend on whether an individual engineer remembers to be careful that day. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Adding a checklist item such as "are live inputs represented in the data the model was validated on?" turns a general worry into something that can be inspected.
statements.explanation: A specific question with a yes or no answer can be assigned, answered and audited.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Setting the failure condition and metric threshold in a monitoring alert before launch removes the need for someone to remember to ask the question later.
statements.explanation: A pre-set alert applies the criterion automatically, whether or not anyone is thinking about it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Once checks are written into the process, no one needs to understand what they are for, since the process will apply them correctly.
statements.explanation: Checks applied without understanding go stale or are satisfied in form while missing their purpose.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A check is more useful when a named person has the authority to hold a release if it fails.
statements.explanation: A check that cannot stop or delay anything records a problem without anyone being able to act on it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Even with checks in the process, someone still has to review whether the checks continue to test the right thing as the system and its use change.
statements.explanation: A check that was well aimed at launch can drift away from the real risk as conditions change.

questions.stem: A forecasting service publishes these probabilities for one day: P(rain) = 0.60, P(snow) = 0.50 and P(rain or snow) = 0.70. For an unrelated question it publishes P(outage) = 0.70 and P(no outage) = 0.40. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The rain and snow figures imply P(rain and snow) = 0.40.
statements.explanation: Inclusion-exclusion gives P(rain and snow) = 0.60 + 0.50 - 0.70 = 0.40.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For any two events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), so the rain and snow figures should have totaled 1.10 and the published 0.70 is a mistake.
statements.explanation: Simple addition holds only for mutually exclusive events; rain and snow can occur together, so the sum overcounts the overlap.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A counterparty who treats the outage figures as fair betting prices could place offsetting bets that win money against the service whichever outcome occurs.
statements.explanation: Prices that sum to 1.10 for a set of outcomes that must resolve to exactly 1 allow a guaranteed profit by trading the opposite side of both bets (a Dutch book).

statements.label: D
statements.text: The outage figures are incoherent, because an event and its complement must have probabilities that sum to 1.
statements.explanation: P(outage) + P(no outage) = 1.10, which violates normalization and the complement rule P(not A) = 1 - P(A).

statements.label: E
statements.text: P(rain and snow) cannot exceed 0.50 here, because "rain and snow" is contained within the snow event.
statements.explanation: If one event is contained in another its probability cannot be larger, so P(rain and snow) <= P(snow) = 0.50; the actual value of 0.40 satisfies this.

questions.source: Conditional probability — the probability that updates on what you know
questions.stem: A triage model attaches an abnormal-lab flag to some incoming cases. In a log of past cases, 70% carry the flag, 40% turn out to be high-acuity, and 25% are both flagged and high-acuity. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: P(high-acuity | no flag) is 0.15.
statements.explanation: 0.15 is P(high-acuity and no flag) = 0.40 - 0.25; dividing by P(no flag) = 0.30 gives a conditional probability of 0.50.

statements.label: B
statements.text: P(high-acuity | flag) is about 0.36.
statements.explanation: P(high-acuity | flag) = 0.25 / 0.70, about 0.357.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Learning that a case carries the flag raises its probability of being high-acuity above the overall 0.40.
statements.explanation: The conditional probability 0.357 is below 0.40, so the flag is mild evidence against high acuity because it is very common.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With these proportions, the flag and high acuity are independent events.
statements.explanation: Independence would require P(both) = 0.70 x 0.40 = 0.28, but the joint is 0.25.

statements.label: E
statements.text: P(flag | high-acuity) has the same value as P(high-acuity | flag).
statements.explanation: P(flag | high-acuity) = 0.25 / 0.40 = 0.625; reversing the conditioning changes the denominator and so the value.

questions.source: The multiplication rule — building joint probabilities from conditionals
questions.stem: An agent must complete three tool calls in order, and the task succeeds only if all three succeed. Measured separately on fresh inputs, the three calls succeed with probabilities 0.95, 0.90 and 0.90. In real runs the first call succeeds with probability 0.95; given that the first succeeded, the second succeeds with probability 0.85; given that both earlier calls succeeded, the third succeeds with probability 0.80. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Relative to the correct joint probability, the independence-based figure of about 0.77 overstates the chance of success by roughly 12 percentage points.
statements.explanation: 0.7695 - 0.646 is about 0.12, so assuming independence here would overstate success by roughly twelve points.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The chain rule can be applied using only the three unconditional success rates.
statements.explanation: The chain rule multiplies each step's probability conditional on the earlier steps having happened, which are different numbers from the unconditional rates.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The probability that all three calls succeed in real runs is 0.95 x 0.85 x 0.80 = 0.646.
statements.explanation: The chain rule gives P(A1) x P(A2 | A1) x P(A3 | A1, A2) = 0.95 x 0.85 x 0.80 = 0.646.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the three calls were independent with the separately measured rates, the probability that all succeed would be 0.95 x 0.90 x 0.90, about 0.77.
statements.explanation: Under independence the joint probability is the product of the marginals: 0.95 x 0.90 x 0.90 = 0.7695.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Multiplying the separately measured rates (about 0.77) gives the correct probability that all three calls succeed in these runs, because the calls run in sequence.
statements.explanation: A product of unconditional rates is the joint probability only under independence; here the later calls are less reliable once the earlier ones have run.

questions.source: The total probability theorem — decomposing complex problems
questions.stem: A fraud-screening service routes each case to one of three model versions. V1 handles 50% of cases and is wrong on 1% of them, V2 handles 30% and is wrong on 4%, and V3 handles 20% and is wrong on 10%. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The overall error rate of the service is 3.7%.
statements.explanation: The law of total probability gives 0.5 x 0.01 + 0.3 x 0.04 + 0.2 x 0.10 = 0.037.

statements.label: B
statements.text: V1 handles the most traffic, so it produces the largest share of the service's errors.
statements.explanation: V1's share of errors is 0.005 / 0.037, about 13.5%, because its error rate is so low.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Given that a case was handled incorrectly, the probability that V3 handled it is about 0.54.
statements.explanation: Bayes' rule gives P(V3 | error) = 0.02 / 0.037, about 0.54.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The overall error rate equals the simple average (1% + 4% + 10%) / 3 = 5%, whatever the traffic shares are.
statements.explanation: The correct overall rate weights each version's error rate by its traffic share; an unweighted average ignores how often each version runs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If traffic were rerouted to 20% V1, 30% V2 and 50% V3 with no model changed, the overall error rate would rise to about 6.4%.
statements.explanation: 0.2 x 0.01 + 0.3 x 0.04 + 0.5 x 0.10 = 0.064, so routing changes alone move the system-level error rate.

questions.source: The test that is 99% accurate, and the patient it kills
questions.stem: A screening test for a condition has sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%. The condition's prevalence in the screened population is 2%. Imagine 10,000 people are screened. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Doubling the prevalence to 4% would double the proportion of positive results that are true cases.
statements.explanation: At 4% prevalence there are 360 true positives and 480 false positives per 10,000, a proportion of about 43%, not double 27%, because the proportion depends nonlinearly on prevalence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: About 490 people without the condition are expected to test positive.
statements.explanation: 9,800 people without the condition times a 5% false-positive rate is 490.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because the test's overall accuracy is about 95%, a person with a positive result has about a 95% chance of having the condition.
statements.explanation: Overall accuracy mixes both classes and is dominated by the many healthy people; the chance that a positive is real is a different conditional probability.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Roughly 27% of the people who test positive are expected to have the condition.
statements.explanation: True positives are 180 and false positives 490, so 180 / 670 is about 0.27.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Raising sensitivity to 100%, with specificity unchanged, would lift the proportion of positives that are true cases above 50%.
statements.explanation: With sensitivity 100%, true positives are 200 against 490 false positives, a proportion of about 29%.

questions.source: The test that is 99% accurate, and the patient it kills
questions.stem: A rare condition affects 1 in 10,000 people. A test is described as "99% accurate" in the sense that it returns positive for 99% of people who have the condition and negative for 99% of people who do not. One person drawn at random from the population tests positive. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because the test is 99% accurate in both directions, the probability that this person has the condition is about 99%.
statements.explanation: 99% describes how the test behaves given the true status; the probability of the condition given a positive result also depends on the 1-in-10,000 base rate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Raising sensitivity to 100%, with specificity left at 99%, would bring that probability above 10%.
statements.explanation: Sensitivity 100% leaves the roughly 10,000 false positives per million unchanged, so the probability stays near 1%.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In 1,000,000 people, about 9,999 true cases and 99 healthy people are expected to test positive.
statements.explanation: The counts are reversed: about 99 true cases and about 9,999 healthy people test positive per million.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The probability that this person has the condition is about 1%.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Raising specificity to 99.9% would bring that probability to about 50%.
statements.explanation: At 99.9% specificity the probability is only about 9%; it takes roughly 99.99% specificity to reach about 50%.

questions.stem: A DNA profile found at a crime scene matches a suspect. The probability that a randomly chosen unrelated person would match is 1 in 100,000. The true source is known to be one person in a region of 1,000,000 people, each equally likely beforehand, and the suspect was identified only because a search of a database covering all 1,000,000 people returned this match. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The probability that a matching person is innocent equals the random-match probability, 1 in 100,000, because both describe the same profile.
statements.explanation: The random-match probability is P(match | innocent); the probability asked about is P(innocent | match), and swapping them is a transposed-conditional error.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The probability that the matching suspect is the true source is about 0.09.
statements.explanation: One true source plus about 10 coincidental matches gives 1 / 11, about 0.09, which Bayes' rule confirms from the prior of 1 in 1,000,000.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If independent evidence had already made the suspect 50% likely to be the source, the same match would raise that probability above 0.99.
statements.explanation: With prior odds of 1 to 1 and a likelihood ratio of 100,000, the posterior probability is about 0.99999.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A probability of about 0.09 means the match carries little evidential value.
statements.explanation: The match raised the probability from 0.000001 to 0.09, a factor of about 90,000, which is strong evidence even though it is not conclusive.

statements.label: E
statements.text: About 10 unrelated people in the region are expected to match by chance.
statements.explanation: 999,999 unrelated people times 1 in 100,000 is about 10.

questions.stem: A condition has prevalence 0.1%. A test has sensitivity 95% and specificity 95%. A person tests positive. The test is then run again, and the second result is also positive. Assume that, given the person's true status, the two results are independent. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: After both positive results, the probability of the condition is about 27%.
statements.explanation: Each positive multiplies the odds by 0.95 / 0.05 = 19, so prior odds of about 0.001 become about 0.36, a probability near 0.265.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the second run reused the same specimen with the same interference as the first, treating the two positives as independent would overstate the probability of the condition.
statements.explanation: A repeat that shares the same error source is not independent given the true status, so it adds less evidence than the independence calculation credits.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The final probability would differ if the two positive results had arrived in the opposite order, because the first result sets the prior for the second.
statements.explanation: Odds updates multiply, and multiplication is commutative, so the order of two positives does not change the posterior.

statements.label: D
statements.text: After the first positive result alone, the probability of the condition is about 1.9%.

statements.label: E
statements.text: After both positive results, the probability of the condition is 0.95 x 0.95 = 0.9025, the product of the test's sensitivity and specificity.
statements.explanation: 0.95 x 0.95 ignores the prior; the posterior depends on the base rate as well as on the test's sensitivity.

questions.stem: A detector has sensitivity 90% and specificity 90%, measured on a labeled evaluation set. It is first deployed where 20% of cases are truly positive, and later redeployed where 2% are. Assume the detector behaves identically on positive cases and on negative cases in both places. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The share of flagged cases that are truly positive is about 0.69 at 20% prevalence and about 0.16 at 2% prevalence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A posterior probability for the new setting can be obtained by combining the detector's likelihood ratio with the new prior odds.
statements.explanation: Posterior odds equal prior odds times the likelihood ratio (here 9), so a new base rate gives a new posterior.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A probability score that was calibrated in the first setting stays calibrated in the second setting without any adjustment.
statements.explanation: Calibration depends on the base rate of the population; a score tied to a 20% prior is too high when the prior is 2%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Sensitivity and specificity remain 90% in both deployments.
statements.explanation: With identical behavior on each class, these class-conditional rates do not depend on prevalence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The drop in the share of flagged cases that are truly positive shows the detector became worse at recognizing positive cases.
statements.explanation: Sensitivity and specificity are unchanged by assumption; the change comes from the lower prior, not from any change in the detector.

questions.source: When the Central Limit Theorem politely declines to help
questions.stem: A model's response time is measured on 25 independent requests. The sample mean is 100 ms and the sample standard deviation is 15 ms. Assume response times are roughly normal. The t critical value for a two-sided 95% interval with 24 degrees of freedom is 2.064. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: About 95% of individual future requests should fall between 93.8 ms and 106.2 ms, since that is the 95% interval computed from the sample.
statements.explanation: The interval 93.8 to 106.2 describes uncertainty about the mean, not the spread of individual requests, which has a standard deviation of 15 ms.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A 95% confidence interval for the mean response time is about 93.8 ms to 106.2 ms.
statements.explanation: The standard error is 15 / 5 = 3 ms, and 100 plus or minus 2.064 x 3 gives about 93.8 to 106.2.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A Bayesian 95% credible interval for the mean, computed from a stated prior and model, can be read as a 95% probability statement about the mean given the data.
statements.explanation: A credible interval contains the parameter with the stated posterior probability, conditional on the model and the prior, which is the interpretation many people wrongly give to a confidence interval.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A 95% prediction interval for a single new request is wider than the confidence interval for the mean, roughly 68.4 ms to 131.6 ms.
statements.explanation: The prediction half-width is 2.064 x 15 x sqrt(1 + 1/25), about 31.6 ms, which adds the variability of one new observation to the uncertainty about the mean.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With 2,500 requests and the same mean and standard deviation, the interval for the mean narrows to about plus or minus 0.6 ms while the prediction interval stays near plus or minus 29 ms.
statements.explanation: The mean's interval shrinks with the square root of n, but individual variability (about 1.96 x 15 = 29 ms) does not shrink with more data.

questions.source: When the Central Limit Theorem politely declines to help
questions.stem: An evaluation team computes a 95% confidence interval for a model's accuracy from each of 100 independent test sets, each drawn afresh from the same population. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 95% describes how often the procedure captures the true accuracy over repeated samples, not a probability attached to any one computed interval.
statements.explanation: Confidence refers to the long-run coverage of the method; once computed, a given interval either contains the fixed true value or does not.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If each of the 100 test sets were much larger, the intervals would be narrower and the share of them containing the true accuracy would rise above 95%.
statements.explanation: Larger samples make intervals narrower, but nominal coverage stays at 95%; it does not increase.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If a test set of 400 items is really 40 distinct items each reworded ten times, an interval computed as if the 400 items were independent will be too narrow.
statements.explanation: Near-duplicates are strongly correlated, so the effective sample size is closer to 40 than 400 and the true uncertainty is larger than the formula suggests.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A very narrow interval shows that the test set is representative of the population where the model will be deployed.
statements.explanation: Interval width reflects sampling noise only; a biased or unrepresentative sample can give a narrow interval around the wrong value.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A 95% interval for the difference in accuracy between two models that excludes zero corresponds to rejecting "no difference" at the 5% level in a two-sided test.
statements.explanation: The duality between two-sided tests and intervals means a 95% interval excluding the null value rejects it at the 5% level.

questions.stem: A team observes 19 correct answers in 20 independent test items. With a uniform Beta(1, 1) prior on the model's accuracy, the posterior is Beta(20, 2), with mean 0.909 and a central 95% interval of about 0.762 to 0.988. With a different prior, Beta(50, 5), concentrated near 0.91, the posterior is Beta(69, 6), with mean 0.92 and a central 95% interval of about 0.849 to 0.970. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A credible interval and a confidence interval are the same quantity and are always numerically equal.
statements.explanation: The two answer different questions and can differ, especially with small samples or informative priors; they roughly agree only under certain diffuse-prior conditions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Given the model and the uniform prior, the probability that the accuracy lies between 0.762 and 0.988 is 95%.
statements.explanation: A central 95% credible interval holds 95% of the posterior probability, conditional on the assumed model and prior.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Under the uniform prior, the posterior probability that the accuracy exceeds 0.90 is above 95%.
statements.explanation: Under Beta(20, 2), P(accuracy > 0.90) is about 0.64, so it is far from 95%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Since the posterior mean is 0.909, the model's accuracy is known to within about one percentage point.
statements.explanation: With only 20 items the interval spans over twenty percentage points, so the accuracy is far from pinned down.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The two intervals differ partly because a credible interval depends on the prior as well as on the data.
statements.explanation: The informative prior narrows the interval and moves the posterior mean, showing that the stated prior contributes to the result.

questions.source: When the Central Limit Theorem politely declines to help
questions.stem: Model P is evaluated on 20 test items and gets 19 right (95%). Model Q is evaluated on 1,000 items and gets 940 right (94%). Approximate 95% Wilson intervals for true accuracy are 0.764 to 0.991 for P and 0.924 to 0.953 for Q. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: P's interval is wider because it rests on far fewer test items.
statements.explanation: Interval width scales with 1 / sqrt(n), and P has 20 items against Q's 1,000.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The data are compatible with P's true accuracy being lower than Q's.
statements.explanation: Q's whole interval lies inside P's, so P's true accuracy could easily be 0.90 or lower.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Roughly four times as many test items would be needed to halve the width of Q's interval, if the observed accuracy stayed about the same.
statements.explanation: Width shrinks with the square root of n, so halving the width requires about four times as many items.

statements.label: D
statements.text: P's observed accuracy is higher than Q's, so P has been shown to be the more accurate model on the strength of a one-point gap.
statements.explanation: A one-point gap in observed accuracy on 20 items is well within sampling noise and does not establish a difference.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Doubling the number of test items for Q would halve the width of its interval, since the standard error is inversely proportional to n.
statements.explanation: Doubling n reduces the width by a factor of about sqrt(2), roughly 29%, not by half.

questions.stem: A model forecasts the probability that each of five loans defaults: 0.8, 0.6, 0.3, 0.9, 0.2. The outcomes are 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, where 1 means the loan defaulted. The Brier score is the mean of the squared differences between forecast probability and outcome. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Classifying a loan as a default when its forecast is at least 0.5 gives an accuracy of 0.8 on these five loans.
statements.explanation: Forecasts of 0.6 (outcome 0) and 0.2 (outcome 1) are on the wrong side of 0.5, so accuracy is 3 of 5 = 0.6.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The single largest contribution to the total squared error comes from the 0.9 forecast.
statements.explanation: The squared errors are 0.04, 0.36, 0.09, 0.01 and 0.64; the 0.9 forecast contributes only 0.01, and the largest is the 0.2 forecast for a loan that defaulted.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The Brier score of these forecasts is 0.228.
statements.explanation: The sum of squared errors is 1.14, and 1.14 / 5 = 0.228.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A Brier score of 0.228 means the forecasts are off by 0.228 probability points on average.
statements.explanation: The Brier score is a mean of squares, not of absolute errors, so it is not an average miss in probability units.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A forecaster who said 0.5 for every loan would score 0.25, so these forecasts score better than that constant.
statements.explanation: A constant 0.5 gives 0.25 for any outcomes, and 0.228 is lower, which is better.

questions.stem: Eight cases have true labels 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0. Model A gives probabilities of the positive class 0.60, 0.70, 0.55, 0.40, 0.30, 0.45, 0.35, 0.60. Model B gives 0.95, 0.90, 0.90, 0.10, 0.05, 0.10, 0.05, 0.95. Each model predicts the positive class when its probability is at least 0.5. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Model B's greater confidence on the cases it gets right gives it the better Brier score.
statements.explanation: Both models get cases 7 and 8 wrong, and B's confident errors (0.05 for a positive, 0.95 for a negative) cost far more than its gains on the correct cases.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Both models have the same accuracy, 0.75.
statements.explanation: Each model errs on the seventh and eighth cases, so 6 of 8 are correct.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Model B's Brier score (about 0.231) is worse than Model A's (about 0.211).
statements.explanation: A's squared errors average about 0.211 and B's about 0.231, because B's two confident errors cost 0.9025 each, more than its sharper correct forecasts save relative to A.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Model B's log loss is higher than Model A's.
statements.explanation: Log loss punishes confident wrong answers even more heavily than Brier does, about 0.81 for B against 0.61 for A.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Brier score separates these two models while accuracy at a 0.5 cutoff cannot.
statements.explanation: Accuracy depends only on which side of 0.5 each forecast falls, so it cannot see the difference in confidence that the Brier score picks up.

questions.stem: On a test set in which 20% of cases are positive, a model's Brier score is 0.12. A reference forecaster always predicts the base rate, 0.20. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Relative to the reference forecaster, the model's Brier skill score, 1 - 0.12 / 0.16, is 0.25.
statements.explanation: A skill score measures improvement over the reference: 1 - 0.12 / 0.16 = 0.25.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Brier scores measured on test sets with different base rates can be compared directly, without a reference, as measures of model quality.
statements.explanation: The score of a trivial forecast is p(1 - p), which depends on the base rate, so a given score means different things at different base rates.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A Brier score of 0.12 means that 12% of the model's forecasts were on the wrong side of 0.5.
statements.explanation: The Brier score is a mean squared probability error, not an error rate at a cutoff.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The reference forecaster has a Brier score of 0 because its forecasts are perfectly calibrated.
statements.explanation: A constant forecast at the base rate is calibrated but has no discrimination, and its Brier score is p(1 - p), well above zero.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The reference forecaster's Brier score is 0.16.
statements.explanation: With p = 0.20 the reference scores 0.20 x 0.80 = 0.16.

questions.stem: A classifier outputs the probability of the positive class for four cases: 0.9, 0.7, 0.2, 0.95. The true labels are 1, 0, 0, 0. Log loss is the mean of -ln(probability assigned to the true class), using natural logarithms. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The largest single penalty comes from the 0.95 forecast on a negative case.
statements.explanation: Per-case penalties are about 0.105, 1.204, 0.223 and 2.996, and the last is the 0.95 forecast on a negative case.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Like the Brier score, log loss cannot exceed 1 for a binary problem.
statements.explanation: Log loss is unbounded above because the penalty grows without limit as the probability given to the true class approaches 0.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A predictor that always outputs 0.5 has log loss of about 0.69, so this classifier beats the constant predictor.
statements.explanation: The classifier's 1.13 is worse than the 0.69 of the constant 0.5 predictor, so it does not beat it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The mean log loss of this classifier is about 1.13.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the classifier had output exactly 0 for a case that turned out positive, that case's log loss would be large but finite.
statements.explanation: -ln(0) is infinite, which is why implementations clip probabilities away from 0 and 1.

questions.stem: An analyst believes an event has true probability 0.7 and will report a probability p. Compare four scoring rules by expected score: Brier score, log loss, absolute error |p - y| (where y = 1 if the event occurs and 0 otherwise), and accuracy at a 0.5 cutoff (a report counts as correct if it is on the right side of 0.5). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Under Brier score, expected loss is minimized by reporting 0.7.
statements.explanation: The expected Brier score 0.7(1 - p)^2 + 0.3p^2 is minimized at p = 0.7.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Under absolute error, expected loss is minimized by reporting 0.7.
statements.explanation: Expected absolute error is 0.7(1 - p) + 0.3p = 0.7 - 0.4p, which falls all the way to p = 1, so it rewards exaggeration.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Under log loss, expected loss is minimized by reporting 0.7.
statements.explanation: Expected log loss is minimized at the true probability, which is the defining property of a proper rule.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Under accuracy at a 0.5 cutoff, reporting 0.7 earns a higher expected score than reporting 0.99.
statements.explanation: Both reports fall on the same side of 0.5 and are correct with probability 0.7, so they earn the same expected score.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A rule is strictly proper if its expected loss is minimized only by reporting one's true belief, and accuracy at a cutoff meets this definition.
statements.explanation: Many different reports earn the same expected accuracy, so honesty is not uniquely rewarded and the rule is not strictly proper.

questions.stem: A classifier scores four positive cases at 0.9, 0.8, 0.6 and 0.55 and four negative cases at 0.7, 0.5, 0.4 and 0.3. Define AUC as the probability that a randomly chosen positive case scores higher than a randomly chosen negative case, with ties counting one half. Predict positive when the score is at least 0.5. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Replacing every score by its square leaves the AUC unchanged.
statements.explanation: AUC depends only on the ordering of scores, and squaring is strictly increasing on non-negative numbers.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The AUC is 0.875, since 14 of the 16 positive-negative pairs are ranked correctly.
statements.explanation: The only misordered pairs are the positive 0.6 against the negative 0.7 and the positive 0.55 against the negative 0.7, so 14 of 16 are correct.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An AUC of 0.875 means the classifier is correct on 87.5% of cases at the 0.5 cutoff used for predictions.
statements.explanation: AUC is a ranking measure; accuracy at a cutoff is a separate quantity that depends on the threshold.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Accuracy at the 0.5 cutoff is 0.75.
statements.explanation: At the 0.5 cutoff the negatives scored 0.7 and 0.5 are called positive, so 6 of 8 cases are correct.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Adding many more negative cases with the same score distribution as the existing negatives would leave the expected AUC unchanged.
statements.explanation: AUC compares the positive and negative score distributions and does not depend on the class proportions in the sample.

questions.stem: A disease has 10% prevalence. Model M1 outputs 0.10 for every patient. Model M2 outputs a score between 0.60 and 1.00 for every patient, and every patient with the disease scores above every patient without it. Model M3 outputs well-calibrated probabilities and has an AUC of 0.85. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: M2's high AUC means its scores can be read directly as probabilities of disease for individual patients.
statements.explanation: AUC measures ranking only; M2's scores of at least 0.6 for patients in a population with 10% disease are far too high as probabilities.

statements.label: B
statements.text: M1 is calibrated in aggregate but has an AUC of 0.5, so it cannot separate patients.
statements.explanation: Predicting the base rate for everyone matches the observed frequency overall but gives no way to rank patients.

statements.label: C
statements.text: M1 would be preferred over M3 for deciding which patients to examine first, because M1's probabilities match the prevalence exactly.
statements.explanation: Prioritizing patients requires a ranking, which M1 cannot supply and M3 can.

statements.label: D
statements.text: M2 has an AUC of 1.0 yet its scores are badly calibrated for a 10% prevalence.
statements.explanation: Perfect ranking is consistent with scores that bear no honest relation to the actual frequency of disease.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Applying a strictly increasing rescaling to M2's scores, fitted on labeled data, could bring its probabilities much closer to the observed frequencies without changing its AUC.
statements.explanation: A strictly increasing map preserves the order of scores, so AUC is unchanged while the stated probabilities can be brought much closer to the observed frequencies (exact calibration with perfectly separated classes would need values of 0 and 1, which a strictly increasing map cannot give, so the fit is approximate).

questions.stem: A reliability diagram for a binary classifier uses four bins of 400 cases each. For each bin it shows the pair (mean predicted probability, observed fraction of positives): (0.15, 0.22), (0.45, 0.47), (0.75, 0.62), (0.95, 0.80). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because the observed rates rise with the predicted probability, the probabilities are shown to be calibrated.
statements.explanation: A rising curve shows the model ranks cases sensibly, but calibration requires the points to lie near the diagonal, which they do not at the ends.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The 0.02 gap in the second bin is smaller than the standard error of an observed rate of about 0.47 from 400 cases, which is roughly 0.025.
statements.explanation: The standard error is sqrt(0.47 x 0.53 / 400), about 0.025, so a gap of 0.02 is within ordinary sampling variation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In the lowest bin the event occurs more often than predicted, so the model understates risk there.
statements.explanation: An observed rate of 0.22 against a mean prediction of 0.15 means positives are more common than the model says there.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The diagram shows the model is miscalibrated by a similar amount in every bin, so one constant shift would repair it.
statements.explanation: The gaps are about 0.07, 0.02, 0.13 and 0.15, so the miscalibration is small in the middle and large at the ends.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In the two highest bins the predicted probabilities exceed the observed rates, a sign of overconfidence at high predicted risk.
statements.explanation: At 0.75 and 0.95 the observed rates are 0.62 and 0.80, below the predictions, which is the signature of overconfidence.

questions.stem: A classifier's top-label confidence on 1,000 test cases is grouped into four bins. For each bin the table gives the number of cases, the mean stated confidence and the observed accuracy: (500, 0.60, 0.58), (300, 0.80, 0.70), (150, 0.92, 0.80), (50, 0.99, 0.78). The expected calibration error (ECE) is the count-weighted mean of the absolute gap between mean confidence and accuracy across bins. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Mean stated confidence (about 0.73) exceeds overall accuracy (about 0.66), so the classifier is overconfident on average.
statements.explanation: The weighted mean confidence is 0.7275 and accuracy is 0.659, so on average confidence is about 7 points too high.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The ECE is about 0.07.
statements.explanation: The weighted gaps are 0.010, 0.030, 0.018 and 0.0105, which sum to 0.0685.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An ECE of about 0.07 means the classifier's predictions are wrong about 7% of the time on these cases.
statements.explanation: ECE measures the gap between confidence and accuracy, not the error rate; the error rate here is about 34%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The bin with the largest gap, 0.21, makes the largest contribution to the ECE, since the ECE is dominated by its worst bin.
statements.explanation: The 50-case bin contributes only 0.0105 because it has few cases; the 300-case bin contributes the most at 0.030.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Averaging the four bin gaps without weighting gives the same value as the count-weighted ECE.
statements.explanation: The unweighted mean of the gaps (0.02, 0.10, 0.12, 0.21) is about 0.11, while the count-weighted ECE is about 0.0685.

questions.stem: A model's 200 test predictions in the range 0.5 to 1.0 consist of 100 cases predicted at 0.60, of which 80 are positive, and 100 cases predicted at 0.90, of which 70 are positive. The expected calibration error (ECE) is the count-weighted mean absolute gap between mean predicted probability and observed frequency within bins. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: ECE values computed with different numbers of bins are directly comparable as measures of the same quantity.
statements.explanation: The ECE changes with the number and placement of bins, so values from different binning schemes measure different things.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Splitting bins into finer sub-bins can only lower the measured ECE, because each sub-bin is more homogeneous.
statements.explanation: Refining the bins can only keep ECE the same or raise it, because averaging within a bin lets opposite-signed gaps cancel.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The single-bin ECE of 0 shows the model is well calibrated across this range of predictions.
statements.explanation: The single-bin value arises from cancellation: the model is underconfident at 0.60 and overconfident at 0.90 by equal amounts.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the 0.60 cases and the 0.90 cases are placed in separate bins, the ECE is 0.20.
statements.explanation: The gaps are |0.6 - 0.8| = 0.2 and |0.9 - 0.7| = 0.2, and the equal weights give an ECE of 0.20.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If all 200 cases fall in one bin covering 0.5 to 1.0, that bin has mean prediction 0.75 and observed frequency 0.75, giving an ECE of 0.
statements.explanation: The pooled mean prediction is (0.6 + 0.9) / 2 = 0.75 and the pooled frequency is 150 / 200 = 0.75, so the gap is zero.

questions.stem: A forecaster is perfectly calibrated by construction: a case predicted at p has an event probability of exactly p, and predictions are spread roughly evenly across 0 to 1. Its expected calibration error (ECE) is estimated on a finite test set using 10 equal-width bins. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The expected measured ECE is greater than zero at any finite test set size.
statements.explanation: Observed frequencies fluctuate around their expectations, and absolute gaps do not average to zero, so the estimate is biased upward even for a perfectly calibrated model.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With 100 test cases, a measured ECE of about 0.08 would be unsurprising for this forecaster.
statements.explanation: Random scatter in small bins gives a typical ECE near 0.10 at this size, so 0.08 does not indicate miscalibration.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reporting an ECE without the test set size and the binning scheme is enough for others to compare it with another model's ECE.
statements.explanation: The ECE depends strongly on how many bins are used and how many cases there are, so both must be reported.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The expected measured ECE decreases as the test set grows.
statements.explanation: Sampling noise in each bin falls roughly with the square root of the bin size, so measured ECE shrinks toward the true value as n grows.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Using 20 bins instead of 10 on the same 100 test cases would, on average, lower the measured ECE.
statements.explanation: More bins mean fewer cases per bin and more noise in each observed frequency, which raises the average measured gap.

questions.stem: A classifier reports top-class confidence of 0.90 for every one of 1,000 held-out cases. Group X contributes 500 cases, 80% of which are classified correctly. Group Y contributes the other 500, all of which are classified correctly. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The pooled reliability diagram has a single point, at confidence 0.90 and accuracy 0.90, which lies on the diagonal.
statements.explanation: Every case has confidence 0.90 and the pooled accuracy is (400 + 500) / 1,000 = 0.90.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Confidence is too high for group X and too low for group Y.
statements.explanation: Group X has accuracy 0.80 against stated confidence 0.90, and group Y has accuracy 1.00 against 0.90.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because the pooled data are calibrated, each group is calibrated, since the group errors average out.
statements.explanation: Opposite-signed errors in the two groups cancel in the pooled data, so aggregate calibration does not imply group-level calibration.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A single global rescaling of confidence fitted on the pooled data would find nothing to correct and leave both group-level gaps in place.
statements.explanation: The pooled data already match the stated confidence, so a one-parameter fit would leave it unchanged and the group gaps would remain.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Pooled calibration guarantees that a decision rule based on confidence is equally reliable for both groups.
statements.explanation: A confidence of 0.90 means an 80% hit rate for one group and 100% for the other, so decisions based on it are not equally reliable.

questions.stem: A forecaster states a 90% interval for each of 20 independent questions and later counts how many intervals contain the true value. Assume that, if the forecaster is well calibrated, each interval has a 90% chance of containing the truth, independently of the others. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the intervals are well calibrated, the expected number that contain the true value is 18.
statements.explanation: The expected count is 20 x 0.90 = 18.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Hitting 17 of 20 would be strong evidence that the intervals are miscalibrated, since 17 is below the expected 18.
statements.explanation: For a calibrated forecaster, P(17 or fewer) is about 0.32, so 17 hits is entirely ordinary.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A result of 14 of 20 shows that the intervals are too wide to be informative.
statements.explanation: Intervals that miss the truth too often are too narrow, which means the forecaster was overconfident.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A result of 14 or fewer of 20 would be rare for a well-calibrated forecaster, with a probability of about 1%.
statements.explanation: Under a binomial model with n = 20 and p = 0.9, P(X <= 14) is about 0.011.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A well-calibrated forecaster must hit exactly 18 of 20, since the long-run hit rate is 90%.
statements.explanation: Even a perfectly calibrated forecaster would hit exactly 18 only about 29% of the time, because the count is random.

questions.stem: A binary classifier outputs the probability sigma(z) from a logit z, where sigma is the logistic function. Temperature scaling replaces it with sigma(z / T), where T > 0 is a single number fitted on held-out data. For one case with z = 3, sigma(3) is about 0.953. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A value of T fitted on validation data from last year restores calibration after the population the model sees changes.
statements.explanation: A single parameter fitted to one distribution does not track later changes in the population, and calibration can go stale silently.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With T = 2, that case's probability becomes about 0.82.
statements.explanation: sigma(3 / 2) = sigma(1.5), which is about 0.818.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Dividing by a positive T changes which cases receive a probability above 0.5.
statements.explanation: Dividing a logit by a positive number never changes its sign, so cases above 0.5 stay above 0.5 and predicted classes are unchanged.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Temperature scaling can repair a classifier whose ranking of cases is poor.
statements.explanation: Temperature scaling changes only the stated confidence, not the ordering of cases, so it cannot improve ranking.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because dividing the logit by T preserves the ordering of cases, the classifier's AUC is unchanged by any T > 0.
statements.explanation: sigma(z / T) is a strictly increasing function of z, and AUC depends only on the ordering of scores.

questions.source: Synthesis — four questions that prevent most deployment disasters
questions.stem: A clinic can follow up a flagged patient at a cost of $20. A positive case that is missed costs $400. A model gives each patient a probability of being positive. For statements A, B, D and E, assume the probabilities are calibrated (statement C considers miscalibrated probabilities). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A 0.5 cutoff minimizes expected cost, as it minimizes the number of classification errors.
statements.explanation: Minimizing error count weights both mistakes equally, but here a miss costs twenty times as much as a follow-up.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Following up whenever the probability exceeds about 0.048 minimizes expected cost.
statements.explanation: Following up costs $20 and not following up costs 400p in expectation, so follow up when 400p > 20, that is p > 20 / 420, about 0.048.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the model's probabilities are miscalibrated, the cutoff of about 0.048 still minimizes expected cost, because the cutoff depends only on the cost ratio.
statements.explanation: The cutoff is valid only if the stated probabilities equal the true frequencies; otherwise the wrong patients cross the cutoff.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A patient with a calibrated probability of 0.10 should be followed up even though most such patients are negative.
statements.explanation: At p = 0.10 the expected cost of not following up is $40, which exceeds the $20 follow-up cost.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the cost of a missed case fell to $100, the cost-minimizing cutoff would rise.
statements.explanation: The cutoff is the follow-up cost divided by the total of both costs, 20 / 120 = 0.167, which is higher than 0.048.

questions.stem: A language model answers 800 factual questions and appends a stated confidence to each answer. On the 400 answers where it wrote 95%, 288 were correct. On the 400 answers where it wrote 70%, 232 were correct. Correctness was judged against verified references. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 95% group is more accurate than the 70% group, so the stated numbers still carry some information about which answers are more likely to be right.
statements.explanation: Accuracy of 72% against 58% on 400 answers each is a difference far larger than sampling noise, so the ordering of the stated values is informative even though their levels are wrong.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Verbalized confidences cannot be corrected using held-out labeled data, so they must be discarded rather than recalibrated.
statements.explanation: Stated confidences can be treated as a score and mapped to observed accuracy using labeled held-out data, then validated on fresh data.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Among answers stated at 95%, the observed accuracy is 72%, so the stated confidence overstates reliability by about 23 points.
statements.explanation: 288 / 400 = 0.72 against a stated 0.95, a gap of 23 points.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A precise stated figure such as 95% shows that the model computed a 95% probability internally before writing it.
statements.explanation: A generated number is text produced by the model and does not by itself show that a probability of that size was computed or that it matches any frequency.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because the model writes the number in fluent text, the stated confidences can be treated as calibrated probabilities.
statements.explanation: Fluency is not evidence of calibration; the observed accuracies of 72% and 58% are well below the stated 95% and 70%.

questions.stem: A team wants to check whether the confidence scores emitted by a deployed classifier can be read as probabilities. Check each statement that is true about a sound way to check.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Collect labeled outcomes from data that resemble the population the classifier will serve, not only from the training distribution.
statements.explanation: Calibration is a property of a model on a population, so it must be measured on data that resemble where the scores will be used.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Report the number of cases in each confidence bin alongside the observed rate, since sparse bins give noisy estimates.
statements.explanation: Counts reveal which bins can support a conclusion; a bin with a handful of cases can show a large gap by chance.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Repeat the check separately for subgroups and for different time periods, because an aggregate can hide offsetting errors and calibration can drift.
statements.explanation: Pooled data can look calibrated while subgroups are not, and a model calibrated at one time can degrade as inputs or base rates change.

statements.label: D
statements.text: After fitting a recalibration map, judge the recalibrated model on the same labeled data used to fit it, which gives an honest estimate of calibration.
statements.explanation: Evaluating on the fitting data overstates quality because the map was tuned to it; a separate held-out set is needed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Use a proper score such as the Brier score or log loss as a complement to binned plots, since it does not depend on the choice of bins.
statements.explanation: Brier score and log loss use every prediction without binning, so they avoid the arbitrariness of bin choice.

questions.source: From Boolean to probabilistic — and why the move is harder than it looks
questions.stem: A loan dashboard shows each decision with a model score such as "87.3% likely to repay." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reporting 87.3% rather than 87% shows that the estimate is accurate to a tenth of a point or better.
statements.explanation: The number of digits displayed is a formatting choice; the real uncertainty, from sampling and from model error, is far larger than the last digit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A high AUC ensures that a score of 87.3% corresponds to an 87.3% repayment rate among loans given that score.
statements.explanation: AUC measures ranking, and a model can rank well while its stated levels are systematically too high or too low.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A score calibrated on last year's loans will still be calibrated after the share of loans that repay changes substantially.
statements.explanation: A change in the base rate or in the inputs moves the relationship between score and outcome, so old calibration can fail.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the model outputs a number labeled as a probability, 87.3% of loans given this score will repay.
statements.explanation: A label on an output does not make it a calibrated probability; the match between score and frequency must be shown with outcome data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: What gives "87%" its meaning is the observed repayment rate among past loans with similar scores, measured on data resembling the deployment population.
statements.explanation: Calibration is established by comparing stated scores with realized frequencies on comparable data.

questions.source: Hume's induction problem, re-translated as distribution shift
questions.stem: A classifier was validated and found calibrated on data from 2024. In 2026 the user population has changed in ways nobody documented. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The classifier's confidence scores can look unchanged while real-world accuracy falls.
statements.explanation: A model computes confidence from its inputs under the assumptions it learned, so scores can stay high and fluent while the world has moved.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A calibration curve measured on 2024 data guarantees calibration on 2026 data, provided the model weights are unchanged.
statements.explanation: A calibration curve describes the population it was measured on; nothing guarantees the same relationship in a different population.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Comparing stated probabilities with realized outcomes, once labels arrive, is the most direct way to detect that calibration has decayed.
statements.explanation: Outcomes are the quantity the probabilities claim to predict, so comparing the two measures calibration directly.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Monitoring only inputs can detect some harmful shifts without labels but cannot reveal a change in the input-outcome relationship when the inputs look the same.
statements.explanation: Input monitoring needs no labels but sees only what the inputs look like, so a shift in the outcome relationship at fixed inputs passes undetected.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If overall accuracy is unchanged, calibration must also be unchanged, since both measure agreement with outcomes.
statements.explanation: Accuracy can stay constant while stated confidence rises or falls relative to it, so a shift in calibration does not require a shift in accuracy.

questions.source: When the Central Limit Theorem politely declines to help
questions.stem: A deployed model's mistakes have this cost distribution: 99.9% of mistakes cost $1 and 0.1% cost $5,000, independently of each other. An audit samples 500 mistakes at random. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The expected cost per mistake is about $6.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The median cost per mistake, $1, is an adequate summary of the risk this model poses to the organization.
statements.explanation: The median ignores the rare $5,000 losses that make up most of the expected cost.

statements.label: C
statements.text: There is about a 61% chance that the 500 sampled mistakes contain no $5,000 mistake.
statements.explanation: 0.999 raised to the 500th power is about 0.606.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In audits with no $5,000 mistake, the sample average is $1 and a standard-error interval computed from the sample has zero width and excludes the true mean.
statements.explanation: When every sampled cost is $1 the sample standard deviation is zero, so a normal-approximation interval collapses to $1 and misses the true mean of about $6.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reporting the frequency and size of the largest losses is needed in addition to the mean.
statements.explanation: With a rare, severe tail, a mean or median alone hides the exposure; tail frequency and size must be reported.

questions.source: When the Central Limit Theorem politely declines to help
questions.stem: Independent draws X1, ..., Xn come from a standard Cauchy distribution, whose tails are so heavy that its mean is undefined and its variance is infinite. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For any independent and identically distributed data, quadrupling the sample size halves the standard error of the mean.
statements.explanation: The standard error formula sigma / sqrt(n) requires a finite variance; for heavy-tailed data with infinite variance it does not apply.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Averaging more draws concentrates the sample mean ever more tightly around 0, the center of symmetry, as it does for normal data.
statements.explanation: The sample mean of Cauchy draws does not settle down as n grows; a single extreme draw can move it a long way.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The average of n such draws has the same distribution as a single draw, for every n.
statements.explanation: The Cauchy distribution is stable under averaging, so the mean of n independent standard Cauchy draws is again standard Cauchy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The usual central limit theorem for the sample mean requires, among other conditions, finite variance.
statements.explanation: The classical theorem assumes independent observations with finite variance; with infinite variance the normalized mean does not approach a normal distribution.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If observations are strongly positively correlated, sigma / sqrt(n) understates the sampling variability of the mean even when the variance is finite.
statements.explanation: Positive correlation makes the observations carry less independent information than n independent ones, so the true variance of the mean is larger than sigma squared over n.

questions.source: Reconstructing the epistemic frame — a working procedure
questions.stem: An analyst receives an export of every insurance claim paid to one hospital system between 2018 and 2023: about 6 million rows, with no blank diagnosis codes. She plans to use it to estimate how common a chronic condition is among adults who live in the surrounding city. Reconstructing the frame behind a dataset means establishing who collected it, for what purpose, who is in and out, and how each variable was measured. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because the data are administrative rather than survey data, they involve no measurement choices, so field names can be taken at face value without any coding documentation.
statements.explanation: Administrative fields are defined by coding rules and reimbursement incentives, and those choices must be documented to interpret them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Residents who are uninsured, use other hospital systems or never seek care are outside the data, so the estimate may be biased for the city.
statements.explanation: A prevalence estimate is only as good as the match between the people recorded and the population the claim is about.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With about 6 million rows, sampling error is negligible, so the prevalence estimate is reliable for the city's adults even though only one system's claims are included.
statements.explanation: Size shrinks random error but not the systematic gap between one system's insured patients and the city's adults.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The export exists to pay claims, so who appears and which fields exist follow billing rules, not a design for measuring the city's health.
statements.explanation: Administrative data inherit the purpose of the system that produced them, and that purpose decides who is recorded and what is captured.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A diagnosis code records what was billed, which can differ from a clinical determination, so how it was measured must be established before it is treated as the condition.
statements.explanation: A code is a measurement produced by billing practice; it is a proxy for the condition, not the condition itself.

questions.source: Reconstructing the epistemic frame — a working procedure
questions.stem: A team inner-joins 100,000 support tickets to a customer table on customer_id to build a modeling table, and the result has 96,000 rows. Tickets from one region (Region N, 10,000 tickets) carry customer IDs with a legacy prefix in the customer table, so 3,200 of them find no match; in the other regions, 800 of 90,000 tickets find no match for unrelated reasons. A missing-value report on the joined table shows 0.0% missing in every column. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because only 4% of rows were lost, a model trained on the table can be expected to perform about equally well in every region.
statements.explanation: Region N falls from 10% of the data to about 7.1%, and its remaining rows may differ from its lost ones, so performance there can be worse.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The zero-missing report shows that the join lost no rows, because dropped rows would appear as blank cells.
statements.explanation: Dropped rows are absent, not blank, so a cell-level report has nothing to flag.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Region N lost 32% of its tickets against about 0.9% elsewhere, so the overall 4% figure hides a concentrated loss.
statements.explanation: 3,200 of 10,000 is 32%, while 800 of 90,000 is about 0.9%; an aggregate rate can mask a severe subgroup rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Comparing 100,000 input rows with 96,000 output rows exposes a 4.0% loss that the missing-value report cannot see.
statements.explanation: Rows removed by an inner join leave no blank cell behind, so only a before-and-after row count reveals them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Region N accounts for about 10% of the dropped rows, matching its 10% share of the input tickets.
statements.explanation: Region N accounts for 3,200 of the 4,000 dropped tickets, which is 80%, far above its 10% share of the input.

questions.source: Reconstructing the epistemic frame — a working procedure
questions.stem: An orders table has six rows, one per order, with customer_id values a, a, b, c, d, d. A customers table has four rows with customer_id values a, b, b, e; the key b appears twice because of a data-entry duplicate. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A full outer join returns 7 rows, the same as the left join, because the customers table contributes no unmatched keys.
statements.explanation: Customer key e matches no order, so a full outer join adds that row and returns 8.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Asserting that customer_id is unique in the customers table before joining would have flagged the problem.
statements.explanation: A uniqueness check on the key catches the duplicate b before it silently inflates the output.

statements.label: C
