statements.text: An inner join on customer_id returns 4 rows: two for order key a and two for order key b.
statements.explanation: Order key a matches one customer row twice (2 rows) and order key b matches two customer rows (2 rows); c and d match nothing.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A left join returns 7 rows, one more than the orders table, because the order for b matches two customer rows.
statements.explanation: Duplicate keys on the right side multiply the matching left rows, so a left join can return more rows than the left table has.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A left join from orders to customers returns 6 rows, one per order, because the left table is preserved.
statements.explanation: The join returns 7 rows: the single order for b matches two customer rows, so it is repeated.

questions.source: The procedural EDA pass — what it sees, and what it structurally cannot
questions.stem: A satisfaction survey appears as a pop-up inside a mobile app after a user completes a purchase, and it cannot be submitted unless every question is answered. The resulting file has 12,000 responses and no empty cells. The company wants to report the satisfaction of 'all customers', a group that also includes web-only customers and people who abandoned a purchase partway. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Customers who abandoned a purchase may differ in satisfaction from completers, so the average can be biased even with 12,000 responses.
statements.explanation: If inclusion is related to the outcome, a large sample reproduces the same systematic error precisely.

statements.label: B
statements.text: No empty cells means the recorded responses are complete; it says nothing about customers who never saw or never submitted the form.
statements.explanation: Completeness of recorded rows is a different property from coverage of the population the rows are supposed to represent.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because every question is mandatory, the respondents must be representative of all customers, since nobody can skip an answer and distort the results.
statements.explanation: Mandatory fields control what each respondent answers, not who is asked or who submits.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A missing-value check on this file would flag the web-only customers as missing, since they appear nowhere in it.
statements.explanation: People who were never recorded are not rows with blanks, so no cell-level check can detect them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Collecting another 12,000 responses through the same pop-up would push the bias toward zero, since a larger sample is closer to the whole customer base.
statements.explanation: More draws from the same selection process reduce random error but leave the systematic bias in place.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.stem: A city has 100,000 adults: 30,000 under 30 and 70,000 aged 30 or older. Under-30s use a transit app 10 hours a month on average and the others 2 hours, so the city-wide mean is 4.4 hours. A researcher draws 1,000 people at random from a phone directory (the sampling frame) that lists 20% of the under-30s and 80% of the older adults, and everyone sampled responds. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Under-30s are about 9.7% of the directory but 30% of adults, so the expected sample mean is about 2.8 hours, below the true 4.4.
statements.explanation: The frame holds 6,000 under-30s and 56,000 older adults, giving an expected mean of (6,000 x 10 + 56,000 x 2) / 62,000, about 2.77.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reweighting respondents so that under-30s count for 30% of the estimate would remove the bias whatever the unlisted people in each age group are like.
statements.explanation: Weighting corrects the age mix only if listed and unlisted people within each age group have the same average usage, which is an assumption.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The undercoverage matters only if the directory lists fewer than half of all adults, since otherwise the majority is represented.
statements.explanation: Coverage of 62% overall still biases the estimate because coverage differs across groups whose outcomes differ.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Enlarging the sample from 1,000 to 20,000 people drawn from the same directory would shrink the gap toward zero, since sampling error falls with sample size.
statements.explanation: A larger sample from the same frame converges to the frame's mean of about 2.8, not to 4.4.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because the 1,000 people are drawn at random, the sample mean is an unbiased estimate of the city-wide mean, whatever the directory covers.
statements.explanation: Random selection within a frame is unbiased only for the frame's population, which here differs from the city's.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.stem: A database lists the annualized returns of investment funds that are still operating today. Ten years ago 1,000 funds were launched. Of these, 600 survive and averaged an 8% annual return over the decade; 400 have closed, and they averaged -2% over the years they existed. The database contains only the survivors. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In a hypothetical in which the same funds had instead closed at random, for reasons unrelated to their returns, the survivors would still be expected to average well above the average over all 1,000 funds.
statements.explanation: If closure were independent of returns, the survivors would be a random subset of the funds and their expected average would match the all-fund average, so the gap arises only because closure is related to returns.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reporting the median instead of the mean of the survivors would remove the bias.
statements.explanation: The median of the survivors is still computed on a filtered group and still excludes the poor performers.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The average over all 1,000 funds was 4%, so the survivor-only average of 8% overstates it by 4 percentage points.
statements.explanation: (600 x 8 + 400 x -2) / 1,000 = 4, so excluding the closed funds raises the average.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A missing-value check on the survivor file would reveal the 400 closed funds as blank rows.
statements.explanation: Closed funds are absent from the file, not present with blanks.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The closures are related to the returns being studied, so the absent funds are not a random subset of all funds.
statements.explanation: Selection that depends on the outcome produces bias that the surviving rows alone cannot show.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.stem: In a city of 100,000 people, disease A affects 10% and disease B affects 10%, independently of each other. A hospital admits every person who has A or B (or both) and 5% of people who have neither; assume it sees nobody else. An analyst uses the hospital's 23,050 admission records to study how A and B are related. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Adjusting for age and sex in a regression on the admission records would restore the population relationship between A and B.
statements.explanation: The selection depends on A and B themselves, so adjusting for unrelated covariates does not undo conditioning on admission.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The negative association in the admission records comes from how patients enter the dataset, not from a biological link between A and B.
statements.explanation: Admission depends on having either disease, so among admitted patients, not having one disease makes the other more likely.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Analyzing ten years of admission records instead of one year would remove the artifact, since the extra records average out the distortion.
statements.explanation: More records collected through the same admission rule reproduce the same distortion.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In the full city population, patients with A are less likely to have B than patients without A, so the two diseases compete with each other.
statements.explanation: The diseases are independent in the population, so the chance of B is 10% whether or not a person has A.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Among admitted patients, about 10% of those with A also have B, compared with about 69% of those without A.
statements.explanation: Admitted with A: 10,000, of whom 1,000 have B. Admitted without A: 9,000 with B plus 4,050 with neither, so 9,000 / 13,050 is about 69%.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.stem: A lender approved 40,000 of 100,000 past applicants using a fixed rule on a legacy score. Repayment outcomes exist only for approved applicants, and 6% of them defaulted. The lender will train a new model on the 40,000 approved loans and use it to score all future applicants, including those the legacy rule would have rejected. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The missing outcomes for rejected applicants are missing completely at random, because a fixed rule rejected them.
statements.explanation: Missingness is determined by the legacy score, which is related to risk, so it is not independent of the data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The training data have no outcomes in the score range the old rule rejected, so predictions there are extrapolation.
statements.explanation: A model cannot be checked against data it never saw; behavior outside the observed range is an assumption.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The 6% default rate describes approved applicants, not all 100,000 applicants.
statements.explanation: Approval was based on a score related to risk, so the approved group is not a random sample of applicants.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Accuracy measured on the 40,000 approved loans is an unbiased estimate of accuracy on all applicants.
statements.explanation: Evaluation on a selected subset reflects that subset only; the rejected region is untested.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Approving a small random share of applicants below the old cutoff would yield outcomes in that range, at a cost to the lender.
statements.explanation: Randomized exploration is the standard way to obtain unbiased labels where a decision rule would otherwise hide them.

questions.source: The procedural EDA pass — what it sees, and what it structurally cannot
questions.stem: A dataset has blank values in several columns. The standard missingness mechanisms are MCAR (missing completely at random), MAR (missing at random, given the observed data) and MNAR (missing not at random). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If younger respondents skip an income question more often and, within each age group, skipping is unrelated to income, the missingness is MNAR because it is related to age.
statements.explanation: Dependence on an observed variable such as age, with nothing further tied to the unobserved value, is MAR; MNAR requires dependence on the unobserved value itself.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Readings lost because a sensor's battery fails at random moments, unrelated to the quantity being measured, are an example of MCAR.
statements.explanation: When the chance of a value being missing is independent of both observed and unobserved data, the mechanism is MCAR.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Statistical tests on the observed data alone can confirm that missingness is MAR rather than MNAR, as long as the sample is large enough.
statements.explanation: MAR and MNAR differ in how missingness depends on unobserved values, and the observed data cannot reveal that dependence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Patients who skip a final visit because the condition measured there has become severe, leaving that measurement blank, are an example of MNAR.
statements.explanation: The reason the value is missing is the value itself, which is the defining feature of MNAR.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If high earners skip an income question because of how much they earn, the missingness is MAR, since income is related to the other columns.
statements.explanation: Missingness driven by the unobserved value itself is MNAR, whatever other columns correlate with income.

questions.source: The procedural EDA pass — what it sees, and what it structurally cannot
questions.stem: A survey of 1,000 people asks for annual income. In the population, 600 people earn 40 (thousand) and 400 earn 100, so the true mean is 64. Each low earner skips the question with probability 0.10 and each high earner with probability 0.50. Averaged over many repetitions, 740 people answer. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: About 26% of income values are expected to be missing.
statements.explanation: Expected skips are 60 + 200 = 260 of 1,000.

statements.label: B
statements.text: High earners are expected to make up about 27% of the answers, against 40% of the population.
statements.explanation: 200 of 740 answers come from high earners, which is about 27%, so they are under-represented among respondents.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The expected mean of the answers is about 56.2, below the true 64.
statements.explanation: Expected answers are 540 low earners and 200 high earners: (540 x 40 + 200 x 100) / 740 is about 56.2.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Filling each blank with the mean of the answers gives an expected overall mean near 64.
statements.explanation: Filling with the answers' own mean leaves the overall mean at about 56.2.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If skipping depended only on an observed column such as job title and not on income itself, analyzing within job-title groups could remove much of the bias.
statements.explanation: Missingness that depends only on observed variables is MAR, and conditioning on those variables can correct it.

questions.stem: A numeric column has 10 rows. Six are observed (30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 100) and four are missing. An analyst fills the four blanks with the observed mean and then computes statistics on all 10 rows. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A standard error computed on the filled column treats ten values as real observations and is therefore too small.
statements.explanation: Only six values carry information; the filled values add no new information but increase the apparent sample size.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The mean of the column stays at 50, because the filled values equal the mean of the observed ones.
statements.explanation: Adding four copies of the mean leaves the sum divided by the count unchanged.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Mean imputation leaves the correlation between this column and other columns unchanged, since the mean is a neutral value.
statements.explanation: Filled rows sit at the mean of this column regardless of the other columns, which pulls correlations toward zero.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Filling the four blanks with the observed median (42.5) instead would also leave the mean at 50.
statements.explanation: Filling with 42.5 gives a mean of 47.0, because the median differs from the mean in a skewed column.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The sample standard deviation falls from about 25.5 to about 19.0, even though no real data were added.
statements.explanation: The sum of squared deviations stays 3,250 while the divisor grows from 5 to 9, so the variance drops from 650 to about 361.

questions.stem: An analyst must decide how to handle blanks in a numeric column. Assume she knows the mechanism that produced them. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the blanks are MCAR, dropping every row with a blank leaves the estimated mean unbiased, though it uses fewer rows and widens the interval.
statements.explanation: Under MCAR the complete rows are a random subset of all rows, so deletion costs precision but not accuracy.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For a categorical column, filling blanks with the column mean is a standard choice.
statements.explanation: A mean of categories is meaningless; the most frequent class or a model-based imputation is used instead.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Multiple imputation creates several completed datasets and pools the results, so the final uncertainty reflects the imputation.
statements.explanation: Variation across the completed datasets is combined with within-dataset variance to avoid overstating precision.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the largest values are the ones that go missing because they are large, dropping those rows leaves the mean unbiased, since the remaining values are real measurements.
statements.explanation: The remaining rows are a truncated subset of the distribution, so their mean is systematically too low.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If blanks depend on an observed column (MAR), imputing from that column, for example within groups, can reduce the bias that dropping rows would introduce.
statements.explanation: Conditioning on the variable that drives missingness lets the imputation model reflect the missing rows' likely values.

questions.source: The procedural EDA pass — what it sees, and what it structurally cannot
questions.stem: A patient table stores age as an integer and uses -999 for 'unknown'. Eight rows have ages 34, 41, 29, -999, 52, 47, -999, 38. A type check confirms the column is entirely integer, and no range check was written. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A summary table showing a minimum of -999 for an age column would reveal the sentinel.
statements.explanation: An impossible minimum for an age column is a standard sign of a placeholder value.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Replacing -999 with 0 gives a mean that is a defensible estimate of the patients' average age.
statements.explanation: Zero is itself an invalid age here and pulls the mean down to about 30.1, which is not the average of any real ages.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The mean computed over all eight values, sentinels included, is about -219.6.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Excluding the two sentinel rows gives a mean of about 40.2 for the six recorded ages.
statements.explanation: The six recorded ages sum to 241, and 241 / 6 is about 40.2.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The mean of 40.2 is guaranteed to equal the average age of all eight patients.
statements.explanation: The two unknown ages could be anything, and whether they are like the recorded ones depends on why they are unknown.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.stem: A pipeline validates a merged patient table against a schema: age is an integer from 0 to 120, weight is a number from 20 to 400, and admission_date and discharge_date are dates. Every row passes. Hospital X records weight in kilograms and hospital Y in pounds, and the table has no unit column. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because every value lies inside 20 to 400, the question of whether the weights are comparable is settled.
statements.explanation: A range check tests plausibility of individual values, not consistency of units across sources.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A discharge date earlier than the admission date can pass a date-type check, yet a cross-field rule would flag it.
statements.explanation: Type validity concerns each value alone; relationships between fields need their own rules.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Both hospitals' weights can satisfy the declared range while differing systematically by a factor of about 2.2.
statements.explanation: One kilogram is about 2.2 pounds, and ordinary adult weights fit inside 20 to 400 in either unit.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding an explicit unit column and validating its values against a list of allowed units would make the mismatch visible.
statements.explanation: Recording and checking the unit turns an implicit assumption into a testable field.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Comparing the weight distribution by hospital would likely expose the unit mismatch.
statements.explanation: A group-wise check shows one source shifted by a constant factor even when the pooled distribution looks plausible.

questions.source: Reconstructing the epistemic frame — a working procedure
questions.stem: A table has 5,000 rows. In the age column, 400 values are missing (NaN), 50 are 0 or negative, and 4,550 are positive. An analyst writes df[df['age'] > 0], intending to remove only the 50 invalid ages. In pandas, comparing NaN with a number using >, <, <= or == gives False, and using != gives True. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 400 rows with missing age are removed silently, with no error or warning.
statements.explanation: The comparison is valid Python and pandas code, so nothing signals that rows with missing values were dropped.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The filter returns 4,550 rows, not the 4,950 the analyst intended to keep.
statements.explanation: NaN > 0 is False, so the 400 missing-age rows are removed along with the 50 invalid ones.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Writing df[df['age'] != 0] instead would also remove the 400 rows with missing age, because NaN fails the comparison.
statements.explanation: NaN != 0 evaluates to True, so those rows would be kept (and the negative ages would also be kept).

statements.label: D
statements.text: Printing the row count before and after the step would have shown 5,000 becoming 4,550 and prompted the question of why 450 rows vanished, not 50.
statements.explanation: A count mismatch against the expected result is the cheapest check for a silent drop.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the missing ages are concentrated in one customer segment, the filter removes that segment's rows disproportionately.
statements.explanation: Dropping on a column that is missing for one segment shifts the segment mix of the table.

questions.source: Reconstructing the epistemic frame — a working procedure
questions.stem: A table has one row per hospital visit: 6,000 rows from 2,000 patients, with a patient_id column and a visit_id column that is unique per visit. To 'remove duplicates', an analyst keeps the first visit for each patient_id, leaving 2,000 rows. Each visit row carries its own label, 'readmitted within 30 days'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Deduplicating on patient_id is correct because a patient is the same person at every visit, so later visits carry no information.
statements.explanation: Later visits carry new events and outcomes; sameness of the person does not make the visits redundant.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Keeping only each patient's first visit is guaranteed to leave the readmission rate unchanged.
statements.explanation: First visits and later visits can have different readmission rates, so the rate generally changes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Rows that repeat the same patient_id and visit_id are the true duplicates to remove.
statements.explanation: A duplicate is a repeated record of one event, which the combination of both identifiers captures.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The step removes 4,000 rows that are distinct visits, not repeated copies of the same record.
statements.explanation: Rows with the same patient_id but different visit_id describe different events.

statements.label: E
statements.text: After the step every patient counts once, whereas before patients with more visits counted more, so the table describes a different population of rows.
statements.explanation: Deduplicating on an entity key changes the unit of analysis and the weighting of frequent users.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.stem: Two annotators independently label 200 items as 'toxic' or 'not toxic'. Both say toxic on 70 items, only the first says toxic on 20, only the second says toxic on 10, and both say not toxic on 100. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Observed agreement between the two annotators is 85%, since they agree on 170 of 200 items.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The 30 disagreements prove the labeling guideline is flawed, since nothing else could explain them.
statements.explanation: Disagreement can also come from ambiguous items, annotator error or legitimate differences in judgment.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Kappa is higher than observed agreement because it adds credit for agreement expected by chance.
statements.explanation: Kappa subtracts chance agreement, so it is lower than raw agreement here (0.69 versus 0.85).

statements.label: D
statements.text: Cohen's kappa is about 0.69, noticeably lower than the raw agreement of 85%.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Expected chance agreement is 50%, because with two labels any two annotators agree half the time.
statements.explanation: Chance agreement depends on each annotator's rate of using each label; here 45% and 40% toxic give 0.45 x 0.40 + 0.55 x 0.60 = 51%.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.stem: A binary classifier has true accuracy 92% on a population. The test labels come from an annotator who flips the correct label on a random 10% of items, independently of what the classifier does. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Suppose the annotator's flips, contrary to the independence stated above, fell mostly on items the model gets wrong; measured accuracy could then exceed the true accuracy.
statements.explanation: Correlated errors make the model agree with wrong labels; if all 8% of the model's errors were flipped and the other 2% of flips hit correct items, measured accuracy would be 0.92 - 0.02 + 0.08 = 98%.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Measured accuracy is higher than true accuracy because the noisy labels add extra correct matches.
statements.explanation: With accuracy above 50% and independent symmetric noise, measured accuracy is lower than the true value.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A second model with true accuracy 93% would show an expected measured advantage of about 0.8 points over the first, not 1 point.
statements.explanation: Measured accuracy is 84.4% versus 83.6%; independent symmetric noise scales true differences by 1 - 2 x 0.10 = 0.8.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The same true difference between two models is harder to detect with noisy labels than with clean labels.
statements.explanation: The measured gap shrinks while sampling variability does not, so the signal-to-noise ratio falls.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The expected accuracy measured against the noisy labels is 83.6%.
statements.explanation: 0.92 x 0.90 + 0.08 x 0.10 = 0.836: correct predictions are marked wrong when the label is flipped, and wrong ones are marked right.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.stem: A model predicts whether a subscriber will cancel within the next 30 days. Features include tenure, plan type, recent logins and cancellation_survey_sent, a flag set by an automated email that goes out at the moment a subscriber cancels. The model scores 0.99 AUC on a random hold-out. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A feature that is strongly associated with the label and has no missing values is safe to keep, since it clearly carries predictive information.
statements.explanation: Strong association and completeness say nothing about whether the feature exists at prediction time.

statements.label: B
statements.text: cancellation_survey_sent is produced by the outcome being predicted, so it is not available when the prediction is needed.
statements.explanation: A feature set after the event cannot be known at prediction time; using it is target leakage.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Removing the flag and re-evaluating is a reasonable check; a large drop would be consistent with the earlier score coming from leakage.
statements.explanation: An ablation isolates how much of the performance depended on the suspect feature; a large drop is consistent with leakage, though a legitimately strong predictor would also cause one, so the timing of the flag is what establishes the leak.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The 0.99 AUC on a random hold-out shows the model will perform about as well on live subscribers.
statements.explanation: The hold-out contains the same leaked flag, so the score measures the leak rather than predictive skill.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A random hold-out split would have detected the leak, because leaked rows would be kept apart from the training rows.
statements.explanation: A random split puts the leaked flag in both partitions, so it cannot reveal a leak.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.stem: A chest-X-ray model is trained on 20,000 images from 5,000 patients, four images per patient. The images are split at random by image: 16,000 for training and 4,000 for testing. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Splitting by patient, so that all four images of a patient fall on the same side, prevents this overlap.
statements.explanation: A group-level split keeps each entity entirely in training or entirely in testing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: About 99% of test images are expected to have at least one training image from the same patient.
statements.explanation: The chance that all three other images of a patient land in the test set is about 0.2^3 = 0.8%, so 99.2% have a training sibling.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the 4,000 test images were also used repeatedly to choose hyperparameters, the final test score would remain an unbiased estimate.
statements.explanation: Repeated selection on the test set fits the choices to it, so the final score is optimistic.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The resulting test accuracy likely overstates performance on patients the model has never seen.
statements.explanation: Images of the same patient share anatomy and acquisition traits that a model can recognize, which is not generalization to new patients.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because test images are never used to update the model's weights, the test set cannot be contaminated.
statements.explanation: Contamination also arises when near-identical or same-entity data sit in training, whatever happens to the weights.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.stem: A text dataset has 10,000 rows. Exactly 800 distinct records each appear twice as byte-identical rows, and the other 8,400 rows appear once. A random 80/20 split by row puts 8,000 rows in training and 2,000 in testing. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Removing exact duplicates before splitting prevents this particular overlap between training and test rows.
statements.explanation: With one copy of each record, no record can appear on both sides.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Exact-match deduplication also removes texts that differ only by trailing whitespace or capitalization.
statements.explanation: Byte-exact comparison treats such texts as different, so near-duplicates need normalization or similarity matching.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Train-test duplicates inflate scores only for neural networks; a nearest-neighbor classifier is unaffected.
statements.explanation: A nearest-neighbor model finds the identical training row and copies its label, so it benefits from leakage at least as much.

statements.label: D
statements.text: About 256 duplicate pairs are expected to straddle the split, so roughly 13% of test rows have an exact copy in the training set.
statements.explanation: Each pair straddles with probability about 2 x 0.8 x 0.2 = 0.32, giving 800 x 0.32 = 256 pairs and 256 / 2,000 = 12.8% of test rows.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The dataset contains 9,200 distinct records, since 800 of them are each counted twice in the 10,000 rows.
statements.explanation: 8,400 records appear once and 800 appear twice, so 8,400 + 800 = 9,200.

questions.source: The procedural EDA pass — what it sees, and what it structurally cannot
questions.stem: A screening dataset has 10,000 cases, of which 200 (2%) are positive. A classifier has recall 80% and a false-positive rate of 5%. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because the classifier's accuracy exceeds 90%, accuracy is an adequate summary of its usefulness here.
statements.explanation: Accuracy is dominated by the majority class; recall, precision and the baseline are needed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A test set rebuilt to be 50% positive gives the best estimate of the precision the classifier will have at 2% prevalence.
statements.explanation: Precision depends on prevalence; on a 50% positive set it would be about 94%, far above the deployment value.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The classifier's precision is about 80%, equal to its recall.
statements.explanation: It flags 160 true positives plus 490 false positives, so precision is 160 / 650, about 25%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A rule that predicts 'negative' for every case has accuracy 98%, higher than this classifier's.
statements.explanation: 9,800 of 10,000 cases are negative, so the trivial rule beats 94.7% while detecting nothing.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The classifier's accuracy is 94.7%, with 9,470 of the 10,000 cases classified correctly.
statements.explanation: True positives 160 and true negatives 9,310 give 9,470 correct out of 10,000.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.stem: A health system builds a model to choose patients for a care-management program, using next-year healthcare spending as the training label. Two groups, A and B, each have 10,000 patients, and 1,000 in each group have the highest illness burden. Group B faces access barriers, so at a given illness burden its patients generate less spending. The program enrolls the 2,000 patients with the highest predicted spending: 1,400 from A and 600 from B. Among the 1,000 highest-illness patients in each group, 870 in A and 520 in B are enrolled. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: 87% of Group A's highest-illness patients are enrolled, against 52% of Group B's.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A larger share of enrolled B patients (about 87%) than of enrolled A patients (about 62%) are among the highest-illness, consistent with B needing to be sicker to reach the same predicted spending.
statements.explanation: 520 / 600 = 86.7% and 870 / 1,400 = 62.1%; a group whose spending understates need must be sicker to clear the same threshold.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The model can predict spending accurately and still enroll fewer of Group B's sickest patients, because spending only proxies illness burden.
statements.explanation: Accuracy on the label does not establish that the label tracks the construct, especially when the gap differs by group.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Removing the group indicator from the features guarantees equal enrollment of equally ill patients from both groups.
statements.explanation: The bias sits in the label, which is also correlated with other features, so dropping the indicator does not remove it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A high R-squared for predicting spending shows that spending is a valid measure of illness burden for both groups.
statements.explanation: Predictive fit to the label says nothing about whether the label measures the intended construct equally for each group.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.stem: A model is trained on data from 2019 to 2021 and run in 2024. A numeric feature is split into four bins. The share of training rows in the bins is 25%, 35%, 25% and 15%; the share of 2024 rows is 15%, 30%, 30% and 25%. The population stability index, PSI = sum over bins of (live share - train share) x ln(live share / train share), is about 0.119. Common rules of thumb call PSI below 0.1 stable and 0.1 to 0.25 a moderate shift. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: PSI is zero only when the binned live shares equal the binned training shares.
statements.explanation: Each term (live - train) x ln(live / train) is nonnegative and equals zero only when the two shares are equal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because 0.119 is below 0.25, the model's accuracy in 2024 is guaranteed to match its accuracy on 2019-2021 data.
statements.explanation: PSI summarizes one feature's shift; accuracy also depends on other features and on whether the input-output relationship changed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The 2024 feature distribution differs from the training distribution, and this can be detected without any outcome labels.
statements.explanation: Covariate shift is a statement about inputs, so comparing feature distributions needs no labels.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The 0.1 and 0.25 cut-offs are derived statistical thresholds above which a model's accuracy is certain to fall.
statements.explanation: They are conventions used to prioritize investigation, not guarantees about performance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If every feature's distribution were unchanged, the model's accuracy could not have changed.
statements.explanation: The relationship between inputs and the outcome can change (concept drift) even when the inputs look the same.

questions.source: The procedural EDA pass — what it sees, and what it structurally cannot
questions.stem: A claims dataset covers 60 months and should hold about 10,000 records per month. A count-by-month plot shows about 5,000 records in each of three consecutive months and about 10,000 in every other month. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Counts by source system or site over the same months would help separate a collection outage from a real change in activity.
statements.explanation: An outage affects specific feeds, while a real change in behavior shows across sources.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Duplicating records from adjacent months to fill the gap restores the missing information, because neighboring months have similar patients.
statements.explanation: Copies of other months' rows add no information about the missing months and distort the distribution.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The total shortfall is 2.5% of the expected 600,000 records, so it can be ignored whatever its cause.
statements.explanation: A small total can hide a large loss in a subgroup or period, and the dip may reflect a changed population.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A drop in counts is a finding only if it coincides with a known external event; an unexplained drop is just noise in the series.
statements.explanation: An unexplained drop is itself a finding that needs an explanation, whether or not an event is known.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The plot shows that something changed but not why; an outage, a policy change and a real drop in activity would all produce it.
statements.explanation: A count series reports a finding without identifying its cause.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.stem: Datasheet proposals for datasets ask questions grouped under motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing, uses, distribution and maintenance. A team is deciding how much to rely on a datasheet written by a dataset's creators. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Preprocessing questions record transformations such as filtering, joining or relabeling that the final numbers no longer show.
statements.explanation: Documented processing steps let users see what was done to the data before they received it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A completed datasheet verifies that the dataset is free of sampling and labeling bias, because each answer is checked against the data.
statements.explanation: A datasheet documents claims and choices; it does not test the data for bias.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Maintenance information, such as who updates the data and which version is current, affects whether a result can be reproduced later.
statements.explanation: A result tied to an unversioned, changing dataset cannot be re-derived.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A datasheet from the creators replaces the user's own exploratory checks, because the creators know the data best and wrote down its limits.
statements.explanation: Documentation can be incomplete or out of date, so users still check the data against what it says.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Answers about collection process and intended purpose help a user judge whether the dataset suits a different purpose.
statements.explanation: Fitness for use depends on how and why the data were gathered, and those facts are rarely visible in the table itself.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.stem: A training table has a column risk_score with no blanks and a smooth, plausible histogram. A colleague says it was produced by an earlier team's scoring model, which was trained on data that included part of the period now being used for evaluation. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because the upstream model saw outcomes from the evaluation period, its score as a feature can leak information about the evaluation labels.
statements.explanation: Information about the outcomes flows through the score into the new model's inputs.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Documenting which model version, inputs and training window produced the column is part of recording its provenance.
statements.explanation: Lineage lets a later user judge availability at prediction time and reproduce the column.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the upstream team retrains its model, the column's meaning and distribution can change even though the raw inputs did not.
statements.explanation: A feature defined by a model changes when the model changes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The column is a prediction by another model, not a raw measurement, so it carries that model's assumptions and errors.
statements.explanation: Derived features inherit the choices and mistakes of whatever produced them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The absence of blanks and a plausible histogram establish that the column measures what its name says, so no further documentation is needed.
statements.explanation: Completeness and a plausible shape are properties of the values and say nothing about what produced them.

questions.source: The procedural EDA pass — what it sees, and what it structurally cannot
questions.stem: A sample of 20 values is: 50, 52, 48, 51, 49, 50, 53, 47, 50, 51, 49, 50, 52, 48, 50, 51, 49, 50, 100, 105. Its mean is 55.25, its sample standard deviation is about 16.2, and its quartiles are Q1 = 49 and Q3 = 51.25. The IQR rule flags values below Q1 - 1.5 x IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 x IQR. The z-score rule flags values with |z| above 3. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The z-score rule flags 105 but not 100, because the two extreme values inflate the mean and standard deviation used to compute z.
statements.explanation: z is about 3.06 for 105 and 2.75 for 100; extremes contaminate the very statistics the rule relies on, which masks the smaller one.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In any sample of 10 values, no value can have |z| above 3 when z uses the sample standard deviation, so the rule can never flag anything there.
statements.explanation: The largest possible |z| is (n - 1) / sqrt(n), which is about 2.85 for n = 10.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The IQR rule can decide whether a flagged value is a data-entry error, because it does not depend on the mean.
statements.explanation: Robustness helps detect candidates, but whether a value is an error is a question about how it was recorded.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The IQR rule flags both 100 and 105.
statements.explanation: The fences are about 45.6 and 54.6, and only 100 and 105 fall outside them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A flagged value should be deleted because outliers always represent errors.
statements.explanation: A flagged value may be a legitimate extreme; the decision to remove, cap or keep it needs domain knowledge.

questions.source: The procedural EDA pass — what it sees, and what it structurally cannot
questions.stem: Four datasets of 11 (x, y) points each have the same mean of x (9), the same mean of y (about 7.5), the same variances, the same Pearson correlation (about 0.82) and the same least-squares line y = 3 + 0.5x. In the fourth dataset, ten of the eleven x values equal 8 and one equals 19. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In the fourth dataset the point at x = 19 alone determines the fitted slope; without it, x has no variation and the correlation is undefined.
statements.explanation: The other ten points share x = 8, so only the lone high-x point separates the slope from zero variation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For x = -5, -4, ..., 5 and y = x^2, the Pearson correlation is exactly 0 even though y is a deterministic function of x.
statements.explanation: The relationship is symmetric and nonlinear, so the linear association cancels out.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Identical summary statistics do not imply similar scatter plots; plotting can reveal curvature or influential points that statistics hide.
statements.explanation: Summary numbers discard shape, which is why four very different point clouds can share them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A correlation of about 0.82 in all four datasets indicates that each relationship is roughly a straight line with random scatter around it.
statements.explanation: Pearson correlation summarizes linear association but is produced equally by curved patterns and by one extreme point.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A correlation heatmap of Pearson coefficients is enough to detect nonlinear dependence between columns, since strong dependence always produces a large coefficient.
statements.explanation: A heatmap of Pearson coefficients can show near-zero for strongly dependent but nonlinear pairs.

questions.source: Statistical checks: test the data before you trust it
questions.stem: A table has 10,000 rows. Group B has 500 rows, 200 of which have a blank income; group A has 9,500 rows, 95 of which have a blank income. A quality gate flags any column whose overall missing rate exceeds 5%. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: About 68% of all blank incomes are in group B, which makes up only 5% of the rows.
statements.explanation: 200 of 295 blanks is about 67.8%, concentrated in a group with 500 of 10,000 rows.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Group B's missing rate for income is 40%, against 1% for group A.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Dropping all rows with a blank income is safe, because it removes under 3% of the rows.
statements.explanation: It would remove 40% of group B, changing the group mix and possibly biasing any result about B.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Missingness concentrated in one group is consistent with the values being missing completely at random.
statements.explanation: If the chance of a blank depends on group, which is observed, the mechanism is not MCAR.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The overall missing rate for income is 2.95%, so the 5% gate does not flag the column.
statements.explanation: (200 + 95) / 10,000 = 2.95%, below the 5% threshold.

questions.source: The access assumption — and where the boundary really lives
questions.stem: A support-ticket table has columns ticket_id, category and body. An analytics tool is granted access to all three columns and to nothing else. The body column is free text in which customers sometimes paste phone numbers, partial card numbers and links to documents held in other systems. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the tool can follow links in body, its effective data scope can extend to documents that the access policy never mentioned.
statements.explanation: References inside data turn a bounded table into an entry point to other data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The tool can reveal exactly what the schema lists, so a review of the three columns' types and permissions covers the exposure.
statements.explanation: Free text can carry identifiers and pointers that the schema does not describe.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The same concern applies equally to a table of numeric temperature readings that contains no text or references.
statements.explanation: A self-contained numeric table has little content that points beyond itself; the concern is greatest for reference-rich data.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Column-level permissions do not limit what sensitive information appears inside the text of a column that is permitted.
statements.explanation: Permissions apply to columns as units, not to the content within them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Scanning free text for patterns such as phone numbers, and listing the references it contains, is a check that type-and-permission validation does not provide.
statements.explanation: Content-level inspection finds what structural validation cannot see.

questions.source: Reconstructing the epistemic frame — a working procedure
questions.stem: Before modeling on a dataset it did not create, a team plans an audit. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The audit is finished once the automated checks on types, ranges, missingness and duplicates all pass, because those cover the main data-quality dimensions.
statements.explanation: Those checks read the data as recorded and cannot detect missing populations, invalid proxies or wrong expectations.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A report that says 'no issues found' is as informative as one that lists the checks run, the checks not run and their limits, since both reach the same conclusion.
statements.explanation: Without the scope of the checks, a reader cannot tell what 'no issues' covers.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Following a few randomly chosen records back to their source systems is unnecessary when documentation exists, since the documentation already describes them.
statements.explanation: Tracing a record can reveal transformations, drops and recodings that documentation omits or has not kept up with.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Writing down the expected row count, time span and population before opening the data keeps a mismatch from being explained away afterward.
statements.explanation: A prior expectation gives the observed numbers something to be compared against, preventing hindsight rationalization.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When the source systems cannot be reached, the audit should assume the supplied documentation is accurate and complete, because nothing better is available.
statements.explanation: Unverifiable documentation is a risk to record, not a reason to trust it; the opacity itself is a finding.

questions.stem: A binary image classifier computes a score s(x) = w·x + b over d = 1000 input values and predicts class 1 when s(x) > 0. Every weight has magnitude |w_i| = 0.02. For one input the score is s = −0.15, so the prediction is class 0. An attacker who knows w may change each input value by at most ε = 0.01 in either direction (an L∞ budget). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the budget were instead an L2 limit of 0.01 on the length of the whole change vector, the largest achievable score change would still be 0.2.
statements.explanation: Under an L2 limit the maximum is ε·‖w‖₂ = 0.01 × 0.02 × √1000 ≈ 0.0063, about 32 times smaller than the L∞ figure.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Within the budget, the largest increase in the score the attacker can cause is 0.2, reached by moving each value by 0.01 in the direction of the sign of its weight.
statements.explanation: For a linear score the change is w·δ, and with |δ_i| ≤ ε it is maximized by δ_i = ε·sign(w_i), giving ε·Σ|w_i| = 0.01 × 1000 × 0.02 = 0.2.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With the original budget the attacker can push the score from −0.15 to a positive value.
statements.explanation: The best case gives −0.15 + 0.2 = +0.05, which is above zero.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If inputs had 4000 values with the same weight magnitude and the same per-value budget, the largest achievable score change would be 0.8.
statements.explanation: The maximum is ε·Σ|w_i|, which grows in proportion to the number of values when per-value weight and budget are fixed (0.01 × 4000 × 0.02 = 0.8).

statements.label: E
statements.text: With a budget ten times smaller (ε = 0.001), the largest achievable increase in the score is 0.02, which cannot flip this input.
statements.explanation: The maximum scales linearly with ε, so 0.001 × 1000 × 0.02 = 0.02, well short of the 0.15 needed.

questions.stem: An image classifier takes 32 × 32 × 3 = 3072 input values scaled to [0, 1]. Robustness claims about it measure the size of a change either as L∞ (the largest change to any single value) or as L2 (the Euclidean length of the whole change vector). Let ε = 8/255 ≈ 0.0314. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A change that moves every one of the 3072 values by exactly ε has an L2 length of about 1.74.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A guarantee that no change with L∞ size up to ε can alter the prediction also covers every change of L2 length up to ε.
statements.explanation: Any change has L∞ size no larger than its L2 length, so the L2 ball of radius ε sits inside the L∞ ball of radius ε.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A guarantee that no change of L2 length up to 0.5 can alter the prediction also guarantees that no change with L∞ size up to ε can alter it.
statements.explanation: The L∞ ball of radius ε contains changes with L2 length up to about 1.74, which exceeds 0.5, so the L2 guarantee does not cover them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A change that moves a single value by 0.5 and leaves the rest alone is inside the L∞ ball of radius ε, because its L2 length of 0.5 is below 1.74.
statements.explanation: The change has L∞ size 0.5, far above ε; a small L2 length does not place a change inside the L∞ ball.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The L∞ ball of radius ε contains every change whose L2 length is at most 1.74.
statements.explanation: The containment runs the other way: the L2 ball of radius 1.74 contains the L∞ ball, and a change of large L2 length concentrated in one value lies outside the L∞ ball.

questions.source: A taxonomy of attacks — what each targets
questions.stem: A 10-class image classifier is attacked, within a fixed L∞ budget, on 1000 test images that it classifies correctly. An untargeted attack (success means any wrong label) succeeds on 940 images. A targeted attack, which must make the classifier output a specific wrong class chosen in advance for each image, succeeds on 610 images. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Every image on which the targeted attack succeeded is also an image on which an untargeted attack with the same budget can succeed.
statements.explanation: A targeted success puts the input in a wrong class, which also counts as an untargeted success, so the targeted successes are a subset of the untargeted ones.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because the untargeted attack succeeds on 94% of images, each of the nine wrong classes is reachable as a target on at least 94% of images.
statements.explanation: The untargeted result says some wrong class is reachable, not that every specified wrong class is; the 61% targeted result shows many specific targets are not.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The gap between 610 and 940 shows that the targeted attack code contains an error.
statements.explanation: Reaching a specified class is a stricter goal than reaching any wrong class, so a lower rate is expected and does not indicate a bug.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A gradient-sign step for a targeted attack increases the loss measured against the chosen target class.
statements.explanation: A targeted step moves toward the target class, so it decreases the loss computed against that class; the untargeted step increases the loss computed against the true class.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A targeted success rate of 61% means an attacker who is satisfied with any wrong output succeeds on at most 61% of images.
statements.explanation: An attacker who only needs some wrong output has the 94% untargeted rate available, so the model is easily pushed off the correct label.

questions.source: A taxonomy of attacks — what each targets
questions.stem: A security team has no access to a deployed image classifier's weights or gradients and can only submit images and read the predicted label. The team trains its own classifier on similar public data, crafts adversarial images against that classifier using its gradients, and submits the crafted images to the deployed system, where a large share are misclassified. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Keeping the weights and gradients secret removes the risk of gradient-based adversarial inputs.
statements.explanation: Attackers have the surrogate route and the query route, so secrecy of weights is not a robustness property.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the crafted images had failed to fool the deployed system, that would show the system resists adversarial perturbations of that size.
statements.explanation: One failed surrogate-based attack is a single weak test; a better surrogate, an ensemble of surrogates or a query-based attack may still succeed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The attack succeeded, so the team must have recovered the deployed model's weights.
statements.explanation: The crafted images used only a surrogate's gradients; transfer works with no knowledge of the target's weights.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This is a transfer attack: perturbations crafted on a surrogate model often also fool other models trained on similar data.
statements.explanation: Models trained on similar data tend to share vulnerable directions, so adversarial inputs often transfer between models.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Attacks that estimate a useful direction from repeated queries of the deployed system's outputs cannot succeed without access to its weights.
statements.explanation: Score-based and decision-based black-box attacks work from outputs alone and have been shown to succeed without weight access.

questions.source: The robustness toolkit — what each tool does and what it costs
questions.stem: A team evaluates a defended image classifier on 1000 test images at a fixed L∞ budget. A white-box gradient attack leaves 74% of the images correctly classified. A transfer attack from a separately trained surrogate model, with the same budget, leaves 41% correctly classified. The defense places a non-differentiable preprocessing step (random rounding of pixel values) in front of the network. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 41% result shows that the model's accuracy under the worst-case perturbation at this budget is exactly 41%.
statements.explanation: Any particular attack gives only an upper bound on worst-case accuracy; a stronger attack could push the figure below 41%.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because a white-box attacker has strictly more information, any particular white-box attack procedure, such as the gradient attack run here, is guaranteed to lower accuracy at least as much as any black-box attack on the same model.
statements.explanation: A white-box attacker could in principle do at least as well, but a particular white-box procedure can fail through optimization difficulty (noisy, shattered or masked gradients) while another route succeeds, so no such ordering is guaranteed for a given attack.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A suitable next test is an adaptive attack that approximates or averages over the preprocessing step.
statements.explanation: Attacks designed with knowledge of the defense, such as approximating the non-differentiable step or averaging over the randomness, are the standard way to test such a defense.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The transfer attack beating the white-box attack points to uninformative white-box gradients (gradient masking), so 74% overstates robustness.
statements.explanation: A defense that only disrupts gradient computation makes the white-box attack fail without making nearby inputs correctly classified, and a different attack route exposes this.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Both 74% and 41% are upper bounds on the model's worst-case accuracy at this budget, and 41% is the tighter one.
statements.explanation: Each attack's accuracy is an upper bound because the true worst case is at most what any attack finds; the lower figure is the tighter bound.

questions.source: Adversarial training and its scaling limits
questions.stem: A team trains an image classifier by adversarial training. For every minibatch, an inner loop runs 10 steps of projected gradient ascent on the loss to find a perturbation inside an L∞ ball of radius 8/255, and then the weights are updated once on the perturbed minibatch. Assume each gradient computation (one forward and backward pass) costs the same. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Each minibatch needs about 11 times as many forward-backward passes as ordinary training.
statements.explanation: Ten inner gradient steps plus one weight-update gradient is 11 passes, against 1 for ordinary training.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the trained model keeps 50% accuracy under a strong 10-step attack at radius 8/255, that is a proof that no perturbation inside the ball can push its accuracy below 50%.
statements.explanation: A measured accuracy is relative to the attacks used; a stronger or adaptive attack may do better, so empirical robustness is not a proof.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Even after such training, the model should still be tested against stronger attacks and against other perturbation types, because the training targeted one threat model.
statements.explanation: Robustness gained against one norm and budget does not automatically carry over to larger budgets, other norms or other perturbation types.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the perturbed inputs act as extra training data, clean accuracy is expected to be unchanged or higher than with ordinary training.
statements.explanation: In standard settings adversarially trained models usually give up some clean accuracy compared with ordinary training.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The inner loop searches for a worst-case perturbation and the outer update lowers the loss on it, so training solves a min–max problem.
statements.explanation: The inner maximization finds a high-loss perturbation in the allowed set and the outer minimization trains on it, which is the min–max formulation.

questions.source: Adversarial training and its scaling limits
questions.stem: Two classifiers with the same architecture are evaluated on a held-out test set. The first is trained normally. The second is adversarially trained against 10-step L∞ perturbations of radius 8/255. Accuracy (%), normal versus adversarially trained: clean inputs 95 vs 85; 10-step L∞ attack at 8/255, 0 vs 50; 10-step L∞ attack at 16/255, 0 vs 14; random Gaussian noise, 60 vs 78; adversarial patch covering one 8 × 8 region, 3 vs 6. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The accuracy under random noise (78%) tells a reader as much about worst-case behavior as the attack results do.
statements.explanation: Random noise is a weak probe in high dimensions; an optimized perturbation of the same size can do far more damage than typical noise.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adversarial training raised accuracy at the trained budget from 0% to 50% at a cost of 10 points of clean accuracy.
statements.explanation: Clean accuracy fell from 95 to 85 (10 points) while accuracy under the 8/255 attack rose from 0 to 50.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The patch result shows that adversarial training left the model less robust to patches than the normal model, trading patch robustness for robustness to small pixel changes.
statements.explanation: The patch accuracy went from 3% to 6%, so it did not get worse; both are close to failure.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Since a 10-step attack leaves 50% at radius 8/255, no stronger attack within that radius, such as more steps or random restarts, can lower the accuracy below 50%.
statements.explanation: A stronger attack can find perturbations the 10-step attack missed, so 50% is only an upper bound on worst-case accuracy.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Robustness gained at one budget does not automatically carry to a larger budget (14% at 16/255) or to another perturbation type (6% under patches).
statements.explanation: Accuracy drops to 14% when the budget doubles and stays near 6% against a patch, so the protection is specific to the perturbation set used in training.

questions.stem: An image classifier with 3072 input values scores 93% on clean test images. Adding random noise of L2 length 1.7 (random direction) lowers accuracy to 91%. An adversarial perturbation of the same L2 length 1.7, found by gradient search separately for each image, lowers accuracy to 2%. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Natural corruptions (blur, fog, compression) and constructed worst-case perturbations are different test conditions; passing one does not settle the other.
statements.explanation: Natural shifts come from the world and worst-case perturbations come from an optimizer, so each needs its own test.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the model were correct on every perturbation of L2 length at most 1.7 around each test image, it would also be correct under the random noise used here.
statements.explanation: The random noise has L2 length 1.7, so each noisy input lies inside the ball and a model correct everywhere in the ball is correct there.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The 91%-versus-2% gap shows random-noise accuracy is a poor predictor of worst-case accuracy at the same size.
statements.explanation: The same perturbation size gives 91% for random noise and 2% for the optimized one, so the first says little about the second.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In high dimensions a worst-case direction shifts a linear score roughly √d times more than a typical random direction of the same length does.
statements.explanation: With a random unit direction the shift has standard deviation ‖w‖₂/√d per unit length, while the aligned direction gives ‖w‖₂, a factor of √d (about 55 for d = 3072).

statements.label: E
statements.text: The 91% figure under random noise shows that the model will also resist a perturbation of that same size when it is chosen by an attacker.
statements.explanation: Noise averages out across coordinates, whereas an optimizer aligns every coordinate with the model's sensitivity, as the 2% result shows.

questions.stem: A model detects pneumonia on chest X-rays. The collection has 10,000 images in all, 5000 from each of two hospitals. Hospital A's images carry a scanner tag and 80% of its patients are positive. Hospital B's images carry a different tag and 10% of its patients are positive. The collection is split at random into training and held-out images, so the held-out set has the same hospital shares and the same tag-label link as the whole collection, and it is large enough that its accuracy figures are accurate to within about one percentage point. On the held-out set the model scores 88% accuracy. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Always predicting the more common class overall would score about 55% on the held-out set.
statements.explanation: Overall prevalence is (4000 + 500)/10000 = 45% positive, so the majority-class baseline is 55%.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Testing on images from a third hospital, whose images carry neither tag and whose prevalence is unrelated to any tag, would test whether the model relies on the tag.
statements.explanation: With no tag and no link between site and label, a model that depended on the tag has nothing to lean on and its accuracy would fall.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Cropping the visible tag out of every image guarantees that the model cannot use any other hospital-specific cue.
statements.explanation: Sites also differ in scanner texture, contrast, positioning and annotation, so removing one visible cue does not remove all site information.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A rule that ignores the lungs and predicts positive for hospital A's tag and negative for hospital B's tag would score about 85% on this held-out set.
statements.explanation: Tag A is right on 4000 of 5000 images (80% positive) and tag B on 4500 of 5000 (90% negative), so 8500 of 10000 are correct.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The 88% score alone does not show that the model reads lung findings, because a rule using only the tag already scores about 85% on this held-out set.
statements.explanation: The held-out set has the same tag-label link as the training data, so only about 3 points (with about 1 point of measurement error) separate the model from the tag rule, which is not enough to show that anything beyond the tag is being used.

questions.stem: A bird-image classifier is evaluated on four groups defined by bird type and background: landbird on land (3000 images, 98% correct), landbird on water (200 images, 62%), waterbird on land (160 images, 55%), waterbird on water (1000 images, 95%). In the training data most landbirds appear on land and most waterbirds on water. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because overall accuracy is about 94%, accuracy on any subgroup of interest is at least about 94%.
statements.explanation: An overall average can hide subgroups far below it; here one group is at 55%.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Worst-group accuracy is 55%, for waterbirds on land.
statements.explanation: The lowest of the four group accuracies is 55%, in the waterbird-on-land group.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Overall accuracy on this test set is about 94%, a weighted average dominated by the two large groups.
statements.explanation: (2940 + 124 + 88 + 950)/4360 = 4102/4360 ≈ 94.1%, and the 3000- and 1000-image groups carry most of the weight.

statements.label: D
statements.text: High accuracy where background matches a bird type's usual background and low accuracy where it does not is consistent with a model that partly relies on the background.
statements.explanation: Accuracy tracking background agreement is what a background-reliant model produces, though other causes such as small group size could also contribute.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The unweighted average of the four group accuracies is higher than the overall accuracy.
statements.explanation: The unweighted mean of 98, 62, 55 and 95 is 77.5%, well below 94% because the small groups count equally.

questions.stem: A classifier has 96% accuracy on customers of type X and 72% on customers of type Y, whatever the mix of customers it is applied to. A vendor reports 93.6% accuracy from a test set that is 90% type X and 10% type Y. A buyer's customers are 70% type X and 30% type Y. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Overall accuracy equals 0.96 × (share of type X) + 0.72 × (share of type Y).
statements.explanation: Overall accuracy is the mix-weighted average of the group accuracies.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the buyer's mix were 50% X and 50% Y, the expected accuracy would remain 93.6% because the model has not changed.
statements.explanation: A 50/50 mix gives 0.5 × 0.96 + 0.5 × 0.72 = 0.84, because overall accuracy depends on the mix as well as on the model.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Whatever the mix, the expected overall accuracy lies between 72% and 96%.
statements.explanation: Overall accuracy is a weighted average of the two group accuracies, so it cannot leave the interval between them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Reporting only the overall figure is enough for a buyer with a different customer mix.
statements.explanation: The overall figure bakes in the vendor's mix; per-group figures are what let a buyer recompute for their own population.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The buyer should expect an overall accuracy of about 88.8%.

questions.stem: Distribution shift is often divided into covariate shift (the distribution of inputs P(x) changes while P(y | x) is unchanged), label shift or prior shift (the class frequencies P(y) change while P(x | y) is unchanged) and concept shift (P(y | x) itself changes). Check each statement that gives the correct name or property.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A diagnostic model trained on one manufacturer's scans is used on another's; pixel statistics differ but the correct diagnosis for a given image is unchanged. This is covariate shift.
statements.explanation: The input distribution changed while the label for a given input did not, which is covariate shift.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Under label shift, the classifier's true and false positive rates change as the class frequencies change, but its precision stays the same because it depends only on the classifier.
statements.explanation: Under label shift P(x | y) is fixed, so true and false positive rates stay the same while precision changes with the class frequencies.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sentiment classifier is trained when a slang word meant "bad". The word now means "good", so the same text carries a different correct label, although the share of positive and negative reviews is unchanged. This is label shift.
statements.explanation: The meaning of the same input changed, so P(y | x) changed; that is concept shift.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A credit model is trained before a regulation takes effect. Afterward, applicant profiles identical to ones previously labeled approvable are labeled not approvable, while the mix of profiles is similar to before. This is covariate shift.
statements.explanation: The correct label for identical inputs changed, which is concept shift, not covariate shift.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A fraud model trained when 2% of transactions were fraudulent is used in a new market where 6% are, and each class looks as before. This is label shift.
statements.explanation: The class frequencies changed while the appearance of each class did not, which is the definition of label shift.

questions.stem: A screening classifier has a true positive rate of 0.80 and a false positive rate of 0.10. Assume pure label shift: these rates are the same in every population and only the prevalence of the condition changes. At the training site prevalence is 10%. At a new site it is 30%. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Prevalence at the new site can be learned only by labeling a sample of that site's cases.
statements.explanation: The fraction flagged positive equals π·TPR + (1 − π)·FPR, so prevalence can be estimated from unlabeled predictions when TPR and FPR are known (0.31 flagged gives π = 0.30).

statements.label: B
statements.text: Precision (positive predictive value) is about 47% at the training site and about 77% at the new site.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Overall accuracy is identical at the two sites, because the true and false positive rates are identical and so the share of correct decisions cannot depend on how common the condition is.
statements.explanation: Accuracy is π·TPR + (1 − π)(1 − FPR), which is 0.89 at 10% prevalence and 0.87 at 30%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A calibrated 0.50 under 10% prevalence becomes about 0.79 after adjusting to 30% prevalence.
statements.explanation: The prior odds ratio is (0.3/0.7)/(0.1/0.9) ≈ 3.86, so posterior odds of 1 become 3.86 and the probability becomes 3.86/4.86 ≈ 0.79.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Recall at the new site would be higher than at the training site, because the condition is more common there.
statements.explanation: Recall is the true positive rate, which is 0.80 at both sites under label shift.

questions.stem: A loan-default model has accuracy 95% for applicants under 40 and 70% for applicants 40 or over. Evaluation used a population that was 80% under 40 and 20% 40 or over. After launch the applicant population is 30% under 40 and 70% 40 or over. Within each age band, the relationship between features and outcome has not changed. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The fall from 90% to 77.5% shows that the relationship between features and outcome must have changed.
statements.explanation: Only the mix of applicants changed; the per-band accuracies were assumed fixed, so the drop is explained by covariate shift alone.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Weighting each evaluation example by launch share over evaluation share gives an estimate that is no noisier than an unweighted estimate from the same sample, because weighting only rescales the examples.
statements.explanation: The 40-or-over band is 20% of examples but carries 70% of the weight, so the effective sample size falls to about 390 of 1000 and the estimate is noisier.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Expected accuracy after launch is 77.5%, down from 90%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the launch population included an age band absent from the evaluation data, the same weighting method could still estimate accuracy for that band.
statements.explanation: Importance weights need the evaluation data to cover every region where launch data has mass; an unseen band has no examples to weight.

statements.label: E
