statements.explanation: The experiment found influences that the text did not report, which is exactly what makes reading the text insufficient.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A fluent, step-by-step justification that supports the final answer is, by itself, good evidence that those steps are what produced the answer.
statements.explanation: Text can be generated to fit an answer after the fact, so fluency and coherence do not show the steps were causal.

questions.source: Model Explainability: Distinguishing Explanation from the Appearance of Explanation
questions.stem: Researchers train a linear probe on a language model's layer-12 activations to predict whether a sentence's subject is singular or plural. The probe reaches 97% accuracy on held-out sentences. A control probe trained to predict a label assigned at random to each word type reaches 55%. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The result shows that the singular-or-plural information is linearly decodable from the layer-12 activations.
statements.explanation: Held-out accuracy of 97% means the label can be read off the activations by a linear function.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Changing the activations along the probe's direction and checking whether verb agreement changes would show whether the information is used.
statements.explanation: An intervention on the representation tests whether downstream behavior depends on it, which decodability cannot.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A probe that is a large nonlinear network can reach high accuracy by learning the task itself, which is why control tasks are used.
statements.explanation: A high-capacity probe can solve the task by itself from weak signals, so accuracy then says less about the activations.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A control probe near chance suggests the probe is not reaching 97% merely by memorizing arbitrary labels.
statements.explanation: A probe able to memorize arbitrary labels would score well on the control task; 55% suggests it cannot do so.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The result proves that the model uses that information when it produces its output; a probe at 97% could not succeed otherwise.
statements.explanation: Information being present is different from the model using it; the model may ignore a variable that is nonetheless decodable.

questions.source: Model Explainability: Distinguishing Explanation from the Appearance of Explanation
questions.stem: A pneumonia classifier is trained on chest X-rays pooled from two hospitals. Hospital 1 contributes 5,000 images, 60% of which show pneumonia. Hospital 2 contributes 5,000 images, 10% of which show pneumonia. Each image carries a small scanner tag in a corner that identifies the hospital, and attribution maps from the trained classifier highlight the tag on most images. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Measuring accuracy within each hospital, and on images from a third hospital, helps check whether the classifier is relying on the tag.
statements.explanation: Within one hospital the tag carries no information, so a collapse in accuracy within hospitals or at a new site indicates reliance on it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A rule that always predicts "no pneumonia" would score 90% accuracy on the pooled data, since most images are negative.
statements.explanation: Pooled prevalence is (3,000 + 500) / 10,000 = 35%, so always predicting negative scores 65%.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A rule that predicts pneumonia exactly when the image comes from Hospital 1 would score 75% accuracy on the pooled data.
statements.explanation: Correct on 60% of Hospital 1 (the positives) and 90% of Hospital 2 (the negatives): (3,000 + 4,500) / 10,000 = 0.75.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The attribution on the tag proves that the classifier contains no information about the lungs and relies on nothing else.
statements.explanation: Attribution to the tag shows the classifier uses it, not that it uses nothing else.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An overall accuracy of 85% would rule out reliance on the tag, because 85% exceeds the 75% that the tag alone can give.
statements.explanation: A model can use the tag and real lung evidence together, so beating the tag-only score does not show the tag is unused.

questions.stem: An autonomous operations agent is told to "delete the customer's record". It runs a command that sets deleted = true on the row in the primary database, then reports: "The customer record has been deleted." The database keeps flagged rows for 30 days and nightly backups keep the row for 90 days. The customer wanted the data to be unrecoverable. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Asking the agent afterwards why it said "deleted" will reliably produce an account that states the retention periods.
statements.explanation: A generated explanation reflects what the model produces when prompted, and can omit facts it never represented.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fluent and confident report makes it unnecessary to check the state of the system; a model that writes well knows what it did.
statements.explanation: Fluency is a property of the text, not evidence about the world.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Querying the database and the backups and checking the retention settings is a verification that the agent's report cannot supply by itself.
statements.explanation: The claim is about the state of the world, so it is checked against that state, not against the agent's description of it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The report can be accurate about the system's own state flag and still mislead a reader who takes "deleted" to mean "no longer recoverable".
statements.explanation: The word "deleted" has a narrow technical meaning inside the system and a stronger meaning to the customer; the report resolves the ambiguity silently.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A feature-attribution method applied to the agent's model would have flagged the mismatch between the agent's wording and the customer's meaning.
statements.explanation: Attribution shows which inputs shaped the output; it does not compare the output's meaning with what the reader will understand.

questions.source: Three words that don't mean the same thing
questions.stem: A hospital buys a sepsis-risk model. The contract says "every prediction must be accompanied by an explainable reason". The vendor publishes the full weights of its 60-million-parameter neural network and supplies, for each patient, the five inputs with the largest Shapley values. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Whether an explanation is adequate depends on who reads it and what decision they must make with it, so one explanation can suit a developer and fail a patient.
statements.explanation: The same attribution can be useful to a developer and useless to a patient; adequacy is relative to the reader and the purpose.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because Shapley values add up exactly to the prediction minus the reference prediction, they establish that the risk would fall if the top input were changed.
statements.explanation: Efficiency makes the values sum correctly; it says nothing about what would happen if an input were changed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Replacing the network with a short scoring rule a clinician can follow step by step would give an explanation that approximates the model, just as the vendor's list does.
statements.explanation: For a short scoring rule the rule itself is the model, so reading it involves no approximation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Meeting the contract's wording means a bedside nurse can use the reason to decide what to do for the patient.
statements.explanation: A list of influential inputs says what moved a number, not what action is clinically appropriate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Publishing all the weights gives access to the model's internals but does not by itself let a clinician predict what the model will do for a new patient.
statements.explanation: Inspecting millions of parameters does not produce a working mental model of behavior on new cases.

questions.stem: To explain a gradient-boosted credit model, an analyst fits a depth-4 decision tree to imitate it, training the tree on the black-box model's decisions and not on the true repayment outcomes. On 2,000 held-out applicants the tree agrees with the black box's decision for 88% of them. Among the 200 applicants under 25, the agreement is 61%. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Agreement with the true repayment outcomes is the correct measure of how faithful the tree is to the black box's decisions.
statements.explanation: Fidelity is agreement with the black box's outputs; agreement with outcomes measures accuracy, which is a different property.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For the 200 applicants under 25, the tree's decision differs from the black box's for 122 of them, about 61% of that group.
statements.explanation: Agreement is 61%, so 122 of the 200 agree and 78 differ; 122 is the number of agreements.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because the tree was trained to match the black box, perfect agreement would still not show that the black box is right about applicants.
statements.explanation: A surrogate trained on model outputs describes the model, and the model can be wrong about the world.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Agreement among the applicants aged 25 or over is 85%, in line with the overall figure of 88% and well above the 61% for the youngest.
statements.explanation: The tree agrees on 1,760 of 2,000 overall and on 122 of the 200 young applicants, so 1,638 of 1,800 others, which is 91%.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An overall agreement of 88% means the tree is a reliable description of the black box for every subgroup, including the youngest.
statements.explanation: Overall agreement can hide a poor match for a subgroup, here 61% for applicants under 25.

questions.stem: A lender removes race from the inputs of its approval model and keeps zip code, which is correlated with race in the applicant population. Shapley explanations for denials show a large value for zip code and no value for race, since race is not an input. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The absence of any attribution to race does not show that approval decisions are independent of race, because correlated inputs can carry the same information.
statements.explanation: A model can reproduce group differences through correlated inputs even when the group label itself is absent.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Removing zip code and retraining guarantees that the new model has no dependence on race, since the proxy is gone.
statements.explanation: Other correlated inputs can carry the same information, so removing one proxy does not guarantee independence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Comparing outcomes such as approval and error rates across groups is a direct way to look for disparities that attribution lists would not reveal.
statements.explanation: Outcome rates by group are measured directly on decisions, independent of how the model is explained.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because race is not an input, approval rates cannot differ between racial groups, whatever the other inputs are.
statements.explanation: Group differences in outcomes can arise from proxies and from differences in the data, whether or not the label is an input.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A large Shapley value for zip code on its own establishes that the lender is discriminating on race.
statements.explanation: A large value shows the model uses zip code; whether that use amounts to discrimination is a further question about proxies, justification and effects.

questions.source: Three words that don't mean the same thing
questions.stem: A logistic regression for loan default uses two nearly duplicate inputs, balance_today and balance_yesterday, with correlation 0.99. On the full data the coefficients are +4.8 and -4.1. On two bootstrap resamples they are (+1.2, -0.5) and (-3.1, +3.8). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The model's predictions can stay similar across resamples even though the coefficients differ, because the data pin down the sum more tightly than each coefficient.
statements.explanation: Predictions depend mainly on the sum for nearly identical inputs, which the data constrain well.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Penalizing the coefficients (ridge) or combining the two inputs into one would make the interpretation more stable.
statements.explanation: A ridge penalty shares weight across the pair and merging them removes the redundancy, both of which stabilize what the coefficients say.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The individual coefficients are unstable across resamples, while their sum (0.7 in each fit) is stable.
statements.explanation: 4.8 - 4.1 = 0.7, 1.2 - 0.5 = 0.7 and -3.1 + 3.8 = 0.7, while each coefficient moves widely and changes sign.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The negative coefficient on balance_yesterday in the full fit shows that a higher balance yesterday lowers default risk.
statements.explanation: With near-duplicates the sign of one coefficient is set by how it offsets the other, not by an independent effect.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reading a coefficient as the effect of changing one input "holding the others fixed" is unreliable when the other inputs cannot realistically be held fixed.
statements.explanation: In nearly duplicate inputs one cannot change without the other, so the "holding fixed" comparison does not occur in the data.

questions.source: What SHAP is, and what SHAP isn't
questions.stem: A team plans several uses for feature attributions (such as Shapley values) computed from a trained model on its validation data. Check each statement that is true about what the attributions can support.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For regulatory review, a list of the top three inputs for each decision shows whether the model treats demographic groups differently.
statements.explanation: Per-decision lists do not compare outcomes across groups; disparities are found by measuring outcomes group by group.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For trust, a user's increased confidence after reading an explanation is evidence that the model is more accurate than was thought.
statements.explanation: Users' confidence can rise with a fluent explanation whether or not the model is correct, so it is not evidence of accuracy.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For debugging, heavy attribution to an input the team did not expect the model to use is a lead worth investigating for leakage or a shortcut.
statements.explanation: Surprising weight on an input is cheap evidence of a data problem and points to where to look.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For safety sign-off, a clean-looking attribution pattern across 1,000 validation cases shows that the model will perform well on a population it has not seen.
statements.explanation: Attributions describe the model on the data used; they do not measure performance under distribution shift.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For recourse, the attribution values alone tell an applicant which actions would change the decision and how large the actions must be.
statements.explanation: Attributions say what contributed to a score, not which feasible changes would flip it; that takes a counterfactual with actionable constraints.

questions.source: Three words that don't mean the same thing
questions.stem: A trial randomizes 100 clinicians to each of two arms. Arm 1 sees an AI recommendation only. Arm 2 sees the recommendation plus a feature-attribution explanation. Each clinician handles one case on which the AI's recommendation is wrong. In arm 1, 46 of 100 clinicians follow the wrong recommendation; in arm 2, 58 of 100 do. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because a 95% interval for the difference includes 0, the data show that the explanation has no effect on whether clinicians follow wrong advice.
statements.explanation: An interval that includes 0 is also consistent with sizeable effects; it shows the data are inconclusive, not that the effect is absent.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A 95% interval for the difference runs from about -2 to +26 points, so these data do not establish that the explanation raises following of wrong advice.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The observed difference is 12 percentage points, in the direction of more following of wrong advice when the explanation is shown.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the 12-point difference is real, it would show that the explanation is an inaccurate description of the model's behavior.
statements.explanation: Higher reliance on a wrong recommendation describes user behavior; an explanation can be accurate about the model and still persuade people to over-trust it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With 400 clinicians per arm and the same proportions, the 95% interval would run from about +5 to +19 points.
statements.explanation: The standard error falls to 0.035, giving 0.12 +/- 0.069, about +0.051 to +0.189.

questions.stem: A city wants to know what share of its residents support a transit levy. The true share is 54%: 40% of residents have a landline and 75% of them support the levy, while the other 60% have no landline and 40% of them support it. A survey firm draws a simple random sample of landline numbers only and reports the sample proportion. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Adding a random sample of residents without landlines and weighting the two groups 40% and 60% would give an estimate centred on 54%.
statements.explanation: The weights 0.4 x 75% + 0.6 x 40% give 54%, and this works only because both strata now have respondents.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The sample proportion has an expected value of 75%, so its bias is about +21 percentage points whatever the sample size.
statements.explanation: Only landline households can be sampled, so the expected value is their 75% support, 21 points above the 54% truth, and that offset belongs to the procedure rather than to n.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Giving the landline respondents a weight so that they count as 40% of the total repairs the estimate, because the weighted sample then matches the population's landline share.
statements.explanation: With no non-landline respondents there is only one stratum to weight, so the weights cancel and the estimate stays at 75%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Raising the sample from 1,000 to 100,000 respondents cuts the standard error about tenfold (1.4 points to 0.14) but leaves the expected estimate at 75%.
statements.explanation: Standard error scales with 1/sqrt(n), so a hundredfold larger sample shrinks it tenfold, while the systematic offset is untouched.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With 100,000 respondents the estimate will very likely land within one point of the true 54%, because sampling error becomes tiny.
statements.explanation: The estimate concentrates ever more tightly around 75%, not around 54%.

questions.stem: A hospital builds a sepsis alert from 10,000 admissions. At triage 2,000 patients are classed unstable (30% develop sepsis) and 8,000 stable (5% develop sepsis), so overall prevalence is 10%. The training data keep only patients who had a lab panel in the first six hours, which happened for 90% of stable and 20% of unstable patients. The triage class is recorded for every patient. Within each triage class, whether a patient had a lab panel does not depend on whether that patient develops sepsis. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Weighting each retained patient by 1 divided by the probability of being retained given triage class recovers a prevalence of 10%.
statements.explanation: Weights of 1/0.9 and 1/0.2 restore each class to its population size, giving (400 + 600) / (8,000 + 2,000) = 10%.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The same weighting would still work if, instead, retention depended on an unrecorded clinician hunch that is related to sepsis.
statements.explanation: Weighting needs a recorded variable that explains who was kept; an unrecorded hunch related to sepsis gives nothing to weight on, so retained patients would stay unrepresentative within each triage class.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Collecting ten times as many admissions under the same lab rule would bring the training prevalence close to 10%.
statements.explanation: The same retention rule yields the same skewed mix at any volume, so more data reproduces 6.3% with a smaller standard error.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The 6.3% training prevalence is the right baseline for calibrating risk scores for all admitted patients.
statements.explanation: Deployment sees all admissions, whose true prevalence is 10%, so a baseline taken from the filtered sample is miscalibrated for them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Sepsis prevalence in the training data is about 6.3%, well below the true 10%.
statements.explanation: The sample has 480 sepsis cases among 7,600 patients, which is 6.3%, because unstable patients are retained at a much lower rate.

questions.source: Leverage analysis — finding the high-leverage intervention point
questions.stem: A lender deletes the column "group" (a protected attribute) from its training table but keeps "neighbourhood". The table covers 1,000 applicants, half living in neighbourhood N1 and half in N2. In N1, 90% of applicants belong to group B; in N2, 10% do. A manager says the model "cannot treat the groups differently, because it never sees group". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A feature that predicts group is, for that reason alone, being used unfairly, whatever else it tells the model about the outcome.
statements.explanation: A feature can predict group and also carry legitimate information about the outcome, so unfair use has to be shown by its effects rather than inferred from correlation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Dropping neighbourhood as well guarantees that no remaining column carries information about group, since the model has nothing left to infer it from.
statements.explanation: Other columns such as employer, school, purchase history or name can also correlate with group, so removing one proxy does not remove the signal.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because the model never sees group, any difference between groups in its approval rates must reflect differences in applicants' true creditworthiness.
statements.explanation: The model can recover much of group from neighbourhood, and the outcomes it learns from can carry group-linked patterns, so outcome differences need not reflect creditworthiness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Guessing group from neighbourhood alone would be right for 90% of applicants, against 50% for a coin flip.
statements.explanation: Of 1,000 applicants, 450 + 450 are classified correctly, so neighbourhood alone recovers most of the group signal.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Auditing outcomes by group requires group labels in the audit data even though the model does not take them as input.
statements.explanation: Without recorded group membership there is no way to compute outcome rates by group, so deleting the field also removes the ability to detect disparities.

questions.stem: A screening model advances 240 of 400 applicants from group A (60%) and 120 of 300 applicants from group B (40%). A reviewer divides the lower selection rate by the higher one and compares the result with 0.8, the benchmark in a common US employment-selection screening heuristic known as the four-fifths rule. A two-proportion z-test on these counts gives z of about 5.2. For reference, if group B had only 20 applicants with 8 advanced (also 40%), the same test would give z of about 1.8, below the 1.96 needed for significance at the 5% level. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A ratio below 0.8 proves that the model uses group membership in its decisions, since the benchmark exists to detect that.
statements.explanation: The ratio is descriptive; a gap can arise from differences between applicant pools, proxies or other causes, and says nothing by itself about whether group is used.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A z of about 5.2 means chance variation in who happened to apply is an unlikely explanation for a gap this large.
statements.explanation: The two-sided p-value is on the order of 10^-7, so sampling noise alone rarely produces such a gap if the underlying rates were equal.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The ratio of the selection rates is about 0.67, which falls below the 0.8 benchmark.
statements.explanation: 40% divided by 60% is 0.667.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A ratio above 0.8 would show that the screening process is free of group-related disadvantage for every subgroup of applicants.
statements.explanation: The benchmark is a screening heuristic on aggregate rates; a ratio above it can coexist with disadvantage hidden in subgroups.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With 20 group B applicants and the same 40% rate, the ratio stays 0.67 but is much weaker evidence of a real gap.
statements.explanation: Fewer applicants widen sampling variability, so the same ratio can fall within chance.

questions.stem: An audit finds that a loan model approves 62% of group X applicants and 48% of group Y applicants. The auditors want to learn which part of the pipeline produced the 14-point gap. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Matching applicants on every observed covariate removes the influence of unobserved differences between the groups.
statements.explanation: Matching balances only what was measured, and unmeasured factors can still differ and drive the gap.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Comparing approval rates among applicants with similar income and credit history shows whether the gap persists among comparable applicants.
statements.explanation: Stratifying on legitimate covariates is the standard first test of whether differences in qualifications account for a gap.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Re-running the model with one input held constant and measuring the change in the gap shows how much of it depends on that input.
statements.explanation: An ablation intervenes on one component and attributes the change in the output gap to it, which narrows the candidate causes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A statistically significant 14-point gap is enough on its own to identify which stage of the pipeline produced it.
statements.explanation: Significance says the gap is unlikely to be noise; it does not say whether data, labels, features, model, cutoff or review produced it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the gap disappears after conditioning on a variable such as job tenure, the decision process must have treated the groups equally.
statements.explanation: The conditioning variable may itself be shaped by group, for example through earlier unequal treatment, so the gap vanishing shows only that it runs through that variable.

questions.stem: A company advanced candidates from two groups into interviews for two roles. For role X, group A had 20 of 100 candidates advance and group B had 100 of 400. For role Y, group A had 240 of 400 advance and group B had 70 of 100. Overall, 260 of 500 group A candidates (52%) and 170 of 500 group B candidates (34%) advanced. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reversal arises because most group B candidates applied to the low-rate role while most group A candidates applied to the high-rate role.
statements.explanation: Group B has 400 of its 500 candidates in role X (a 25% rate) while group A has 400 of its 500 in role Y (60%), and the overall rate is a mix-weighted average.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Applying the same 50/50 role mix to both groups gives about 47.5% for group B and 40% for group A.
statements.explanation: Standardizing gives B = 0.5 x 25% + 0.5 x 70% = 47.5% and A = 0.5 x 20% + 0.5 x 60% = 40%.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The overall rates are the correct basis for comparing the groups, since they include every candidate.
statements.explanation: Which comparison is appropriate depends on the causal question, and the overall figure mixes the groups' different role choices with the process's treatment of them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The pattern cannot occur with correct counts, because a group that leads in every role must also lead overall.
statements.explanation: A reversal is arithmetically routine when groups apply to roles in different proportions; here B leads 25% to 20% in role X and 70% to 60% in role Y.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Group B has the higher advance rate in each role, yet group A has the higher rate overall.
statements.explanation: Role X is 25% against 20%, role Y is 70% against 60%, and overall it is 34% against 52%.

questions.stem: In hospital records, patients given a new drug recovered at a lower overall rate than untreated patients (66% against 76%), yet the drug group did better within each severity level: mild 90% against 85%, severe 60% against 40%. Of the 200 mild patients, 40 received the drug; of the 200 severe patients, 160 did. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Standardizing both groups to a 50/50 severity mix gives 75% recovery with the drug and 62.5% without.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Stratifying on blood pressure measured after dosing would remove part of the drug's effect if the drug works partly by lowering it.
statements.explanation: Conditioning on a post-treatment mediator blocks a path along which the treatment effect travels.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Assigning the drug at random would break the link between severity and treatment, removing that distortion from the overall comparison.
statements.explanation: Randomization makes treatment independent of severity and of other prior factors, measured or not, in expectation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Whenever a reversal like this appears, the stratified table is the correct one, whatever the causal relationships among the variables.
statements.explanation: A variable that is a consequence of the treatment (a mediator) or a collider can distort a stratified comparison, so the right table depends on the causal structure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Severity influences both who receives the drug and who recovers, which makes it a confounder of the overall comparison.
statements.explanation: Doctors gave the drug mostly to severe patients, who recover less often, so the drug group's overall rate is dragged down.

questions.stem: A classifier is tested on 10,000 images: 9,500 from group A, on which accuracy is 95%, and 500 from group B, on which accuracy is 70%. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Pooled accuracy equals the simple average of the two group accuracies, 82.5%.
statements.explanation: It is an average weighted by group size, so the large group dominates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Group B's error rate is about three times group A's.
statements.explanation: 30% against 5% is a factor of six.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Pooled accuracy on the test set is 93.75%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A pooled accuracy of 93.75% implies that every group's accuracy is at least 93.75%.
statements.explanation: A pooled figure is an average, so one group can sit well below it when another sits above it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Pooled accuracy would still exceed 90% if the classifier were wrong on every group B image.
statements.explanation: 9,025 correct out of 10,000 is 90.25%.

questions.stem: On a test set, group A has 2,000 examples with 160 errors (8.0%) and group B has 40 examples with 6 errors (15.0%). A 95% Wilson interval for group B's error rate runs from about 7.1% to 29.1%, and a Fisher exact test of the difference between the two error rates gives p = 0.13. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because 15% is higher than 8%, the model is worse on group B than on group A.
statements.explanation: With only 40 examples the observed difference is compatible with chance, so the point estimate alone does not establish a higher error rate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The non-significant test shows that the two groups have the same error rate.
statements.explanation: Failing to reject is not evidence of equality; with 40 examples the test has little power to detect even sizeable differences.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Group B's interval includes group A's observed 8.0%, so these data do not rule out equal error rates.
statements.explanation: 8.0% lies between 7.1% and 29.1%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Collecting 160 group B examples that also show a 15% error rate would leave the interval about as wide as it is now.
statements.explanation: Quadrupling n roughly halves the width of an interval for a proportion.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Merging group B into one pool with group A and reporting a single error rate of about 8.1% settles the uncertainty about group B.
statements.explanation: Pooling averages group B into a figure dominated by group A and hides exactly the subgroup in question.

questions.stem: An auditor tests a model for an error-rate gap in each of 20 independent subgroups, using a 5% significance level for every test. Suppose the model truly performs identically in all 20 subgroups. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If no subgroup is flagged, the model is shown to perform equally well in all of them.
statements.explanation: A null result may reflect low power in small subgroups, which is not evidence of equality.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The expected number of subgroups flagged by chance is 1.
statements.explanation: Twenty tests at a 5% rate give 20 x 0.05 = 1.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A subgroup found by searching through many possible splits after seeing the data is weaker evidence of a real gap than one chosen in advance.
statements.explanation: Post hoc searching multiplies the number of implicit tests and inflates false findings.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The probability that at least one subgroup is flagged by chance is 5%, since each test has a 5% false-flag rate.
statements.explanation: The 5% applies per test; across 20 independent tests the chance of at least one false flag is much larger.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The probability that at least one subgroup is flagged by chance is about 64%.
statements.explanation: One minus 0.95 raised to the 20th power is 0.64.

questions.stem: A face-attribute classifier is tested on 2,000 images, with 500 images in each combination of gender (men, women) and skin tone (lighter, darker). The error counts out of 500 are: lighter-skinned men 5, darker-skinned men 105, lighter-skinned women 55, darker-skinned women 55. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An audit by gender alone would report an 11% error rate for men and 11% for women.
statements.explanation: Men have 110 errors in 1,000 images and women have 110 errors in 1,000 images.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The error rate for darker-skinned men is 21%, which is 21 times the 1% rate for lighter-skinned men.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With 10 binary attributes there are about 100 intersectional subgroups to evaluate.
statements.explanation: There are 2^10 = 1,024 combinations, and the number grows multiplicatively with each added attribute.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because error rates are equal across men and across women, error rates must also be equal across the four combinations.
statements.explanation: The marginal equality masks wide cell-level differences, from 1% to 21%.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When an intersectional cell has too few examples to estimate error precisely, that cell should be dropped from the audit.
statements.explanation: Dropping it hides subgroups that may be most affected; the right response is to report the wide uncertainty or to collect more data.

questions.stem: Two neighbourhoods, X and Y, each have 10,000 residents, and in each of them 10% commit an offence in a given year. Police patrol X heavily, so 60% of offences there lead to an arrest; in Y only 30% do. A team trains a model to predict "arrested in the next year" from past records. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Recorded arrest rates are 6% in X and 3% in Y even though offending rates are equal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A model that is calibrated to the arrest label within each neighbourhood will, if next year's arrest rates match those above, give residents of X an average score about twice that of residents of Y.
statements.explanation: A model calibrated within a neighbourhood has an average score equal to that neighbourhood's arrest rate, 6% in X against 3% in Y, a ratio of two.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Adding more years of arrest records produced by the same patrol pattern would shrink the gap between X and Y.
statements.explanation: More records from the same process estimate the same distorted rates more precisely; the offset remains.

statements.label: D
statements.text: High accuracy at predicting arrests shows that the model identifies offenders equally well in both neighbourhoods.
statements.explanation: Accuracy is measured against the arrest label, and that label's relationship to offending differs by neighbourhood.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Using victim-reported offences as the outcome, which depends less on patrol patterns, could reduce the distortion but has its own reporting biases.
statements.explanation: Changing the label to a measure less tied to enforcement intensity reduces dependence on patrol patterns.

questions.source: Three flavors of bias, mapped to the ten types
questions.stem: A hospital program enrols patients whose predicted annual cost is at least 7 units, as a stand-in for health need. Need is spread evenly across levels 1 to 10 in two groups of equal size. Group A faces no access barriers, so cost equals need; group B faces barriers, so cost is 0.7 times need. The model predicts cost perfectly for everyone. "High need" means level 7 or above. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: All of group A's high-need patients are enrolled, compared with a quarter of group B's.
statements.explanation: Group A levels 7 to 10 cost 7 to 10 and are all enrolled; in group B only level 10 reaches a cost of 7.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The disparity arises because the model predicts cost less accurately for group B than for group A.
statements.explanation: The model is assumed perfect; the problem is that cost measures need differently in the two groups.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Deleting the group indicator from the model's features would equalize enrolment of high-need patients.
statements.explanation: Enrolment follows predicted cost, and cost itself understates group B's need, so removing the group column does not change what the label measures.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Replacing the label with a direct clinical measure of need would target the intended construct, though it may carry its own distortions.
statements.explanation: The mismatch is between the label and the construct, and a measure closer to the construct reduces it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because cost is predicted accurately, it is a valid measure of health need for both groups.
statements.explanation: Predictive accuracy for a label says nothing about whether the label measures the construct of interest.

questions.stem: A lender approved 4,000 of 10,000 applicants under its scoring policy; 200 of the approved applicants defaulted (5.0%). As an experiment, it approved a random sample of 200 of the 6,000 denied applicants, and 24 of them defaulted (12.0%, with a margin of about 4.5 points either side). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Under the original policy the default outcome of a denied applicant is never observed, because no loan is issued.
statements.explanation: Outcomes exist only for those who receive the favourable decision, so labels are selectively observed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Training a new model on approved applicants only and testing it on held-out approved applicants gives an unbiased estimate of its performance on the full pool.
statements.explanation: Training and test data both come from the selected subgroup, so the estimate says nothing reliable about the denied region.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The 5.0% default rate among approved applicants is the default rate for the whole applicant pool.
statements.explanation: The approved group was selected by the score and contains the applicants least likely to default.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the denied applicants were chosen by the old policy, a random sample of them cannot be representative of the denied group.
statements.explanation: A random draw from the denied group represents that group, whatever process put its members there.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Combining the approved group's rate with the experimental estimate for denied applicants suggests that about 9.2% of the whole pool would default.

questions.source: Leverage analysis — finding the high-leverage intervention point
questions.stem: Two districts have the same true incident rate. Each cycle, 1,000 patrol hours are divided between them, and the number of incidents recorded in a district is proportional to the patrol hours it receives. The first cycle splits hours 600 and 400 between districts 1 and 2. In every later cycle hours are split in proportion to the incidents recorded in the previous cycle. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Each district's recorded count is an unbiased estimate of its true incident rate, because the counts come from real events.
statements.explanation: The counts depend on how many incidents are observed, which depends on patrol hours, so they favour the heavily patrolled district.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Setting aside some patrol hours for randomly chosen districts, or measuring incidents independently of patrol presence, would let the data reveal the equal rates.
statements.explanation: Random or independent measurement breaks the link between past records and where observation happens.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If all hours instead go to the district with more recorded incidents each cycle, district 2 records zero incidents from the second cycle on.
statements.explanation: With no patrol hours no incidents are recorded there, and the data then appear to confirm that district 2 has none.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Under this rule the split stays at 600 and 400 in every cycle, although the true rates are equal.
statements.explanation: Recorded incidents are proportional to patrol hours, so allocating in proportion to records reproduces the same shares.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Given enough cycles, the recorded counts will converge to equal as the system accumulates more and more data.
statements.explanation: The records reflect where patrols went rather than where incidents occur, so the 60/40 split is a fixed point that never corrects.

questions.stem: A training set has 1,000 examples: group A has 360 positive and 240 negative labels, and group B has 120 positive and 280 negative labels. A reweighing scheme gives each combination of group and label the weight P(group) x P(label) / P(group and label), where each P is the share of the training set. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Training on the reweighted data guarantees equal selection rates for the two groups on new data.
statements.explanation: Weights make group and label independent in the training sample; the learned model's predictions on new data can still differ by group.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Group B's positive examples each count 1.6 times as much as an average example.
statements.explanation: P(B) x P(positive) / P(B and positive) = 0.4 x 0.48 / 0.12 = 1.6.

statements.label: C
statements.text: After weighting, the positive-label rate is 48% in both groups.
statements.explanation: Group A gives 288 / (288 + 312) = 0.48 and group B gives 192 / (192 + 208) = 0.48.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Reweighing addresses the association between group and label in the training sample, not whether each individual's label is accurate.
statements.explanation: Weights change how much each row counts, while the label on each row remains as recorded.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Computing the weights requires knowing each training example's group, even if the group is never given to the model as an input.
statements.explanation: The weights depend on P(group), so group membership must be recorded for the training rows even when the model never uses it as a feature.

questions.stem: Two groups of 1,000 applicants each receive integer scores from 1 to 5 from a model. Counts at scores 1 to 5 are 100, 200, 300, 250, 150 for group A and 300, 300, 200, 150, 50 for group B. Under a single cutoff, applicants scoring 4 or 5 are selected. A proposal would instead select scores 4 and 5 in group A and scores 3, 4 and 5 in group B. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If group B's lower scores reflect biased labels, the proposal equalizes selection rates without making the scores a valid measure.
statements.explanation: Post-processing acts on outputs and leaves the learned score relationships, and any bias in them, in place.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The proposal changes the scores the model assigns to each applicant, because the cutoffs are part of the scoring.
statements.explanation: Only the cutoff applied to the scores changes; the scores themselves are untouched.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Under the proposal both groups have a 40% selection rate, yet a group B applicant scoring 3 is selected and a group A applicant scoring 3 is not.
statements.explanation: Group B selects 200 + 150 + 50 = 400, and group A at score 3 falls below its cutoff.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Under the single cutoff, 40% of group A and 20% of group B are selected.
statements.explanation: Group A has 250 + 150 = 400 selected and group B has 150 + 50 = 200.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The proposal can be carried out without knowing an applicant's group at decision time, since the scores already encode it.
statements.explanation: A different cutoff for each group requires knowing which group an applicant belongs to when deciding.

questions.source: Leverage analysis — finding the high-leverage intervention point
questions.stem: A résumé-ranking model trained on a firm's past hiring decisions selects group B candidates less often than group A candidates with the same measured experience. The team considers reweighing the training data, adding a fairness penalty to the training loss, setting score cutoffs separately by group, and changing how human reviewers use the ranking. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reweighing the training data guarantees equal selection rates in the final decisions, whatever happens after training.
statements.explanation: It adjusts the training sample only; cutoffs, reviewers and the learner's behaviour can still produce unequal rates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If most of the disparity arises when reviewers override the model's rankings, changes to the training data will remove most of it.
statements.explanation: A disparity created at review lies outside the reach of the training data.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A drop in agreement with the historical hiring decisions after mitigation shows that the mitigated model has become worse at identifying strong candidates.
statements.explanation: The historical decisions are the thing under suspicion, so lower agreement with them can reflect less copying of past skew rather than lower quality.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Setting cutoffs by group leaves what the model learned from past decisions unchanged and changes only how scores are acted on.
statements.explanation: Post-processing modifies decisions, not the learned scores.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A mitigation applied at one stage of the pipeline makes checks at the later stages unnecessary once it has been validated.
statements.explanation: Disparity can enter or return at later stages such as cutoffs and review, so each stage needs its own check.

questions.source: A limit case: when the leverage is upstream of your pipeline — and who owns it then
questions.stem: A bank buys a credit-risk model from a vendor. The vendor trained it on records bought from a data broker, with "repaid" and "defaulted" labels taken from another lender's earlier approval history. The bank chooses the approval cutoff and sends borderline cases to loan officers. An audit finds a large approval gap between two groups. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Buying the model from a vendor moves responsibility for the outcomes of the bank's lending decisions to the vendor.
statements.explanation: The bank makes the lending decisions and cannot contract away accountability for them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Tracing the largest source of disparity to its step and naming who controls it lets the fix be directed to someone able to make it.
statements.explanation: Remedies fail when aimed at a party with no control over the step where the disparity is created.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The vendor should be held accountable for documenting what the training data contain and what the model has and has not been validated for.
statements.explanation: A deployer cannot judge fitness for use without this information from the party that built the model.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The bank is accountable for its choice of cutoff and for how loan officers use the model's output, because it controls those steps.
statements.explanation: Accountability tracks control: the party that can change a decision point owns the consequences of how it is set.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Assigning accountability for a disparity requires identifying an individual engineer who intended harm or acted negligently.
statements.explanation: Accountability can be assigned to roles and organizations that control a step in the pipeline, with no finding of intent.

questions.source: A limit case: when the leverage is upstream of your pipeline — and who owns it then
questions.stem: A datasheet for a dataset records how and why data were collected, who is and is not represented, how labels were produced, and recommended uses. A model card states a model's intended uses, its evaluation data, and its performance broken down by relevant subgroups. An external audit is an evaluation by a party independent of the developer. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A datasheet's account of how labels were produced lets a team judge whether they measure what the model is meant to predict.
statements.explanation: Label provenance is key evidence on whether the target is a valid measure.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Publishing a model card that lists the model's metrics shows that the model is fair to the groups it will affect.
statements.explanation: A model card is a disclosure; it can report poor subgroup performance and does not by itself make the model fair or its contents correct.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A model card reporting subgroup performance with confidence intervals shows where the model is weaker and how well that is known.
statements.explanation: Disaggregated metrics and their uncertainty make weaknesses and data limits inspectable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An external audit is more informative when the auditor can access the model and data and reproduce the reported numbers.
statements.explanation: Independence plus reproducibility lets an audit check claims instead of accepting them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Stating which uses are out of scope lets reviewers judge whether a deployment went beyond what the developer evaluated.
statements.explanation: An explicit scope statement turns a vague expectation into something a deployment can be checked against.

questions.stem: A model is evaluated on a benchmark that is 90% group A and 10% group B, with accuracy of 95% on group A and 75% on group B. It will be deployed on a population that is 50% group A and 50% group B. Assume each group's accuracy in deployment equals its benchmark accuracy. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Accuracy on the benchmark is 93%.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Expected accuracy in deployment is also 93%, because each group's accuracy is unchanged.
statements.explanation: Overall accuracy depends on the mix of groups tested, and the mix changed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Weighting each group's benchmark accuracy by its deployment share predicts about 85% accuracy without any new data.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Doubling the benchmark's size while keeping its 90/10 composition would reveal the mismatch with deployment.
statements.explanation: A larger sample of the same composition narrows noise but cannot show how the model does on a different mix.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A reported accuracy figure is a property of the model alone and does not depend on who is tested.
statements.explanation: It describes the model's performance on a particular population.

questions.stem: Outcome y depends on a feature x differently in two groups. In group A, y = 2x. In group B, y = 2x + 6. Each group has 11 points, with x = 0, 1, ..., 10. A single least-squares line is fitted to all 22 points; it comes out as y = 2x + 3, with R-squared of about 0.82. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A misfit of this kind arises only when one group is much larger than the other.
statements.explanation: Here the groups are equal in size and the pooled line still misfits both.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Collecting many more points from the same two groups will move the pooled intercept to the correct value for both.
statements.explanation: More data from the same groups estimates the same compromise line more precisely; no single intercept fits both.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An R-squared of 0.82 shows that the pooled line fits each group well.
statements.explanation: R-squared summarizes the pooled fit; every point here misses by 3, and the shared slope hides the group-specific offset.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the mean residual over all 22 points is zero, residual diagnostics on the pooled data cannot reveal a group-specific misfit.
statements.explanation: Residuals split by group show a consistent -3 for group A and +3 for group B.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The pooled line overpredicts every group A case by 3 and underpredicts every group B case by 3.
statements.explanation: At any x the line gives 2x + 3, while group A's true value is 2x and group B's is 2x + 6.

questions.source: Three flavors of bias, mapped to the ten types
questions.stem: A screening device reads each person's true value plus Gaussian noise. True values are 6 for people who have a condition and 4 for people who do not; half of each group has the condition. A reading above 5 is classified as positive. The noise standard deviation is 1 for group A and 2 for group B. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The gap shows that the classifier learned a group-specific decision rule from the training examples.
statements.explanation: A single cutoff is applied to everyone; the difference comes from measurement noise.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Applying the same cutoff to both groups is consistent with unequal error rates, so identical rules need not mean identical error burdens.
statements.explanation: The cutoff is the same but the noisier measurement makes errors more frequent in group B.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Accuracy is about 84% for group A and about 69% for group B, although the same rule classifies both.
statements.explanation: Accuracy is one minus the error rate, 1 - 0.159 and 1 - 0.309.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Collecting more labelled training rows measured with the same device would be expected to remove the gap.
statements.explanation: More rows from the same noisy instrument leave each reading just as noisy; improving the measurement or accounting for the noise is what helps.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The false-negative rate is about 16% for group A and about 31% for group B.
statements.explanation: A positive person is missed when the noise pushes the reading to 5 or below, which has probability 0.159 for sd 1 and 0.309 for sd 2.

questions.stem: A classifier has a true positive rate of 80% and a false positive rate of 20% in each of two groups. The share of truly positive people (the base rate) is 30% in group 1 and 50% in group 2. Positive predictive value (PPV) is the share of flagged people who are truly positive. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: PPV is about 63% in group 1 and 80% in group 2.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If both groups had the same 40% base rate, the same error rates would give both groups a PPV of about 73%.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For a classifier with the same true positive rate and the same nonzero false positive rate in two groups, PPV is higher in the group with the higher base rate.
statements.explanation: PPV = p x TPR / (p x TPR + (1 - p) x FPR), which increases with the base rate p when TPR and FPR are fixed and positive.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The PPV gap shows that the classifier is being applied incorrectly in the group with the lower base rate.
statements.explanation: The gap follows arithmetically from equal error rates and unequal base rates; no misapplication is needed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Group 1's flagging rule could be changed so that its PPV rises to group 2's 80% while its true and false positive rates stay equal to group 2's.
statements.explanation: With rates held at 80% and 20%, group 1's PPV is fixed at 63% by its 30% base rate, so reaching 80% requires different error rates.

questions.stem: A model approves 30% of group A applicants and 18% of group B applicants, a 12-point gap. The same applicants are scored again with the postcode input replaced by a single constant value, and approval rates become 29% and 26%, a 3-point gap. Group membership is not an input to the model. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because group membership is not an input, the remaining 3-point gap must come from the model using group directly.
statements.explanation: Other inputs that correlate with group can carry the remaining gap.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Since the gap shrank, the original 12-point gap can be disregarded as an artifact of one feature and left out of the audit.
statements.explanation: The gap is a real property of the model's decisions, and a feature that contributes to it is part of what needs explaining.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The result shows that postcode causes group differences in approval outcomes in the real world, which is why the gap closed.
statements.explanation: The test intervenes on a model input; it shows how the model works and says nothing about why applicants in different groups differ.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Replacing postcode removed 9 of the 12 points, so most of the model's output disparity depends on that input.
statements.explanation: Three quarters of the gap, (12 - 3) / 12, vanished when the input was neutralized.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The test intervenes on a model input rather than on applicants' lives, so it speaks to how the model uses information.
statements.explanation: It tests whether the output depends on one input, which is a statement about the model.

questions.source: Leverage analysis — finding the high-leverage intervention point
questions.stem: Group A makes up 90% of the data and group B 10%. Three candidate models have error rates (group A, group B) of M1: 5%, 30%; M2: 6%, 20%; M3: 3%, 45%. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Switching from M3 to M2 would raise the average error by more than one percentage point.
statements.explanation: The increase is 0.2 points, from 7.2% to 7.4%.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Average error weights the two groups equally, whatever their share of the data.
statements.explanation: It weights each group by its share of the data, 90% and 10%.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An objective that minimizes average error is neutral between the groups, because it applies one formula to everyone.
statements.explanation: Errors on the larger group count nine times as much, so the objective favours performance there.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Choosing the model with the lowest average error selects M3, which has the highest group B error rate of the three.
statements.explanation: Average errors are 7.5% for M1, 7.4% for M2 and 7.2% for M3.

statements.label: E
statements.text: M2 has both the lowest average error and the lowest worst-group error of the three models.
statements.explanation: M2's worst-group error (20%) is the lowest, but its average (7.4%) is higher than M3's (7.2%).

questions.source: Leverage analysis — finding the high-leverage intervention point
questions.stem: A model flags 20% of applicants in each of two groups for adverse action, and a human reviewer then upholds 50% of the flags in group A and 80% in group B. The final adverse-action rate is the share of all applicants whose flag is upheld. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The gap in upheld rates may partly reflect real differences between the flagged cases, which should be examined before judging reviewers.
statements.explanation: Without comparing like cases, rate differences cannot be attributed to reviewer behaviour.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The different upheld rates alone establish that reviewers are prejudiced against group B.
statements.explanation: The flagged cases may differ in true risk, so the rates call for investigation but do not establish motive.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Final adverse-action rates are 10% for group A and 16% for group B.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Comparing the flag rate, upheld rate and final rate by group at each stage shows where the disparity arises.
statements.explanation: A stage-by-stage breakdown localizes the step at which rates diverge.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Equal flag rates for the two groups guarantee equal final outcomes for the two groups.
statements.explanation: The review step can create or remove disparity after the model has produced equal flag rates.

questions.stem: A text-generating model screens résumés and answers "shortlist" or "reject" for each. Auditors build 200 pairs of résumés that are identical except for a first name signalling group A or group B. Each résumé was submitted once with the model's sampling randomness switched on, so repeating a submission could give a different answer. Results: shortlisted in both résumés of the pair, 90; in neither, 68; only the group A name, 30; only the group B name, 12. Shortlisting rates are 60% for group A names and 51% for group B names. An exact sign test on the 30 against 12 discordant pairs gives p of about 0.008. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The test result shows that the model was trained on discriminatory hiring data and learned to copy it.
statements.explanation: The test shows that outputs depend on the name; the origin of that dependence in training data, tuning or prompt is a separate question.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The 90 pairs shortlisted for both names and the 68 rejected for both play no part in the exact sign test.
statements.explanation: The exact sign test uses only the pairs on which the two names were treated differently, the 30 and the 12, so the concordant pairs do not enter it (they would matter for other quantities, such as the size of the rate difference).

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because each pair differs only in the name, differences in qualifications cannot explain the 30-to-12 split.
statements.explanation: Matching by construction removes the qualification confounder within the tested résumés.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Run-to-run randomness in the model's answers makes the 30-to-12 split uninterpretable as evidence.
statements.explanation: Randomness is already part of the null distribution: with no name effect the 42 discordant pairs would split about evenly, and the test gives p of about 0.008.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because outputs vary between runs, repeating each pair several times would better estimate each name's shortlisting probability.
statements.explanation: Repetitions average out sampling randomness within each pair.

questions.stem: Two annotators label 100 clinical notes as positive or negative for a condition. Both say positive for 85 notes and both say negative for 5; each is alone in saying positive for 5 notes. Each annotator labels 90% of notes positive. Cohen's kappa is (observed agreement - chance agreement) / (1 - chance agreement). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Chance agreement is about 82%, which gives a kappa of about 0.44.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Raw agreement is the better statistic here, because chance agreement is irrelevant when one category dominates.
statements.explanation: Chance agreement is largest exactly when one category dominates, which is when raw agreement misleads.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A high kappa shows that the labels measure the condition accurately, since the annotators agree on them.
statements.explanation: Annotators can agree with each other and still share the same systematic error, so agreement shows consistency rather than validity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If kappa falls sharply once annotators are blinded to a patient's earlier diagnosis, the unblinded labels were probably shaped by it.
statements.explanation: Agreement that depends on seeing a cue indicates annotators are following the cue rather than assessing the note independently.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Kappa is about 0.90, the same as the raw agreement, since kappa simply restates the share of matching labels.
statements.explanation: Kappa corrects raw agreement for agreement expected by chance, and here that correction is large.

questions.source: Three flavors of bias, mapped to the ten types
questions.stem: A skin-lesion classifier has a 12% error rate on images of darker skin and 4% on lighter skin in a held-out test set labelled by the same process as the training data. Darker-skin images are 8% of the training set. A balanced audit set, labelled by an independent expert panel using biopsy results, shows the same 12% against 4% gap. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because the audit labels came from an independent process, the gap is not an artifact of how the original test labels were made.
statements.explanation: The original test labels shared a source with the training labels and could share its errors, whereas independent labels remove that explanation for the measured gap.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adding many more darker-skin images to the training set is certain to close the gap, as those images are the scarce input.
statements.explanation: The gap may come from label quality or measurement differences that more images of the same kind would not change.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The 8% share of darker-skin images establishes that under-representation is the cause of the gap.
statements.explanation: Under-representation is consistent with the gap but has not been tested; label quality, image quality and lesion appearance could also contribute.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the audit labels were independent, differences in image quality between skin tones are ruled out as a cause.
statements.explanation: Independent labelling does not control for how the images were captured, which can still differ by group.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The persistence of the gap shows that the training labels were accurate for both skin tones.
statements.explanation: A model trained on skewed labels would also show a gap against correct labels, so the audit cannot distinguish that case from under-representation.

questions.stem: A binary classifier outputs a decision Ŷ (1 means the favorable decision) for people whose true outcome is Y (1 means the person actually qualifies). People belong to group a or group b. Check each statement that is true about standard group fairness criteria.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Predictive parity requires the precision of favorable decisions, P(Y=1 | Ŷ=1, group), to be equal across groups.
statements.explanation: Predictive parity compares positive predictive value (precision) across groups.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Equalized odds requires both the true-positive rate and the false-positive rate to be equal across groups.
statements.explanation: Equalized odds is the conjunction of true-positive-rate parity and false-positive-rate parity.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Equal opportunity requires the false-positive rate, P(Ŷ=1 | Y=0, group), to be equal across groups, with no condition on people who qualify.
statements.explanation: Equal opportunity is parity of the true-positive rate, P(Ŷ=1 | Y=1, group); false-positive parity is a separate condition.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Equalized odds implies equal opportunity, because equal true-positive rates are one of its two components.
statements.explanation: Equal opportunity asks only for the true-positive half, so anything that satisfies equalized odds satisfies it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Demographic (statistical) parity requires P(Ŷ=1 | group) to be equal across groups, without conditioning on Y.
statements.explanation: It constrains the rate of favorable decisions alone, whatever the people's true outcomes.

questions.stem: A lender's model approves (Ŷ=1) or declines loan applicants. On held-out data, Y=1 means the applicant would have repaid. Group P (1,000 applicants): 240 approved who would repay, 60 approved who would not repay, 160 declined who would repay, 540 declined who would not repay. Group Q (1,000 applicants): 120 approved who would repay, 160 approved who would not repay, 80 declined who would repay, 640 declined who would not repay. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The ratio of approval rates (Q over P) is about 0.93, above a 0.8 screening convention.
statements.explanation: Approval rates are 0.30 for P and 0.28 for Q, and 0.28/0.30 = 0.93.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The true-positive rate is 0.60 in both groups, so equal opportunity holds.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Equalized odds holds in these data.
statements.explanation: Equal true-positive rates are only half of equalized odds, and the false-positive rates differ (0.10 versus 0.20).

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the true-positive rates match, approval precision also matches across groups.
statements.explanation: Precision also depends on the base rate and the false-positive rate; it is 240/300 = 0.80 in P and 120/280, about 0.43, in Q.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Among applicants who would not repay, the approval rate in group Q is twice that in group P.
statements.explanation: False-positive rates are 160/800 = 0.20 for Q and 60/600 = 0.10 for P.

questions.stem: A recruiting model flags applicants (Ŷ=1) for an interview; Y=1 means the applicant was later rated qualified. Group M (500 applicants): 170 flagged and qualified, 30 flagged and not qualified, 80 not flagged but qualified, 220 not flagged and not qualified. Group N (500 applicants): 60 flagged and qualified, 140 flagged and not qualified, 40 not flagged but qualified, 260 not flagged and not qualified. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because demographic parity holds, the groups must have similar false-positive rates.
statements.explanation: Demographic parity ignores true outcomes, so error rates can differ freely; here they are 0.12 and 0.35.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Equal flag rates show the two groups contain the same share of qualified applicants.
statements.explanation: Qualified shares are 250/500 = 0.50 in M and 100/500 = 0.20 in N; the flag rate also depends on the error rates.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The precision of flags is higher in group N than in group M.
statements.explanation: Precision is 170/200 = 0.85 in M and 60/200 = 0.30 in N.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The false-positive rate in group N (0.35) is nearly three times that in group M (0.12).

statements.label: E
statements.text: Both groups are flagged at the same rate, 0.40, so demographic parity holds exactly.
statements.explanation: 200/500 = 0.40 in each group.

questions.stem: A model predicts which patients need follow-up care (Ŷ=1); Y=1 means the patient actually needed it. Group A (1,000 patients): 400 flagged who needed it, 100 not flagged who needed it, 50 flagged who did not, 450 not flagged who did not. Group B (1,000 patients): 160 flagged who needed it, 40 not flagged who needed it, 80 flagged who did not, 720 not flagged who did not. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Equalized odds holds: the true-positive rate is 0.80 and the false-positive rate is 0.10 in both groups.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Demographic parity must also hold here, because equalized odds holds and the error rates are identical in the two groups.
statements.explanation: Flag rate is base rate × TPR + (1 − base rate) × FPR, so equal TPR and FPR still give different flag rates when base rates differ (0.50 versus 0.20).

statements.label: C
statements.text: Even if every group B patient who needed follow-up were flagged, lifting B's flag rate to 0.45 would require a false-positive rate of at least about 0.31 in B.
statements.explanation: B needs 450 flags, only 200 patients needed follow-up, so at least 250 of the other 800 must be flagged: 250/800 = 0.3125.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The gap in flag rates (0.45 versus 0.24) is explained by different shares of patients who needed follow-up, not by different error rates.
statements.explanation: The error rates are identical across groups, so only the 50% versus 20% need rates can produce the gap.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The precision of flags is the same in both groups, since the true-positive and false-positive rates match.
statements.explanation: Precision is 400/450, about 0.89, in A and 160/240, about 0.67, in B.

questions.source: Each metric is a values claim
questions.stem: A resume-screening tool advanced 180 of 600 applicants in group X and 168 of 400 applicants in group Y. A reviewer computes the ratio of the lower group's advance rate to the higher group's advance rate and flags any ratio below 0.8 for further review (a screening convention, not a verdict). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The ratio shows how many qualified applicants were missed in each group.
statements.explanation: The ratio compares selection rates only and uses no information about who was qualified.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The ratio is about 0.71, so the screen is flagged under the convention.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Had group X's advance rate been 0.34 (a ratio of about 0.81), the screen would pass the convention, which would show the process is free of discrimination.
statements.explanation: Passing a ratio threshold does not rule out discrimination, which can exist above the threshold or act through other mechanisms.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Being flagged under the convention shows that the screen is unlawful.
statements.explanation: A ratio below 0.8 is a heuristic that triggers further review; it does not itself establish a legal violation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A gap of 12 percentage points with samples of 600 and 400 applicants is the sort of difference chance alone would plausibly produce between groups with identical true rates.
statements.explanation: A two-proportion z-test gives z of about 3.9 (pooled rate 0.348), far beyond what chance produces at these sample sizes.

questions.source: Each metric is a values claim
questions.stem: A bank's model flags transactions (Ŷ=1) for manual review, which delays the customer, so being flagged is the burden. Over a month, 12% of customers in group R were flagged and 20% in group S. An analyst computes a disparate-impact ratio (lower group rate divided by higher group rate) and compares it with a 0.8 convention that is meant to be applied to the rate of the favorable outcome. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Computed on the rates of not being flagged, the ratio is also 0.60, since the two framings describe the same gap.
statements.explanation: Not-flagged rates are 0.88 and 0.80, and 0.80/0.88 is about 0.91.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Computed on flag rates, the ratio is 0.60.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The gap between the groups is 12 percentage points on the flag rate but only 8 points on the rate of not being flagged, because the two outcomes differ.
statements.explanation: The two rates are complements, so the gap is 8 points either way (0.20 − 0.12 = 0.88 − 0.80).

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because not being flagged is the favorable outcome here, the ratio that matches the convention is about 0.91.
