statements.explanation: The convention is stated on favorable-outcome rates, which here are the not-flagged rates.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The same data can pass or fail the 0.8 convention depending on which outcome is called favorable, so the analyst must state that choice.
statements.explanation: A ratio of 0.60 fails and a ratio of 0.91 passes, so the verdict flips with the framing.

questions.stem: A risk model outputs a probability score, and people with a score of at least 0.5 are flagged. Among flagged people the score takes only two values, 0.6 and 0.9. Group A: 300 flagged people scored 0.6, of whom 180 had the positive outcome, and 100 scored 0.9, of whom 90 had it. Group B: 100 flagged people scored 0.6, of whom 40 had the positive outcome, and 300 scored 0.9, of whom 230 had it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In group B, people who scored 0.9 had the positive outcome about 77% of the time, so the score overstates their risk.
statements.explanation: 230/300 = 0.767, below the stated 0.9.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If a score were calibrated within each group, precision among flagged people would have to be equal across groups.
statements.explanation: Under calibration, precision among flagged people equals their average score, which depends on each group's mix of scores and so can differ.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Among flagged people the positive-outcome rate is 0.675 in both groups, so predictive parity holds at this cutoff.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because predictive parity holds at the cutoff, the score is calibrated within each group.
statements.explanation: Group B's observed rates (0.40 at score 0.6, about 0.77 at score 0.9) do not match its scores, although its overall precision equals A's.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Calibration within groups requires that, at each score value, the observed positive rate matches the score in every group.
statements.explanation: That is the definition: among people given score s, a fraction s should have the positive outcome, in each group.

questions.stem: A model outputs probability scores that take one of three values: 0.2, 0.5 or 0.8. Expected calibration error (ECE) is the sum over score values of (share of people with that score) × |observed positive rate − score|. Group A (1,000 people): score 0.2, 500 people, 105 positive; score 0.5, 300 people, 147 positive; score 0.8, 200 people, 158 positive. Group B (1,000 people): score 0.2, 400 people, 120 positive; score 0.5, 300 people, 165 positive; score 0.8, 300 people, 225 positive. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Equal ECE in the two groups would imply equal true-positive rates.
statements.explanation: ECE measures agreement between scores and outcome frequencies; true-positive rates depend on how scores are turned into decisions and on who actually has the outcome.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Pooling both groups into one ECE calculation gives about 0.04, which hides that group B's calibration error is several times group A's.
statements.explanation: Pooled bins have observed rates 0.25, 0.52 and 0.766, giving ECE of about 0.037, while the group values are 0.01 and 0.07.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With bins of 200 to 500 people, a gap of 0.01 in group A is within what sampling noise could produce.
statements.explanation: The standard error of an observed rate near 0.2 to 0.5 from 200 to 500 people is roughly 0.02 to 0.03.

statements.label: D
statements.text: ECE is about 0.01 for group A and about 0.07 for group B.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In group B, people with score 0.2 had a positive rate below 0.2, so the score overstates their risk and a decision-maker would be too cautious about them.
statements.explanation: Their observed rate is 120/400 = 0.30, above 0.2, so the score understates their risk.

questions.source: The arithmetic — the actual proof, not a gesture
questions.stem: Group 1 has a base rate (share of people with the positive outcome) of 0.5 and group 2 has a base rate of 0.3. A binary classifier is reported to have precision (positive predictive value) of 0.75 and a false-positive rate of 0.10 in both groups. Take these as exact population values. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If both groups instead had base rate 0.4, equal precision of 0.75 and equal false-positive rate of 0.10 would still require different true-positive rates.
statements.explanation: With equal base rates the same relation gives equal true-positive rates, 0.10 × 3 × (0.6/0.4) = 0.45 in both.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The same precision and false-positive rate can be achieved in both groups with a true-positive rate of 0.50 in both.
statements.explanation: A true-positive rate of 0.5 would give precision of about 0.83 in group 1 and 0.68 in group 2, not 0.75 in both.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Collecting more labeled data and training a more flexible model would bring the two true-positive rates together while holding precision and false-positive rate fixed.
statements.explanation: The relation is arithmetic on population rates; with these precision and false-positive values the true-positive rates are pinned at 0.30 and 0.70 whatever the model.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In this example the group with the higher base rate has the higher true-positive rate.
statements.explanation: Group 1, with base rate 0.5, has the lower true-positive rate (0.30 versus 0.70).

statements.label: E
statements.text: Bayes' rule implies the true-positive rates must be about 0.30 in group 1 and 0.70 in group 2.
statements.explanation: Precision odds equal base-rate odds × TPR/FPR, so TPR = 0.10 × 3 × (1−p)/p, which is 0.30 for p = 0.5 and 0.70 for p = 0.3.

questions.source: The arithmetic — the actual proof, not a gesture
questions.stem: Two groups have base rates of 0.5 and 0.2. Consider two classifiers: (i) one that approves every person in both groups regardless of features, and (ii) a perfect classifier that approves exactly the people who have the positive outcome. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Classifier (i) satisfies predictive parity.
statements.explanation: Its precision equals each group's base rate, 0.5 versus 0.2.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Classifier (ii) satisfies equalized odds and predictive parity but violates demographic parity.
statements.explanation: Perfect prediction gives TPR 1, FPR 0 and precision 1 in both groups, but selection rates equal the unequal base rates.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Classifier (i) satisfies equalized odds, because its true-positive rate and its false-positive rate are both 1 in each group.
statements.explanation: Approving everyone gives TPR = FPR = 1 in every group, so the rates match.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because classifier (i) satisfies two of the three criteria, it is a useful way of resolving the conflict between them without giving up predictive value.
statements.explanation: It carries no information about individuals, so it avoids the conflict only by being useless as a predictor.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Classifier (i) satisfies demographic parity.
statements.explanation: Both groups are approved at rate 1.

questions.source: The toolkit and what it cannot do
questions.stem:
A lender scores applicants and approves anyone whose score is at or above a cutoff. On held-out data, group G has 1,000 people who would repay and 1,000 who would not; group H has 400 who would repay and 1,600 who would not. The table gives, for each cutoff, how many of each kind score at or above it.

| Cutoff | G would repay | G would not | H would repay | H would not |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.4 | 900 | 500 | 340 | 720 |
| 0.5 | 800 | 350 | 280 | 480 |
| 0.6 | 700 | 250 | 220 | 320 |
| 0.7 | 550 | 150 | 140 | 160 |

Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With a single cutoff of 0.6, the true-positive rate is 0.70 in G and 0.55 in H.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Using cutoff 0.6 for G and 0.5 for H makes both the true-positive rates and the false-positive rates equal across the two groups, so equalized odds holds.
statements.explanation: True-positive rates are both 0.70, but false-positive rates are 250/1000 = 0.25 for G and 480/1600 = 0.30 for H.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Under cutoffs of 0.6 for G and 0.5 for H, an applicant in G and an applicant in H who both score 0.55 receive different decisions.
statements.explanation: The G applicant is declined (0.55 < 0.6) and the H applicant is approved (0.55 ≥ 0.5), the individual-level objection to group-specific cutoffs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Even if both groups had identical true-positive rates and identical false-positive rates, their base rates (0.5 versus 0.2) would still leave the precision of approvals unequal.
statements.explanation: Precision odds equal base-rate odds × TPR/FPR, so identical rates with base-rate odds of 1 and 0.25 give unequal precision (for example TPR 0.70 and FPR 0.25 give about 0.74 versus 0.41); in the table the gap is wider (0.74 versus 0.37) partly because H's false-positive rate is also higher.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Using cutoff 0.6 for G and 0.5 for H makes the precision of approvals about equal in the two groups, since the true-positive rates match.
statements.explanation: Precision is 700/950, about 0.74, for G and 280/760, about 0.37, for H.

questions.source: Each metric is a values claim
questions.stem: Two equal-sized groups have true base rates of 0.6 and 0.3, and the recorded labels are exactly correct. A perfect classifier predicts every label correctly. Here demographic parity means equal selection rates in the two groups. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Any classifier with equal selection rates in the two groups must have overall accuracy of at most 0.85.
statements.explanation: If both groups are selected at rate s, their error rates are at least |0.6 − s| and |0.3 − s|, which average at least 0.15, so accuracy is at most 0.85.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reaching demographic parity here means moving some decisions away from the true labels in one group or both.
statements.explanation: Closing the gap in selection rates means moving decisions away from the true labels in one or both groups.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The perfect classifier satisfies equalized odds but violates demographic parity.
statements.explanation: It has TPR 1 and FPR 0 in both groups, while its selection rates equal the unequal base rates.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The perfect classifier's selection rates are 0.6 and 0.3, a ratio (lower over higher) of 0.5.
statements.explanation: A perfect classifier selects exactly those with the positive outcome, and 0.3/0.6 = 0.5.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Demographic parity can be reached here without adding misclassifications, since the recorded outcomes are correct.
statements.explanation: Any move toward equal selection rates departs from the true labels, so errors rise, to at least 0.15 of people.

questions.stem: A lender removes the field recording applicants' ethnicity from its model's inputs but keeps postal code, first name and school attended. The company concludes that outcomes cannot differ by ethnicity. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Without the field in the model, no one can measure group-level error rates.
statements.explanation: Group labels can be kept in the evaluation data, apart from the model's inputs, and used to compute rates by group.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A rule that never uses the protected attribute cannot be found to have disparate impact in legal frameworks that recognize it.
statements.explanation: Disparate-impact doctrine concerns facially neutral practices that burden a group, so a rule can be neutral on its face and still be challenged.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Dropping the field guarantees equal false-positive rates across ethnic groups.
statements.explanation: Removing an input guarantees nothing about error rates, which depend on how outcomes and the remaining features relate to group.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Postal code and similar fields can correlate with ethnicity, so the model may still produce outcomes that differ by ethnic group.
statements.explanation: Proxies can carry much of the information in the removed attribute, so group-correlated outcomes can persist.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Keeping the field in the evaluation data, while excluding it from the model's inputs, lets analysts audit outcomes by group.
statements.explanation: Auditing needs the attribute at evaluation time even when the model is not allowed to use it.

questions.stem: Individual fairness in its Lipschitz form requires that for any two people x and y, the distance between their outcome distributions is at most a task-specific distance d(x, y) between the people. A scoring system gives each person a probability of approval, so the distance between two people's outcome distributions is the absolute difference of their approval probabilities. Four people have approval probabilities M(x1) = 0.70, M(x2) = 0.55, M(x3) = 0.60 and M(x4) = 0.20, and pairwise distances d(x1,x2) = 0.10, d(x1,x3) = 0.30, d(x1,x4) = 0.50, d(x2,x3) = 0.35, d(x2,x4) = 0.40, d(x3,x4) = 0.45. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Whether the pair (x1, x2) counts as a violation depends on the similarity distance chosen, not only on the model's outputs.
statements.explanation: With d(x1,x2) = 0.20 the same outputs satisfy the condition.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The pair (x1, x4) violates the condition, because their outputs differ by as much as their distance.
statements.explanation: Their outputs differ by exactly 0.50, equal to d(x1,x4), and the condition allows equality.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The pair (x1, x2) violates the condition.
statements.explanation: Their outputs differ by 0.15, which exceeds d(x1,x2) = 0.10.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If x1 and x2 belong to different demographic groups, the violation shows a group-level disparity in approval rates.
statements.explanation: The condition compares individual pairs; one violating pair says nothing about the groups' overall approval rates.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Changing M(x1) to 0.62, with all other values unchanged, would remove the violation without creating a new one.
statements.explanation: The gaps become 0.07 (limit 0.10), 0.02 (limit 0.30) and 0.42 (limit 0.50).

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about individual fairness (similar individuals should be treated similarly) and its relation to group fairness criteria.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Checking all pairs of individuals becomes expensive for large populations, so audits often sample pairs.
statements.explanation: The number of pairs grows quadratically with the population.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A model can satisfy demographic parity while treating two near-identical people very differently.
statements.explanation: Parity constrains group rates; it does not limit which individuals within a group receive the favorable decision.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A model can treat similar people alike under a chosen metric and still show different selection rates between groups.
statements.explanation: If the groups differ on features the metric counts as relevant, consistent treatment of similar people coexists with unequal group rates.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Individual fairness can be evaluated from per-group confusion matrices alone, since they contain every person's outcome.
statements.explanation: It needs a notion of which individuals are similar and a comparison of their treatment, which group-level matrices average away.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The choice of similarity metric is a technical detail that does not affect the fairness conclusion, since any reasonable metric agrees.
statements.explanation: Different metrics give different verdicts on the same pair; deciding which differences between people are relevant is a substantive judgment.

questions.source: Causal fairness: what the data cannot tell you
questions.stem: In a causal model of a loan decision, a protected attribute A influences an education credential E, and E is an input to a predictor Ŷ. Unobserved background factors U also influence E. A predictor is counterfactually fair for an individual if its prediction would have had the same distribution had A taken a different value, with that individual's background factors U held fixed. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A predictor that takes E as an input is in general not counterfactually fair here, because changing A changes E.
statements.explanation: With U fixed, a different A produces a different E, which moves the prediction.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Judging counterfactual fairness requires assumptions about the causal structure; observed data alone does not settle it.
statements.explanation: Different causal structures can produce the same observed distribution while implying different counterfactuals.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Counterfactual fairness implies equalized odds, because a predictor that ignores the protected attribute's effects must have equal error rates.
statements.explanation: It is an individual-level causal condition and places no constraint on error rates conditional on the true outcome.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Which paths from A to the prediction are acceptable is a value judgment that the causal graph does not supply.
statements.explanation: The graph shows which paths exist; whether a path through a credential is legitimate is a normative question.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A predictor using only variables not causally downstream of A is counterfactually fair with respect to this model.
statements.explanation: Its inputs do not change when A is changed counterfactually, so neither does its output.

questions.stem: A system allocates a benefit b_i to each of eight people. Generalized entropy with parameter 2 is GE(2) = (1/N) Σ ½[(b_i/μ)² − 1], where μ is the mean benefit; this equals half the squared coefficient of variation (population standard deviation divided by the mean, squared). Group P has benefits 0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 0.8 and group Q has benefits 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5. The between-group component is GE(2) computed after replacing each person's benefit by their group's mean benefit; the within-group component is the remainder. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Most of GE(2) comes from the between-group component.
statements.explanation: Both group means are 0.5, so the between-group component is 0 and all of GE(2) is within-group.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A comparison of the two groups' mean benefits would show no group-level disparity.
statements.explanation: The means are 0.5 and 0.5.

statements.label: C
statements.text: GE(2) for the eight people is 0.09.
statements.explanation: The mean is 0.5 and the population variance is 0.045, so GE(2) = ½ × 0.045/0.25 = 0.09.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Doubling every person's benefit would double GE(2).
statements.explanation: GE depends on b_i/μ, so multiplying all benefits by a constant leaves it unchanged.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because the group means are equal, the benefits are distributed fairly and no further inequality analysis is needed.
statements.explanation: Members of group P receive very unequal benefits (0.2 versus 0.8), a large within-group inequality that group means hide.

questions.source: The arithmetic — the actual proof, not a gesture
questions.stem: A risk tool assigns each person a score in [0, 1]. Assume the two groups have different base rates (0.4 and 0.2) and that the score is imperfect, meaning it does not separate all positives from all negatives. Three properties are of interest: (1) calibration within groups, meaning among people with a given score the positive rate equals the score in each group; (2) equal average score among actual positives in the two groups; (3) equal average score among actual negatives in the two groups. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The conflict is a property of the groups' base rates and the score's imperfection, not of any particular learning algorithm.
statements.explanation: The argument uses only population rates, so any scoring method with these properties is subject to it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The result implies that calibration within groups cannot hold in any form, even for a single group considered alone.
statements.explanation: Calibration within groups can hold by itself; the result says it cannot be combined with both balance properties under these assumptions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Gathering more labeled data does not remove the conflict; it only makes the group rates better estimated.
statements.explanation: The impossibility concerns the population quantities themselves.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the two groups had equal base rates, a score with the same distribution in both groups could satisfy all three properties.
statements.explanation: With equal base rates and identical joint distributions of score and outcome, calibration and both balance conditions hold together.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Under these assumptions, properties (1), (2) and (3) cannot all hold.
statements.explanation: With unequal base rates and an imperfect score, calibration within groups forces the average scores among positives or among negatives to differ.

questions.source: The COMPAS case — the theorem in public
questions.stem: A pretrial risk tool labels each person high-risk or low-risk. An analyst finds that among people who were not re-arrested, 45% of group X and 20% of group Y were labeled high-risk. The vendor replies that among people labeled high-risk, 60% of both groups were re-arrested, and that the groups' re-arrest base rates are 0.5 for X and 0.3 for Y. Take all figures as exact. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The analyst's finding by itself shows that the tool uses group membership as an input.
statements.explanation: A tool that never sees group membership can still show different error rates through correlated features and differing base rates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The analyst's figures and the vendor's figures can both be correct at the same time.
statements.explanation: They measure different quantities, error rates conditional on the true outcome and precision conditional on the tool's output, and with unequal base rates they can differ in this way.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The disagreement is a factual one that more data would settle by showing which set of figures is correct.
statements.explanation: Both statements are already accurate; the dispute is over which criterion should take priority.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the tool were adjusted until the false-positive rates matched while precision stayed equal, the false-negative rates would have to differ.
statements.explanation: Equal precision and equal false-positive rate force the true-positive rates apart when base rates differ and the tool is imperfect.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Equal precision of the high-risk label means wrongly labeled people in the two groups bear the same burden.
statements.explanation: The false-positive rates are 0.45 and 0.20, so non-re-arrested people in X are labeled high-risk far more often.

questions.source: Each metric is a values claim
questions.stem: An organization must choose which group fairness criterion to prioritize for two systems. System one is a cancer-screening aid: a missed case can be fatal, and a false alarm leads to an inexpensive follow-up test. System two flags benefit claims as suspected fraud: a flagged person's payments are frozen during review. Check each statement that is a sound argument about choosing criteria.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For the screening aid, comparing false-negative rates (equivalently, true-positive rates) across groups targets the main harm.
statements.explanation: The costliest error is a missed case, and equal true-positive rates ask that this error not fall more heavily on one group.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Demographic parity is the right criterion for both systems whenever base rates differ, since base rates are irrelevant to harm.
statements.explanation: Equal selection rates ignore who is harmed by which error, and base-rate differences change what equal rates would mean.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For the fraud flag, comparing false-positive rates across groups targets the harm that matters most.
statements.explanation: A wrongly flagged person bears the cost, and the false-positive rate measures how often that happens to people who did nothing wrong.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Which criterion to prioritize can be derived from the confusion matrices alone, without knowing who bears the cost of each kind of error.
statements.explanation: The matrices give rates, but the choice depends on the cost of each error type to the people affected.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The criterion that gives the highest overall accuracy is the right one for both systems, since accuracy summarizes every error.
statements.explanation: Overall accuracy weights all errors equally and says nothing about which group bears which error.

questions.stem: A team has built a loan-approval model by minimizing overall log loss and is now deciding how to report fairness. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Choosing which error rates to equalize trades one group's harms against another's, so accountable people should make and record the choice.
statements.explanation: A value-laden trade-off should be owned by someone with authority and accountability, with reasons on the record.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If a regulator requires a specific metric, decisions remain open, such as which groups to compare and what tolerance counts as equal.
statements.explanation: A named metric fixes the formula but not its application.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A tool that computes every fairness metric can identify which metric is correct for the deployment, since the best one scores highest.
statements.explanation: Metrics describe consequences; choosing among them depends on values and on who bears the costs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the model passes the chosen metric, there is no need to document which other criteria were traded away, since the chosen one was met.
statements.explanation: Passing one criterion can mean others fail, and affected parties and reviewers need to know what was given up.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because the loss function never mentions groups, minimizing overall log loss has no bearing on how errors are distributed across groups.
statements.explanation: Minimizing an average loss over all examples weights every example equally, which determines which errors the model tolerates and so how error rates fall across groups, whether or not anyone chose it.

questions.stem: A model predicts whether a person will be arrested within two years. An audit finds equal true-positive and false-positive rates across two neighborhoods, measured against arrest records. Suppose one neighborhood is patrolled much more heavily, so the same behavior is more likely to lead to an arrest there. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Using different cutoffs per neighborhood would correct the measurement problem by rebalancing who is flagged.
statements.explanation: Cutoffs change decisions, not how the recorded outcome relates to behavior; the measurement problem remains.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A metric on this label measures agreement with arrest patterns, which reflect enforcement as well as behavior.
statements.explanation: The model is scored on matching the recorded outcome, not on matching the behavior the outcome stands in for.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The audit certifies that neither neighborhood is disadvantaged by the tool, since the error rates are equal.
statements.explanation: It certifies parity with respect to a label that may itself encode the disparity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Equal error rates against recorded arrests do not establish equal error rates against actual offending.
statements.explanation: If arrest probability given behavior differs by neighborhood, the recorded outcome measures something different in each.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An independent measure of the behavior would let the team estimate how far the arrest label departs from it.
statements.explanation: A second measure gives a check on the recorded outcome's validity.

questions.stem: In an audit sample, 300 of 400 truly qualified applicants in group A were approved (true-positive rate 0.75) and 24 of 40 truly qualified applicants in group B were approved (true-positive rate 0.60). Approximate 95% intervals for the true-positive rate are 0.71 to 0.79 for A and 0.45 to 0.74 for B. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The interval for B is wider than A's because B's true-positive rate is lower.
statements.explanation: Width depends mainly on sample size (40 versus 400); a rate nearer 0.5 widens it only slightly.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A non-significant result for the small group shows that the two groups have equal true-positive rates, since no difference was detected.
statements.explanation: Low power means a real gap can go undetected; absence of evidence of a gap is not evidence of equality.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Testing many small subgroups at the 5% level makes it likely some gap looks significant by chance.
statements.explanation: With many comparisons, false positives accumulate unless the analysis accounts for multiple testing.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A 15-point gap in the point estimates is enough to conclude with certainty that the true rates differ, since it is large.
statements.explanation: Sampling variation can produce a gap of this size, especially with 40 observations; the conclusion carries uncertainty.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The interval for B is wide, so B's true-positive rate is estimated imprecisely.
statements.explanation: With only 40 qualified applicants the standard error is large.

questions.stem: A screening tool's selection rates, with 500 people in each of four cells, are: women in the north 0.50, women in the south 0.30, men in the north 0.30, men in the south 0.50. A reviewer flags any ratio of lowest rate to highest rate below 0.8. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Passing the check on gender and the check on region separately implies the check on gender-by-region will also pass.
statements.explanation: This example passes both margins and fails the cells.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The ratio of the lowest to the highest of the four cell rates is 0.6, which is flagged under the convention.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Women overall and men overall are both selected at 0.40, and the north and the south are both at 0.40.
statements.explanation: Each margin averages one 0.50 cell and one 0.30 cell.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Checking intersections as well as single attributes multiplies the number of groups, so cells become small and estimates noisy.
statements.explanation: The number of cells multiplies with each attribute while the sample is split among them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Since the single-attribute comparisons show no gap, no subgroup can be disadvantaged within either attribute's categories.
statements.explanation: Disparities can cancel in the margins and appear only in the combinations.

questions.source: The toolkit and what it cannot do
questions.stem: Practitioners distinguish pre-processing, in-processing and post-processing methods for reducing group disparities in a classifier. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reweighting training examples so that group-and-label combinations are balanced is a pre-processing method.
statements.explanation: It changes the data the model is trained on, before training.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Group-specific cutoffs applied to a frozen model's scores require the group attribute at decision time.
statements.explanation: The cutoff to apply depends on which group the person is assigned to.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Adversarial debiasing, where a second network tries to predict the group from the model's representation, is an in-processing method.
statements.explanation: It alters the training objective rather than the data or the final decisions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Any of the three families can remove bias built into the recorded labels without further information about how those labels were produced, because they adjust the data or the decisions.
statements.explanation: These methods act on data, objective or decisions; they cannot know that a label is mismeasured unless that is learned some other way.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Any method that leaves both the training data and the trained model unchanged and adjusts only the final decisions is a post-processing method.
statements.explanation: Post-processing is defined by acting on the model's outputs after training, with the data and the model itself left as they were.

questions.stem: A classifier has a true-positive rate of 0.80 and a false-positive rate of 0.10 in both group 1 and group 2. At validation both groups had base rate 0.30. After deployment, group 2's base rate rises to 0.50, while the classifier's true-positive and false-positive rates in each group stay the same. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: After the shift, precision of positive predictions is about 0.77 in group 1 and about 0.89 in group 2.

statements.label: B
statements.text: After the shift, the ratio of selection rates (group 1 over group 2) falls to about 0.69.
statements.explanation: Selection rates are 0.31 and 0.45, and 0.31/0.45 = 0.69.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Equalized odds stops holding after the shift because the base rate changed.
statements.explanation: Equalized odds is defined by rates conditional on the true outcome, and those are unchanged.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because true-positive and false-positive rates are unchanged, no group metric needs rechecking after the shift.
statements.explanation: Selection rates and precision shifted, so other criteria must be re-measured on live data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Precision parity was robust to the change in base rate.
statements.explanation: Precision depends on the base rate, and moved from equal (0.77 in both) to unequal.

questions.source: The arithmetic — the actual proof, not a gesture
questions.stem: A score is perfectly calibrated within each of two groups. In group 1, 60% of people have score 0.2 and 40% have score 0.7. In group 2, 80% have score 0.2 and 20% have score 0.7. People with a score of at least 0.5 are flagged. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The base rates are 0.40 in group 1 and 0.30 in group 2.
statements.explanation: Under calibration, the base rate is the average score: 0.6×0.2 + 0.4×0.7 = 0.40 and 0.8×0.2 + 0.2×0.7 = 0.30.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The true-positive rates at the 0.5 cutoff are equal in the two groups, because calibration makes the scores mean the same.
statements.explanation: They are 0.28/0.40 = 0.70 in group 1 and 0.14/0.30 ≈ 0.47 in group 2.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The false-positive rates at the 0.5 cutoff are equal in the two groups, because the score is calibrated in both.
statements.explanation: They are 0.12/0.60 = 0.20 in group 1 and 0.06/0.70 ≈ 0.09 in group 2.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Among people who actually have the positive outcome, the average score is about 0.55 in group 1 and about 0.43 in group 2.
statements.explanation: Weighting by outcome probability gives 0.22/0.40 ≈ 0.55 and 0.13/0.30 ≈ 0.43.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The two groups are flagged at equal rates, because the score is calibrated in both groups.
statements.explanation: Flag rates are 0.40 in group 1 and 0.20 in group 2.

questions.stem: A hospital tests a language-model assistant that triages patient messages as urgent or not and states its own confidence in words (for example, "I am 90% sure this is urgent"). The team wants to know whether the assistant's stated confidence means the same thing for patients writing in English and for patients writing in other languages. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the assistant says "about 90% sure" equally often for both groups, that shows its stated confidence is calibrated in each group.
statements.explanation: Calibration compares stated confidence with observed outcomes; how often a number is stated says nothing about that.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A calibration check by group can be done without any outcome labels, by comparing stated confidence across groups.
statements.explanation: The check needs the true outcome to compare against the stated confidence within each group.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Hedged wording in the assistant's replies is good evidence that its stated numbers are calibrated.
statements.explanation: Tone is not evidence of calibration; only agreement with observed frequencies is.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A confidence a language model states in words is a claim to test against outcomes, not an established probability.
statements.explanation: Fluent statements of confidence need not track how often the model is right.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A calibration check done for one model version and prompt remains valid after either is changed.
statements.explanation: Changing the model or the prompt can change the confidence statements, so the check must be repeated.

questions.source: Causal fairness: what the data cannot tell you
questions.stem: General legal and ethical frameworks for decisions made with algorithms distinguish different kinds of unequal treatment. Check each statement that is true in general terms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Satisfying one statistical fairness metric establishes legal compliance, since the metric measures whether the system is fair.
statements.explanation: Legal compliance depends on the applicable law and its facts, not on any single metric.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A ratio of 0.8 between group selection rates is a bright-line legal test in every jurisdiction, not merely a rule of thumb.
statements.explanation: It is a rule of thumb used in some settings, not a universal legal standard.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Using different cutoffs for protected groups to reduce a disparity can itself raise disparate-treatment concerns in some jurisdictions.
statements.explanation: Explicit group-based decision rules can be restricted even when the aim is to reduce a disparity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In some legal regimes a practice with disparate impact can be justified by a legitimate need and is then checked for less discriminatory alternatives.
statements.explanation: Disparate impact is not automatically unlawful; justification and the availability of alternatives enter the analysis.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Disparate treatment concerns decisions that differ by protected attribute; disparate impact concerns neutral-looking practices with disproportionate effects.
statements.explanation: That is the standard distinction between the two doctrines.

questions.stem: A risk model flags people (Ŷ=1) for an intervention; Y=1 means the person truly needed it. Group A (1,000 people): 400 flagged who needed it, 100 flagged who did not, 0 not flagged who needed it, 500 not flagged who did not. Group B (1,000 people): 300 flagged who needed it, 0 flagged who did not, 100 not flagged who needed it, 600 not flagged who did not. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Equal accuracy means the two groups bear the same cost from the model's mistakes.
statements.explanation: An unneeded intervention and a missed need can differ greatly in cost, so equal error counts do not mean equal burden.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Group B's true-positive rate is 1.0 and group A's is 0.75.
statements.explanation: The values are swapped: group A's is 400/400 = 1.0 and group B's is 300/400 = 0.75.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Accuracy is 0.90 in both groups, so accuracy parity holds.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Equalized odds holds, since the groups have equal accuracy and equal numbers of errors.
statements.explanation: True-positive rates are 1.0 and 0.75, and false-positive rates are about 0.17 and 0.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Every error in group A is a false positive and every error in group B is a false negative.
statements.explanation: Group A has 100 false positives and 0 false negatives; group B has 0 false positives and 100 false negatives.
